title: How to Use Chopsticks in Japan — and What Never to Do
excerpt: Using chopsticks correctly in Japan is less about technique and more about knowing the four things that are genuinely offensive. The technique is optional. The four things are not.
heroImageAlt: A pair of wooden chopsticks resting on a ceramic chopstick rest beside a bowl of rice
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The two that are genuinely serious
paragraphs: Tatehashi: standing chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. This is how rice is offered to the dead at a funeral and at a household altar. It is not a minor breach of form; it is placing a funeral object on a dinner table, and it will stop conversation.

Passing food directly from your chopsticks to someone else's is the other one, and it comes from the same place: at a Japanese cremation, the bones are passed between relatives chopstick to chopstick. If you want to share something, put it on the other person's plate.

Both are known to every Japanese person and explained to children. Seeing a foreign visitor do either is understood as unfamiliarity rather than disrespect, but they are the two worth actually remembering.

sections.heading: The everyday ones
paragraphs: Sashi-bashi: spearing food with a chopstick as if it were a fork. Mayoi-bashi: hovering over the dishes while deciding, which is read as indecisive and slightly greedy. Yose-bashi: dragging a dish towards you with your chopsticks instead of picking it up. Saguri-bashi: rummaging through a communal dish for the piece you want.

Neburi-bashi is licking the ends, and namida-bashi is letting food drip across the table on the way to your mouth — the name means 'crying chopsticks'. Watashi-bashi, laying them across the top of a bowl, is common enough in practice but the correct signal is the rest.
None of these will cause offence in the way the first two do. They are closer to eating with your elbows on the table: nobody says anything, everybody notices.

sections.heading: Where to put them down
paragraphs: The hashioki is the small ceramic rest beside your plate, and it is what it is for. Chopsticks go on it with the tips pointing left, parallel to the edge of the table, whenever you are not using them.

If there is no rest — common at casual places — the paper sleeve the disposable chopsticks came in can be folded into one in about five seconds, which is a small trick that Japanese diners do without thinking about it. Otherwise, resting the tips on the edge of a small dish is fine.
At the end of the meal, put them back in the paper sleeve if there was one, or lay them neatly on the rest. Leaving them crossed on the table is untidy rather than taboo.

sections.heading: How to actually hold them
paragraphs: The lower stick does not move. It sits in the crook between thumb and index finger and rests on the ring finger, and it stays exactly where it is for the whole meal. The upper stick is held like a pencil, between thumb, index and middle finger, and it is the only one that moves.
Almost everyone who struggles with chopsticks is moving both sticks. Fixing the bottom one solves most of it in about ten minutes of practice.

Grip near the top third rather than close to the tips. It feels less controlled and gives you far more reach and leverage — and holding chopsticks very low down is a childish grip that adults notice in the same way an adult holding a pen in a fist would be noticed.

sections.heading: Technique is not the point
paragraphs: Many restaurants that serve foreign visitors have forks available on request. If you cannot use chopsticks comfortably, ask for one. Nobody will be offended.

Struggling badly for an entire meal while declining a fork is not a gesture of cultural respect — it is inconvenient for you and creates mild concern for everyone eating with you. Use the fork. Practise the chopsticks when you have time and are not hungry.

And expect to be complimented on doing it badly. 'O-hashi ga jouzu desu ne' — you are good with chopsticks — is offered to foreigners with real warmth and very low standards. Take it as the kindness it is.

sections.heading: Shared dishes
paragraphs: At a shared meal — izakaya, shabu-shabu, hot pot — there may be serving chopsticks, toribashi, for moving food from the central dish to your plate. Use them if they are there.

If there are none, the convention in informal settings is to turn your own chopsticks around and use the clean ends. This is widely practised, though some etiquette purists dislike it on the grounds that the ends you are now handling have been in your hand. Either is acceptable; taking directly from a communal pot with the ends you have been eating from is not.
Take from the side of the dish nearest you rather than reaching into the middle for the best piece, and take one thing at a time.

sections.heading: Disposable chopsticks
paragraphs: Waribashi are the disposable wooden chopsticks served at casual restaurants and convenience stores. Split them apart holding them horizontally and pulling gently sideways — done vertically, they tend to split unevenly and take half the table with them.

Rubbing them together to remove splinters is poor form at a proper restaurant, because it implies the chopsticks are cheap, which implies the restaurant is cheap. At a convenience store on a park bench, nobody is watching and the rule is not in operation. Context applies.
Convenience stores will ask whether you want chopsticks and will give you exactly as many pairs as there are meals. Saying no if you do not need them is normal.

sections.heading: The bowl in your other hand
paragraphs: The rule that surprises Western diners most is that small bowls are lifted. Rice and miso soup are held up near the chest in the left hand and eaten from there, not left on the table and leaned over. Leaving a rice bowl on the table and bending down to it is the actual bad manners here.

Soup is drunk directly from the bowl; there is no spoon, and the chopsticks are for the solid pieces in it. Anything larger than about a hand's width — a donburi, a plate, a serving dish — stays on the table.
For noodles, the bowl stays down, the noodles come up, and slurping is normal and functional. It cools them on the way in.

sections.heading: The chopsticks themselves
paragraphs: Japanese chopsticks are shorter than Chinese ones and taper to a fine point, which is a design for picking bones out of fish rather than for reaching across a large round table. That difference is why they feel unfamiliar even to people confident with Chinese chopsticks.

Households here have personal chopsticks — each person's own pair, not interchangeable, in a way that plates and glasses are not. Lengths differ by hand size, and there are shorter pairs for children. That personal quality is exactly what makes a good pair a genuinely thoughtful souvenir.

A lacquered pair from a specialist shop costs a few thousand yen and will last decades if you keep it out of the dishwasher, which will strip the lacquer. Buy a rest to go with them; that is how a set is given.

title: The Rules of Gift Giving in Japan: What to Give, How to Give It, When Not To
excerpt: Gift giving in Japan is governed by a set of conventions that are invisible until you get them wrong. Here is what they are.
heroImageAlt: An elegantly wrapped Japanese gift box with a noshi ribbon on a wooden surface
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The presentation matters as much as the gift
paragraphs: In Japan the wrapping of a gift is not separate from the gift — it is part of it. A well-chosen item presented unwrapped or in a plastic bag conveys carelessness. A modest item in beautiful wrapping conveys consideration. Department stores wrap purchases without being asked, with a precision that takes real skill.

If you are bringing something from abroad, find a way to present it wrapped. The intent is not to disguise value; it is to show that the presentation was thought about. Any Japanese department store will wrap a gift you bought elsewhere if you ask at the service counter.

For formal occasions there is a layer above wrapping: noshi, a printed paper band placed over the parcel carrying the occasion and the giver's name. Shops sell and apply it, and asking for it signals that the gift is a proper one rather than a casual one.

sections.heading: Numbers and colours to avoid
paragraphs: Avoid sets of four, since shi sounds like the word for death, and nine, since ku sounds like suffering. Three, five and seven are the auspicious counts and are what shops package in anyway.

White wrapping alone, and black-and-white ribbon combinations, belong to funerals and should not appear on a celebratory gift. Red and gold are strongly positive. Red-and-white cord is for happy occasions; black-and-white or silver for condolences, and the two are not interchangeable.

One more that catches people: giving a clock or a knife carries unfortunate connotations, and potted plants are traditionally avoided as a get-well gift because the roots suggest an illness taking hold. None of these will cause genuine offence from a foreign visitor, and all are easy to sidestep.

sections.heading: Gifts are not opened in front of the giver
paragraphs: The convention is to receive a gift graciously, set it aside, and open it privately later. Opening it immediately, examining it, exclaiming over it, asking what it cost — none of that is standard.

If a Japanese host opens your gift on the spot, that is a gesture of warmth towards you specifically. If they set it aside, do not read it as indifference. The gift has been received and will be appreciated; the appreciation is simply expressed later, and often in writing.
The mirror image applies when you are the recipient. Take it with both hands, thank the person, and put it down. You can open it after they leave.

sections.heading: Giving with two hands, and what to say
paragraphs: Gifts, business cards, money envelopes and anything given as a gesture of significance are presented with both hands and a slight bow, and received the same way. Handing something over one-handed while doing something else with the other reads as inattentive in a formal setting.

There is a set phrase that accompanies it and it is worth understanding even if you never use it: 'tsumaranai mono desu ga' — this is a boring, trifling thing, but. It is not false modesty about the object so much as a way of removing any suggestion that the recipient now owes you something. The modern, softer version is 'kokoro bakari desu', just a small token.
Whatever you say, keep it brief and do not talk up the gift. Explaining that it was expensive or hard to find inverts the whole exchange.

sections.heading: The occasions that have rules
paragraphs: Temiyage is the gift you bring when visiting someone's home — food or drink, bought that day, handed over at the door after you have removed your shoes and been shown in, not thrust forward on the doorstep. Never arrive empty-handed.

Ochugen in midsummer and oseibo in December are the formal seasonal gift exchanges between businesses, clients and families. Department stores build entire floors around them for a few weeks a year. As a visitor you will not be expected to participate, but it explains why the gift halls are suddenly enormous in July and December.

Weddings and funerals run on money in specially printed envelopes, with the design, the cord and the amount all governed by convention — and with real rules about which notes to use. If you are ever invited to either, ask a Japanese friend rather than improvising; this is the one area where getting it wrong is genuinely awkward.

sections.heading: Reciprocation is expected
paragraphs: Japanese gift culture is reciprocal by default. A substantial gift creates an expectation of okaeshi, a return gift, conventionally at around half the value of the original. This is why calibration matters so much.

The practical consequence for a visitor: an expensive present to a casual acquaintance is not generous, it is a burden. You have obliged someone to spend money and time working out how to respond. A modest, consumable, clearly-from-abroad gift lands better and closes the loop cleanly.
Consumables are the elegant solution precisely because they are used up. Food, drink and good-quality cosmetics discharge the obligation by being consumed, which is why they dominate the category.

sections.heading: What makes a good gift from abroad
paragraphs: Regional food from where you actually live, something associated with your country that is not a cliché, or anything that reflects genuine thought about the person. Packaged sweets, good tea or coffee, decent whisky, and local specialities all work.

Individually wrapped portions are better than one large item, for the same reason omiyage is: it may be shared around an office. Something with English packaging is a feature rather than a problem — it is visibly from elsewhere.

What to avoid: luxury branded goods, which create the reciprocation problem; anything requiring refrigeration; and anything that needs explaining at length. If the gift needs a paragraph of context to make sense, it is the wrong gift.

sections.heading: When not to give a gift
paragraphs: Do not tip in lieu of a gift, and do not give cash to anyone outside the formal envelope contexts. Do not give a gift to someone in a customer service role unless you have a genuine personal relationship with them — it puts them in an awkward position, and many workplaces do not allow it.
Do not give a gift that clearly exceeds the social context. The gift economy here runs on calibration: the value reflects the relationship, and mismatching in either direction creates discomfort.
And do not press a refused gift. If someone declines twice, the answer is no, and continuing is the one move that turns a small awkwardness into a real one.

title: Tattoos and Onsen in Japan: What the Policy Actually Is
excerpt: Most onsen ban tattoos. Fewer than you'd think actually enforce it. Here is how to navigate it honestly.
heroImageAlt: Steam rising from an outdoor onsen rotenburo surrounded by autumn trees
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the ban exists
paragraphs: The tattoo ban at Japanese onsen traces to the historical association between full-body tattoos and organised crime. It was introduced not as a statement about tattoos generally but as a practical measure to keep criminal organisations out of communal bathing facilities, and it has persisted for decades largely through institutional inertia.

It is worth knowing that this association is relatively recent in a long history. Tattooing in Japan goes back thousands of years and had a substantial decorative tradition in the Edo period among firefighters, labourers and merchants, before being banned outright by the Meiji government as part of a broader project of appearing modern to Western eyes. The criminal association hardened during the twentieth century.

Attitudes have shifted significantly since Japan began preparing for large numbers of international visitors, and the shift is ongoing. The situation now is meaningfully different from ten years ago, and it will be different again in another ten.

sections.heading: The official policy versus practice
paragraphs: Official policy at most large resort onsen and hotel spa facilities is no tattoos, regardless of size. Enforcement varies enormously. At a small neighbourhood sento run by the same family for forty years, nobody is checking anything. At a large facility near a tourist area, staff may ask at the desk, and there are sometimes signs with illustrations at the entrance.

The underlying concern has always been the comfort of other bathers rather than the tattoo itself. A visible, extensive tattoo in a shared bath makes some Japanese guests — particularly older ones — genuinely uneasy, and the facility is managing that rather than expressing an opinion about your arm.
Some places have moved to a no-visible-tattoo policy rather than a blanket ban, which in practice means a small tattoo that a cover patch will hide is fine and a full sleeve is not.

sections.heading: The options, in order of reliability
paragraphs: A private bath is the cleanest answer. Kashikiri-buro — family baths bookable by the hour — are offered by a great many ryokan and onsen hotels, and there are no other guests and therefore no policy. Rooms with their own open-air bath attached cost more and solve the problem permanently. This is often the more relaxing option regardless of whether you have tattoos.

Tattoo-friendly facilities exist and their number grows every year. Several online directories maintain lists; treat them as a starting point and confirm directly, because policies change and listings go stale.

Covering works for small tattoos only. Waterproof cover patches are sold at some facilities and at drugstores, and they need to actually stay on in hot water. A patch peeling off mid-bath is a worse outcome than not going in.

The last option is simply the day-use bath at a place that does not care. Small municipal sento in ordinary neighbourhoods are the most relaxed category in the country, and they are also cheap, unglamorous and among the better things to do in Japan.

sections.heading: How to ask, and when
paragraphs: Ask before you book, not on arrival. Most facilities have handled the question many times and will give you a straight answer. Email works better than the phone for a foreign visitor, and hotel concierges will call on your behalf.

The phrase is 'tattoo wa daijoubu desu ka' — is a tattoo all right. If you want to be precise, 'chiisai tattoo ga arimasu' means I have a small tattoo. Bringing a photograph on your phone is more useful than any description.

Arriving, undressing, and being asked to leave at the threshold of the bath is unpleasant for you and for the staff member who has to do it. That scenario is entirely avoidable and avoiding it is the whole of the advice here.

sections.heading: It is not only onsen
paragraphs: The same restriction turns up in places visitors do not anticipate: public swimming pools, hotel gyms and pools, water parks, some beaches with managed facilities, and occasionally capsule hotels and gyms.

Water parks and municipal pools tend to be stricter than onsen, not more relaxed, and they are the ones most likely to enforce at the entrance. If a day at a pool is part of your plan, check that specifically.

Conversely, ordinary daily life is entirely unaffected. Nobody cares about a visible tattoo on the street, on a train, in a restaurant or in a shop, and the idea that Japan is generally hostile to tattooed visitors is not accurate.

sections.heading: The honest approach
paragraphs: Ask first, respect the answer, and do not attempt to argue the policy at a front desk. The person you would be arguing with did not write it and cannot change it, and the conversation has a guaranteed outcome.

It is reasonable to find the rule outdated. It is also somebody else's bath, in somebody else's country, and the practical position — book a private bath, find a facility that welcomes you, or use a neighbourhood sento — costs you almost nothing and works every time.

The direction of travel is clear. More facilities open to tattooed guests every year, tourism bodies have been pushing for exactly that, and younger Japanese people increasingly have tattoos themselves. It is a problem that is slowly solving itself.

title: Meishi: The Japanese Business Card Ritual and Why It Matters
excerpt: In Japan, the business card is not a piece of paper. It is a physical representation of the person. Treating it as stationary is the fastest way to start a professional relationship poorly.
heroImageAlt: A Japanese business card (meishi) held with two hands against a wooden meeting table
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What a business card represents
paragraphs: In Japan, the meishi (business card) exchange is a ritual that establishes who you are, your position, and your company — in one gesture, at the start of every professional interaction. Cards are not handed out casually. They are exchanged at the beginning of a meeting with a formality that can feel significant to those not used to it. Understanding why makes the ritual easier: the card is standing in for a formal introduction that would otherwise take several minutes of verbal exchange.

The card also settles the question that Japanese professional interaction cannot proceed without: relative seniority. Japanese has different registers of politeness depending on who outranks whom, and you cannot construct a normal sentence until you know. The card tells everyone in the room how to speak to everyone else, which is why it is exchanged before the conversation rather than after it.

Note the order of information printed on it. Company first, then division, then title, then name. That sequence is not a design choice — it is the order of importance, and it is the opposite of the Western convention. You are being introduced as a representative of an organisation who happens to be a particular person.

sections.heading: Before the meeting: what to have ready
paragraphs: Bring more cards than you think you need. A single meeting with a mid-sized company can involve six people, and running out halfway around the table is the failure mode you are trying to avoid. Twenty in the case for a day of meetings is not excessive.

Carry them in a meishi holder — a slim leather or metal card case — not loose in a wallet or a jacket pocket. The case matters for a practical reason as well as an aesthetic one: cards produced from it are flat, clean and unbent, which is the entire point. Cases are sold in any department store and in most stationery shops.

Have the card printed with Japanese on one side and English on the other. Any print shop in Japan will do this in a day or two, and several online services will do it before you travel. If you cannot manage a translated side, an English-only card is acceptable; a card with a Japanese side you had machine-translated and never checked is worse than no Japanese side at all.

sections.heading: How to present your card
paragraphs: Hold the card with both hands, text facing the recipient so they can read it immediately, and offer a slight bow as you present it. Say your name and company as you do. If you are handing out cards in a group, the most senior person goes first. Do not hand out cards across a table — walk around or hand directly.

Hold it by the corners or the lower edge. Covering the company name or your own name with your thumbs is the small error people make most often — you are presenting the information, so leave it visible.

Height carries meaning. The more junior party offers their card slightly lower than the more senior one. You are not expected to calibrate this precisely as a visitor, but if you are clearly the one asking for the meeting, presenting a little low reads as courteous and costs you nothing.

Very often both people present at the same time. The convention is to offer with the right hand while receiving with the left, then immediately bring the second hand to the received card. It feels awkward the first time and stops feeling awkward around the fourth.

sections.heading: How to receive a card
paragraphs: Receive the card with both hands. Take a moment to read it — not a cursory glance, but actually look at it. Acknowledge the person's name and company.

Say something. Reading the name aloud to confirm the pronunciation is welcome, because Japanese surnames are written in characters with multiple possible readings and even Japanese colleagues ask. A remark about the office location or the division is enough. What you are demonstrating is that you read the card rather than pocketed it.

sections.heading: The cards stay on the table
paragraphs: If you are sitting down at a meeting, place the cards on the table in front of you, arranged to mirror where people are sitting, with the most senior person's card at the top of your arrangement. Keep them there for the duration.

This is not ceremony for its own sake. It is a seating chart. Six unfamiliar names in a language you do not read are impossible to hold in your head, and everyone in the room is using the same trick. Referring down to the cards during the meeting to get someone's name right is expected, not a lapse.

Put them away only once the meeting has finished and people are standing up, and put them into the case rather than a pocket. The card on the table means the person is still present in the meeting, literally and symbolically.

sections.heading: What not to do
paragraphs: Do not write on a business card in front of the person who gave it to you. Do not fold it. Do not put it in your back pocket and sit on it. Do not place anything on top of it (not a cup, not another card). These actions read as treating the card — and by extension the person — carelessly.

Do not slide a card across a table, do not deal them out like playing cards to several people at once, and do not hand one over with a drink in your other hand. If you need to make a note about someone, make it afterwards and out of sight.
After the meeting, file cards appropriately. Japanese professionals use meishi holders and binders specifically for this purpose, and many will genuinely still have your card two years later.

sections.heading: Reading the titles
paragraphs: A card is only useful if you can decode it, and Japanese corporate titles map onto a fairly consistent ladder. From the top: shacho (president), senmu and jomu (executive directors), bucho (department head), kacho (section head), kakaricho (subsection head), and shain (staff, usually with no title printed at all).

The one worth recognising on sight is bucho. A department head is typically the most senior person who will attend a working meeting, and is usually the person whose agreement actually decides the outcome. Kacho is the level that does most of the real coordination.
Also look for a name in katakana or romaji alongside the kanji. If it is there, the person has put it there so foreigners can read it, and using that reading is what it is for.

sections.heading: If you don't have cards
paragraphs: Arriving at a Japanese business meeting without cards is not a catastrophe, but it is noticed. A brief explanation — 'I apologize, I have run out of cards' — is appropriate. Most Japanese businesspeople will accept this gracefully.

Receiving a card when you have none to give creates a small debt, and the graceful way to settle it is to follow up by email the same day with your full details. If you are in Japan for a week and expect more meetings, get cards printed while you are there; same-day services exist in every business district.

sections.heading: Where the ritual is relaxing
paragraphs: The formality is not uniform. Startups, creative agencies, foreign-owned firms and younger teams handle meishi far more loosely than a bank or a manufacturer will, and in some rooms the exchange is barely a pause. Digital card apps — Eight and Sansan are the common ones — are now normal, and being asked to scan rather than swap is not a snub.
The safe approach is to arrive prepared for the full version and follow the room. Nobody has ever been thought worse of for handling a card carefully. The reverse is not true.

It is also worth keeping the ritual in proportion. Getting it slightly wrong will not end a negotiation, and your Japanese counterparts know you are a visitor. What the effort communicates is that you looked into how things are done before you arrived — which is, in the end, the same thing the ritual itself communicates.

title: How to Order and Drink Sake in Japan Without Getting It Wrong
excerpt: Sake is Japan's most misunderstood drink. Most people drink it too warm, in the wrong glass, with the wrong food. This is how to do it correctly.
heroImageAlt: A small ceramic tokkuri flask and ochoko cups of sake on a wooden table at an izakaya
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Sake is not always drunk hot
paragraphs: The most persistent misunderstanding about sake outside Japan is that it is drunk hot. It is drunk across a range of temperatures — cold, room temperature, gently warmed, hot — and which one depends on the sake and on preference.

Premium ginjo and daiginjo are almost always served cold or at room temperature, because heat destroys the delicate aromatics that justify the price. Warming suits fuller, more robust honjozo and everyday futsushu, and warm sake is a genuinely underrated pleasure that gets dismissed because so much bad sake has been served hot to disguise it.

The temperature words are worth having: reishu is chilled, hiya is room temperature, nurukan is around body-warm, atsukan is hot. Asking which is recommended for a specific bottle is a reasonable question and will get a thoughtful answer.

sections.heading: You pour for others, not yourself
paragraphs: The central social convention is that you pour for others and they pour for you. You do not fill your own cup. If someone's cup is empty and the flask is nearest you, pour. If yours is empty, lift it slightly towards whoever has the flask — that is the signal, and it is silent.
Pour with two hands: one on the flask, one supporting it underneath. One-handed pouring is casual and reads as inattentive in any semi-formal setting.

At a very informal dinner among close friends the rule relaxes and people top themselves up. Anywhere with colleagues, hosts or people you have just met, it applies. Pouring for yourself while others sit with empty cups is the version that lands badly.

sections.heading: The receiving gesture
paragraphs: When someone pours for you, do not leave the cup on the table. Lift it, hold it with both hands or support it from below with one, and hold it steady while they pour. This is the same gesture as receiving anything with both hands: it says you are receiving attentively.
Take at least a sip before setting it down, then pour in return. The exchange is the point rather than the drink.

If you have had enough, leave your cup full. A full cup is the polite signal that you are done, and it prevents the loop from continuing. Covering the cup with your hand or turning it over works too, but the full cup is the gentlest version.

sections.heading: The vessels
paragraphs: Sake arrives in a tokkuri, the small ceramic flask, and is drunk from an ochoko, the small cup. Both are sized so that pouring for each other happens constantly, which is the entire design intention.

A masu is the square wooden box, originally a rice measure, and it appears in two ways. Sometimes you drink from it directly, in which case you drink from a corner rather than a flat edge. More often it holds a glass, and the server deliberately overflows the glass so that the masu fills too — this is mokkiri, and the overflow is generosity, not clumsiness. Drink the glass down before lifting it, then tip the box into the glass.
At a serious sake bar you may be given a wine glass instead, which is not an affectation: a wide bowl is the only way to smell an aromatic daiginjo properly.

sections.heading: Ordering
paragraphs: At an izakaya the standard entry is a carafe rather than a bottle. They come in one go, about 180ml, and two go, about 360ml. The small one is the right first order while you work out what you like.

At a specialist, the menu will list classifications — junmai, honjozo, ginjo, daiginjo — often with a region and sometimes a sweetness and acidity figure. The useful question is 'osusume wa nan desu ka', what do you recommend, followed by whether you want something light or rich, dry or fruity. Staff at a sake-focused place enjoy this question.
Tasting sets of three small glasses are common and are the efficient way to find out what you like. Order one before committing to a flask.

sections.heading: Kanpai, and the pace of the evening
paragraphs: The toast is kanpai. Make eye contact, touch cups gently — ceramic chips — and drink together. Wait for it before drinking, even if your glass arrived first, and if you are the most junior person present, let your cup sit slightly lower than the others when they meet.

Japanese drinking is paced around food and conversation rather than around finishing what is in front of you, and the first drink at an izakaya is usually beer with the second round moving to sake. Nomihodai — all-you-can-drink for a fixed time — is common and is not an invitation to race.
Declining a drink is entirely acceptable. 'Kekkou desu' or simply covering the cup works. Nobody will push, and the days when refusing was socially difficult are largely gone.

sections.heading: What to drink it with
paragraphs: Sake is built for food and shows badly on its own. It has less acidity than wine and a great deal of umami, which is why it sits well beside grilled fish, tofu, pickles and anything salty, and why it does not fight delicate flavours the way a tannic wine does.

The one pairing debate worth knowing: sake with sushi is a little contentious among purists, because both are rice, and many sushi chefs prefer you drink tea or beer with the meal and sake before or after. This is a preference rather than a rule and nobody will stop you.

Alongside it, a glass of water — yawaragi-mizu, softening water — is the single best habit to adopt. Drinking it between cups is standard practice at any serious sake bar and is the difference between a good evening and a bad morning.

title: The Japanese Breakfast: What It Is and Why It Will Change Your Morning
excerpt: A traditional Japanese breakfast is not a quick meal. It is a composed sequence of small things done well, and eating it once will make every hotel breakfast you eat for the rest of your life feel like a concession.
heroImageAlt: A traditional Japanese breakfast set with rice, miso soup, grilled fish, pickles, and tofu
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What a Japanese breakfast is
paragraphs: A traditional Japanese breakfast consists of steamed white rice, miso soup, a piece of grilled fish, a small selection of pickled vegetables, a square of tofu, a small egg dish, and nori. Everything arrives simultaneously. Nothing is sweet. Coffee, if it appears, comes afterwards.

The structure has a name — ichiju-sansai, one soup and three dishes — and it is the underlying grammar of Japanese meals generally rather than a breakfast-specific idea. Rice is the centre, the soup supports it, and the small dishes are there to make the rice interesting.

This is the standard morning meal at ryokan, traditional hotels and in the homes of people who still cook breakfast, though it is worth knowing that a great many Japanese people eat toast and coffee on a weekday like everyone else.

sections.heading: The grilled fish
paragraphs: The fish is the anchor. A properly grilled piece of salmon or mackerel — salted, left, then grilled slowly — has crisp skin, a slightly smoky interior, and a flavour that is to a hotel buffet as a proper espresso is to an office coffee machine.

At a ryokan it was grilled minutes before it arrived, sometimes on a small charcoal grill at your table. Eat it immediately and eat the skin, which is the best part and which visitors routinely leave.
The bones are left in and are removed at the table with chopsticks, working along the spine. This takes practice and nobody is judging the outcome.

sections.heading: Miso soup and the small dishes
paragraphs: Miso soup at a proper breakfast is made from dashi — kombu and dried bonito — with miso stirred in off the heat, not from powder. The difference is obvious. It arrives hot in a lacquer bowl with a lid; lift the lid, invert it beside the bowl, and drink directly from the bowl, using chopsticks for the solids.

The pickles are not a garnish. They are there to punctuate the rice, and eating a little between mouthfuls is the intended rhythm. Takuan, the bright yellow daikon, is the most common and the most divisive.

Tamagoyaki, the rolled omelette, is slightly sweet and served cold or warm. Onsen tamago — an egg cooked slowly in its shell until the white is barely set — is the other common version and is poured over rice.

sections.heading: Natto, and whether you have to
paragraphs: Fermented soybeans, brown, sticky, strong-smelling, and stringy in a way that has to be seen. It is the single most divisive item on a Japanese breakfast tray and it appears constantly, especially east of Nagoya.

The preparation matters: open the pack, add the sachets of mustard and soy-based sauce, and stir hard for twenty or thirty seconds until it goes pale and foamy. Unstirred natto is much harder going. Then tip it over rice, or eat it alongside.

You do not have to eat it and nobody expects you to like it. It is genuinely good for you, it is genuinely cheap, and about half of foreign visitors who try it properly stirred find it fine. The other half do not, and that is a completely normal outcome that Japanese people from Osaka will sympathise with.

sections.heading: How to eat it
paragraphs: Everything arrives at once and you move between the dishes rather than finishing one and starting the next. A mouthful of rice, a piece of fish, a sip of soup, a pickle, back to the rice. The rice is the constant and everything else is there to keep it interesting.

The rice bowl and the soup bowl are lifted; the plates stay on the table. Do not put anything on top of the rice unless it is meant to go there — natto, raw egg and the seaweed do, the fish generally does not.

The nori is for wrapping: take a sheet, dip a corner in soy sauce, pick up a little rice with it, eat. At a ryokan the nori arrives in a sealed packet to keep it crisp, and opening it at the last moment is the point.

sections.heading: Where to eat one
paragraphs: The best is at a ryokan, where it arrives in your room or a dedicated dining room at a fixed time and takes forty-five minutes to eat properly. It is frequently the meal people remember longest from a trip.

The second-best is a business hotel that has opted for a proper Japanese breakfast rather than a buffet, which is a common and underrated feature of chains like Dormy Inn. A teishoku shop — a set-meal restaurant — will serve the same thing to office workers for under ¥1,000, and some are open from six in the morning.

The other genuinely Japanese breakfast is the kissaten morning set: coffee with toast, a boiled egg and sometimes a small salad, thrown in free or nearly free with the price of the coffee before eleven. It is a different tradition entirely, it dates to the post-war cafés of Nagoya, and it is excellent.
The convenience store version — onigiri, a boiled egg, a carton of miso soup — is fast, cheap and perfectly decent. It is not the same experience and it is what most of Tokyo actually eats.

sections.heading: What it teaches you
paragraphs: Eating one properly, without hurrying, resets certain assumptions about what mornings can be. The meal is light enough that you feel alert afterwards rather than heavy. The flavours are savoury and complex at seven in the morning in a way that feels strange until it feels obvious.
The effort is visible in every dish, and none of the dishes is large. That is the argument the whole meal is making: several small things done carefully beat one big thing done quickly.
Arrive at the dining room at the time you were given, sit down properly, and give it the three quarters of an hour it is asking for.

title: The Best Time to Visit Japan: An Honest Month-by-Month Guide
excerpt: Spring cherry blossoms and autumn foliage are spectacular. They are also the two most crowded periods of the year. Here is what every month actually offers.
heroImageAlt: Mount Fuji reflected in a lake surrounded by summer wildflowers
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: January and February: crowds at minimum
paragraphs: January is Japan's quietest month for tourism. After New Year, which is busy with domestic travel until around the 3rd, the country empties. Hotels are cheaper, Shinkansen seats are available, and famous sites are accessible at human scale. Tokyo and Kyoto sit around 4–10°C, cold but dry and mostly clear — Japan's winter is much sunnier than northern Europe's.

Onsen towns are at their best, because sitting in outdoor hot water is a different proposition when the air is near freezing. Hakone, Kinosaki and Beppu all reward a winter visit in a way they do not in July. February adds Sapporo's Snow Festival in the first week and the best of the ski season.
The trade-offs are real: short days, some mountain routes closed, and Kyoto gardens at their barest. If what you want is the country without the crowd premium, this is when to come.

sections.heading: March and April: cherry blossom
paragraphs: Sakura season typically runs from late March to mid-April depending on location and year. Tokyo usually peaks in the last days of March, Kyoto about a week later, and northern Japan and higher elevations into late April and beyond. The flowers last roughly a week to ten days at any one place, less if it rains hard.

This is the most visited season, the most expensive, and the most beautiful. Book accommodation four to six months ahead. The famous viewpoints are genuinely crowded; the less-visited spots — riverside embankments, canal paths, ordinary neighbourhood parks — offer the same flowers with a fraction of the people, and there are cherry trees on practically every street.

The forecast is published from January and revised weekly, and it is the thing to watch. Be aware that a trip booked to hit peak bloom on a fixed date is a gamble: the front moves by up to a week in either direction, and the only real hedge is being willing to travel north or uphill to catch it.

sections.heading: May: the sweet spot
paragraphs: Late May, after Golden Week has cleared, is one of the best times to visit Japan and it is consistently underrated. Temperatures sit at 15–22°C across central Japan, the humidity has not arrived, and the rates have dropped back to normal.

The specific pleasure of this month is the new green. Shinryoku — the fresh leaf on the maples before summer darkens it — is a season Japanese people actively travel for and almost no foreign visitor has heard of. The same Kyoto gardens that are impassable in November are quiet and luminous in the third week of May.
Roughly May 10 to 30 is the window. It is the answer for a first visit with no fixed seasonal target.

sections.heading: June to August: rain, then heat
paragraphs: June brings the rainy season to most of Honshu — several weeks of grey skies and intermittent rain from early June. It is frustrating for sightseeing and it is also the cheapest and quietest period outside winter, and hydrangea season, which is genuinely lovely in temple gardens.

July and August are hot and humid in a way that surprises people: 30–36°C in Tokyo and Osaka with humidity above 80%, and nights that do not cool down. This is not merely uncomfortable, it is a health consideration — heatstroke cases spike every summer, and walking a full sightseeing day in August is a bad plan.

The compensations are the summer festivals, which are spectacular and are what the season is for, and the fireworks displays. If you must come in summer: go to Hokkaido, which is cool and green and dry; or restructure the day around early mornings, air-conditioned afternoons and evenings outside.

sections.heading: September to November: typhoons, then the best weather
paragraphs: September carries the highest typhoon risk of the year, mostly affecting Kyushu, Shikoku and Okinawa but capable of shutting down trains and flights nationally for a day or two. It is worth travel insurance and a flexible day in the itinerary rather than a reason to avoid the month; the heat breaks and late September is pleasant.

October is arguably the best weather in the Japanese year: clear, dry, 15–25°C, minimal rain. It is the month to come if the weather itself is what matters and you do not need a specific natural event.

November brings the autumn colour, peaking across central Honshu in the middle of the month, and with it the second great crowd of the year. Kyoto in the third week of November requires the same planning discipline as cherry blossom season. Late November in Tokyo, by contrast, is beautiful and manageable.

sections.heading: The weeks to avoid regardless of season
paragraphs: Three periods are about domestic travel rather than weather, and all three are worth planning around. Golden Week, from April 29 to May 5, when the whole country travels at once. Obon in mid-August, when it does the same in worse heat. And New Year, December 29 to January 3, when the issue is not crowds but closure — restaurants, museums and small businesses simply shut.
None of the three is unmanageable if you are already committed. All three will cost you more, book out earlier and move slower than the weeks either side of them.

sections.heading: The country is longer than you think
paragraphs: Japan spans about three thousand kilometres from north to south, and national seasonal advice hides a lot. Okinawa is subtropical: cherry blossom in January, swimmable sea from April, and a summer that is hot but less oppressive than Tokyo's because there is wind.

Hokkaido runs on a different calendar entirely — a genuine Northern European summer in July and August, autumn colour in early October, and a winter cold enough to support the best powder skiing in the world.

Which means the honest answer to 'when should I visit Japan' is partly 'where in Japan'. August is a bad month for Kyoto and an excellent one for Hokkaido; February is bleak in Tohoku and pleasant in Okinawa.

sections.heading: What to pack, briefly
paragraphs: Winter: layers rather than one heavy coat, because buildings and trains are heated hard. Spring and autumn: a light jacket and something waterproof. Summer: the lightest clothing you own, a hand towel — which is what the small cloth everyone carries is for, since public lavatories often have no dryer — and sun protection.

Year-round: shoes you can walk fifteen kilometres in and remove easily, because you will be taking them off at temples, some restaurants and any traditional accommodation. This is the single most consequential packing decision for a Japan trip and most people get it wrong.

sections.heading: The recommendation
paragraphs: For a first visit with no fixed seasonal preference: late May or October. Both give you good weather, normal prices and manageable crowds, which is a combination the famous seasons cannot offer.

For a trip structured around a natural event: cherry blossom in late March to early April, autumn leaves in the first half of November, and book far ahead for either. For minimum crowds and maximum value: January, accepting the cold, or June, accepting the rain.
The worst time to book without planning is Golden Week or mid-August — not because they are bad, but because accommodation disappears months in advance and the prices reflect it.

title: Taking a Taxi in Japan: What to Know Before You Get In
excerpt: Japanese taxis are expensive, exceptionally clean, and almost entirely driven by people who know exactly where they are going. The main things to know are not about navigation.

factsExpire.what: Tokyo fares were revised April 2026; re-check roughly a year on

heroImageAlt: A black Toyota Crown Japanese taxi cab waiting at a Tokyo intersection at night
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The door opens automatically
paragraphs: Japanese taxi doors open and close automatically, controlled by the driver. Do not touch the door. Attempting to open or close it manually will work but is unnecessary and slightly startles the driver. This catches almost every first-time visitor. Stand near the door, wait for it to open, get in. When you arrive, the driver will open it for you. Get out, step away, the door closes.
Only the rear left door is automatic — the one on the kerb side. If you get in on the road side, which you generally should not, you are opening that one yourself.

sections.heading: Show the destination in writing
paragraphs: Most taxi drivers in Japan speak limited English. The reliable approach: have your destination written in Japanese characters, either on your phone (from Google Maps, copy the Japanese name) or on a piece of paper from your hotel. Pronunciation of Western place names in Japanese is often different enough from English pronunciation to cause confusion. A screen showing the map with the destination pinned is universally understood. Your hotel's front desk should always be able to provide you with a card showing the hotel address in Japanese — ask for one at check-in.

The method that works even better: give the driver a phone number. Japanese taxi navigation systems search by telephone number, and every restaurant, hotel and shop has one listed. Reading out ten digits gets you to the door with no ambiguity about which of the four branches with the same name you meant. This is what locals do, and drivers visibly relax when you do it.

Addresses themselves are the weak option. Japanese addresses describe nested blocks rather than positions along a street, and a written address alone can leave a driver hunting the last hundred metres. Name plus phone number, or a dropped map pin, beats an address every time.

sections.heading: Fares and metering
paragraphs: Fares are metered. In Tokyo the base fare is ¥500, which since the April 2026 revision covers the first kilometre rather than the 1.096 km it used to, and every further ¥100 buys about 232 metres. A short hop across a couple of neighbourhoods lands around ¥1,000; a five-kilometre ride across the city is more like ¥2,500. Between 10pm and 5am everything is 20% higher, so that ¥500 flagfall starts at ¥600. Fares are set regionally, so other cities differ. There is no tip. Pay exactly what the meter says.

Two things get added to the meter legitimately. Expressway tolls are passed through at cost, which matters on airport runs and is worth agreeing to before the driver takes the ramp. And the meter also ticks over slowly while stationary, so heavy traffic costs you even when you are not moving.

Fares vary by region. Tokyo is the expensive end; a ride in a smaller city can be noticeably cheaper for the same distance. What does not vary is the honesty of the meter. Deliberate long-hauling of tourists is close to unheard of, and if a driver takes a route that looks odd it is almost always a one-way system or a traffic avoidance, not a scam.

sections.heading: Paying, and the small tray
paragraphs: Credit cards are accepted in most Tokyo taxis now; IC cards (Suica) are accepted in many. Check the payment stickers on the rear side window before you get in if you're unsure. Outside the big cities, assume cash and carry it — a rural taxi that cannot take your card at midnight is a genuinely bad situation.

Money is exchanged on a small tray, not hand to hand. Put your notes in the tray; change and receipt come back the same way. This is standard everywhere in Japan, not a taxi quirk, and it is not rudeness — it is simply how the transaction is done.

There is no tipping. Not a small one, not rounding up, not leaving the coins. Attempting it produces a driver chasing you down the pavement to return your money, which is a worse outcome for everyone than simply taking the change. If you want a receipt, ask for a ryoshusho.

sections.heading: When to use a taxi
paragraphs: Taxis are worth the cost in specific situations: after the last train, with heavy luggage between hotel and station, when traveling with elderly or young children, in cities with infrequent bus service, or when the destination is not near a train line. In Tokyo during normal hours, taxis are significantly more expensive than the train and not faster — traffic density means trains win on time and price for most inner-city routes. Outside Tokyo, in smaller cities, taxis become more valuable as transit alternatives are thinner.

The case that justifies the fare most often is the last train. Tokyo's network stops around midnight and does not resume until roughly 5am, and there is no night service to fall back on. A taxi home at 1am is expensive; the alternative is a capsule hotel, an all-night cafe, or four hours in a bar you have stopped enjoying. Budget for one or two of these rides on a trip rather than treating each as a failure of planning.

The other strong case is rural. In the countryside, buses can run four times a day and stop in the early evening, and a taxi from the station to a remote ryokan is not a luxury but the only way to arrive. Ask the ryokan to book it — many will send one, and some will collect you free.

sections.heading: Hailing and apps
paragraphs: Taxis in Japan are hailed from the street — stand at the curb, extend your arm, and a cab with a lit red indicator will stop. The red character in the windscreen, 空車, means vacant; a green or orange display generally means occupied or on call, which is the opposite of what visitors from most countries expect. Do not try to hail a cab at a zebra crossing or intersection.

At any significant station there is a taxi rank, and the rank is the better option. Queue at the head of it and take the front car; do not walk down the line picking one. In the rain, at a busy station, the rank will still be moving when the street has nothing free on it at all.

Taxi apps: GO (Japan-specific, major cities, English available), Uber (operates in some Japanese cities but uses licensed taxis rather than private drivers), DiDi, and S.RIDE in Tokyo. GO is the most widely used and works in Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto, and most other large cities. Having it installed before you need it at midnight is a better plan than finding it at midnight — and note that most of these want a Japanese phone number or a working data connection at sign-up, which is an argument for sorting your eSIM at the airport rather than later.

sections.heading: The etiquette that is not obvious
paragraphs: Sit in the back. The front passenger seat is not off limits but is unusual for a lone visitor, and the rear left seat is the conventional one. Seatbelts are required in the back as well as the front.

Do not eat in the taxi, and keep drinks closed. The interiors are immaculate — white lace seat covers, spotless floor mats, a driver in a suit and often white gloves — and that standard is maintained deliberately. Treat the car the way it is being presented to you.

Large luggage goes in the boot; the driver will handle it and does not expect help or payment for doing so. If you need space, look for a JPN Taxi, the tall boxy hybrid now common in cities. It has a sliding door, a wheelchair ramp, and considerably more room for suitcases than the older sedans.

sections.heading: Where taxis let you down
paragraphs: Airports are the main one. A metered taxi from Narita into central Tokyo runs well over ¥20,000 and can take ninety minutes in traffic; the Narita Express or the Keisei Skyliner does it for a tenth of that. Some companies sell fixed-price airport transfers, which at least remove the uncertainty, but the train is nearly always the right call unless you are arriving at 2am with three suitcases and a toddler.

The second is Kyoto in peak season. The city's traffic during autumn foliage and cherry blossom is genuinely bad, taxis sit in it with the meter running, and a bicycle or a bus lane beats a car by a wide margin. The third is anywhere a Shinkansen goes: at intercity distances the fare becomes absurd long before the journey becomes convenient.

title: Matsumoto: The Castle Town That Gets Everything Right
excerpt: Two and a half hours from Tokyo, a city with one of Japan's three great original castles, a mountain backdrop, an excellent food scene, and a fraction of Kyoto's visitor numbers. There is no explanation for why more people don't come here.
heroImageAlt: Matsumoto Castle reflected in the surrounding moat on a clear autumn morning with the Japanese Alps behind
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The castle
paragraphs: Matsumoto Castle is one of Japan's twelve surviving original castles — meaning it was not destroyed, bombed, or rebuilt in concrete in the postwar era. The main tower (tenshu) dates to 1593. It is black, which is unusual (most Japanese castles are white), and it sits in a moat surrounded by mountains that the castle architects clearly intended as a backdrop. In spring there are cherry trees around the moat. In autumn there are maple trees. In winter there is snow on the Alps. In summer the castle is reflected in the moat in the early morning before the crowds arrive. Every season offers something specific. Entrance is ¥700.

sections.heading: Inside the castle
paragraphs: The interior is original — steep wooden staircases (more ladder than stair in the upper floors), low beams, the smell of old timber, defensive features like gun ports and stone-drop windows. It is small enough to feel like a real building rather than a museum installation, and large enough to spend an hour in. The views from the top floor extend across the city to the Alps. The interior can be crowded at peak times; arrive at 8:30am when it opens and you will often have the upper floors largely to yourself.

sections.heading: The old town
paragraphs: The Nakamachi and Kaichi districts preserve Edo-period kura (storehouses) that have been converted into craft shops, sake breweries, coffee shops, and restaurants. The streets are genuinely old and genuinely in use — not a preserved historical theme zone but a working neighborhood that has been lived in continuously. The Kaichi School building (1876), built in a hybrid Japanese-Western style unique to Meiji-era architecture, is worth the five-minute detour.

sections.heading: Food and sake
paragraphs: Matsumoto is in Nagano Prefecture, which produces excellent sake, buckwheat, and mountain vegetables. The soba in Matsumoto is made from local buckwheat and is a different thing from the Tokyo variety — coarser, darker, more robust. Mameichi, a small soba restaurant near the castle, is consistently recommended. The local sake breweries in Nakamachi offer tastings. Basho, a specialist sake bar near the station, has one of the better regional sake selections in the area.

sections.heading: Getting there
paragraphs: From Tokyo (Shinjuku): the Azusa Limited Express to Matsumoto takes 2h30m, costs around ¥6,500 one-way, and is covered by JR Pass. From Nagoya: 2h by Shinano Limited Express. The city is small enough to walk everywhere once you arrive — the castle is 15 minutes from the station on foot. A single full day is enough for the castle, old town, and a proper meal. Two days allows excursions to Kamikochi (30 minutes by bus, one of Japan's most beautiful alpine valleys) or Hotaka (20 minutes by train, a shrine with an unusual collection of religious art).

sections.heading: The other reasons to stop here
paragraphs: Matsumoto is Yayoi Kusama's home town, and the city art museum holds a substantial permanent collection of her work along with the polka-dotted vending machines outside it. If the Naoshima pumpkins were on your list, this is the same artist at greater length and with no ferry.

The Suzuki method of teaching violin was developed here, and the city runs a serious classical music festival in late summer founded by the conductor Seiji Ozawa. Both facts explain a town that is noticeably more cultured than its size suggests.

Twenty minutes north by train, the Daio wasabi farm sits on spring water from the Alps and is the largest in Japan — rows of wasabi under black shade cloth in clear running streams, with wasabi ice cream at the end. It is a strange and pleasant hour.

sections.heading: Using it as a base for the Alps
paragraphs: The stronger argument for Matsumoto is what it reaches. Kamikochi, the alpine valley under the Hotaka range, is about ninety minutes by bus and is among the most beautiful places in Japan — a flat river walk under three-thousand-metre peaks, no private cars allowed, and a season running roughly mid-April to mid-November.

Norikura and the Tateyama Kurobe route are both reachable from here, and Shirahone Onsen, a small milky-white sulphur spring village in a gorge, is an hour and a half by bus and barely changed in a century.
This is why two nights beats one. Day one is the castle and the old town; day two is a mountain. A single overnight gets you the castle and a train.

sections.heading: Doing the castle properly
paragraphs: Go at opening. The interior is a single narrow route up six floors of original timber with staircases closer to ladders than stairs, and once it fills there is no overtaking — the whole building becomes one slow queue. At half past eight you can climb it at your own pace; by eleven on a weekend the wait to enter can be an hour.
Socks matter, because shoes come off at the entrance and you carry them with you in a bag. The floors are cold, worn and steep, and this is not a building to attempt in anything slippery.

Outside, walk the full circuit of the moat rather than photographing from the front. The reflection shot everyone takes is from the south-east; the quieter north side gives you the black tower against the Alps, which is the better picture and the reason the castle was built where it was.

sections.heading: The Alps in winter
paragraphs: Matsumoto in winter — December through February — is exceptional if you are prepared for cold. The Alps are fully snowcapped. The castle moat reflects a stark black tower against white mountains on clear mornings. Visitor numbers are low. The onsen around the city (Asama, Utsukushigahara, Shirahone) are at their best in cold weather. Shirahone Onsen specifically, 90 minutes by bus from Matsumoto, is a small valley onsen village that has barely changed since the Edo period and is close to empty outside of August.

title: Kyoto in Three Days: What to Actually See and What to Skip
excerpt: Kyoto has over 1,600 temples and shrines. You will not see them all. Here is how to choose the ones that matter — and what makes them worth choosing over the others.
heroImageAlt: The vermilion torii gates of Fushimi Inari at dawn with no crowds visible
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Day one: the east side
paragraphs: Start at Fushimi Inari. The torii gate path that runs up Mt. Inari is the most photographed image in Japan, and the photographs don't exaggerate it. The path continues for four kilometers past the main tourist zone, thinning to almost nothing by the second kilometer. Arrive at 6:30am or earlier and walk past the first major platform — the mountain path above it is genuinely quiet until 9am. In the afternoon: Kinkaku-ji (the Golden Pavilion). Arrive between 2pm and closing. It is always crowded; go anyway, because the building and its reflection in the pond are one of those things that maintains its impact despite the crowds. This is rarer than it sounds.

sections.heading: Day one: evening in Gion
paragraphs: After 5pm, walk through Gion. The most famous streets (Hanamikoji, Shimbashi) are genuinely beautiful in the evening light. In summer (July), the Gion Matsuri preparations fill the streets with yamahoko floats. In autumn, the maple trees along Shimbashi turn. Come to look, not to photograph — or at minimum, look before you photograph. The neighborhood has been fighting the worst effects of mass tourism for several years, and the experience of being there is different when you are present rather than performing.

sections.heading: Day two: the northwest
paragraphs: Arashiyama is the west side's major district, accessible by the Sagano Scenic Railway or the Randen tram. The bamboo grove is a ten-minute walk from the Arashiyama station and genuinely spectacular — and very crowded by 10am, nearly empty at 7am. After the grove: Tenryu-ji, one of Kyoto's great Zen gardens, with a pond framed by borrowed scenery (shakkei) of the mountains behind it. In autumn the maple trees around the pond are what the photographs in every Japan feature show. After Tenryu-ji, walk the Sagano path north to Jojakko-ji — a moss-covered temple on a hillside that appears in almost no itineraries and is about as far from the crowd as you can get while staying in Arashiyama.

sections.heading: Day two: Nishiki Market
paragraphs: Return to central Kyoto in the afternoon for Nishiki Market — a covered arcade called Kyoto's Kitchen, narrow, parallel to Shijo Street, with stalls selling pickled vegetables, grilled mochi, tofu, Kyoto-style dashi components, fresh yuba, and specialty food items. Eat as you walk (this is one of the exceptions to the no-eating-while-walking rule, since the market format makes stationary eating difficult). The market closes early — most stalls done by 6pm.

sections.heading: Day three: what most itineraries miss
paragraphs: Philosopher's Path (Tetsugaku no Michi): a two-kilometer canal-side walkway between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji in the northeastern hills. In cherry blossom season the canal is lined with sakura. At any time of year it is quieter than the central tourist circuit and lined with small cafés, tofu restaurants, and craft shops. Walk it slowly, south to north. At the northern end: Nanzen-ji, a Zen temple complex with an aqueduct running through the grounds — one of the odder visual combinations in Kyoto and one of the most memorable.

sections.heading: How to move around, which decides everything
paragraphs: Kyoto's buses go everywhere and are slow, packed and stuck in traffic during any busy season. The two subway lines are fast and cover very little. The trains — JR, Keihan, Hankyu, Eizan, Randen — are excellent along their own corridors and useless between them.

The answer most residents will give you is a bicycle. The city is flat, compact and on a grid, and almost everything in this itinerary is within a twenty-minute ride. Rentals are inexpensive and widely available; park only in marked bays, because Kyoto impounds bikes left on pavements.

Where you stay matters more here than in Tokyo, because crossing the city eats an hour. Staying near Karasuma or Kawaramachi puts you within reach of both halves. Staying at the station is convenient for arrival and inconvenient for everything else.

sections.heading: The season changes the plan
paragraphs: In cherry blossom season and in the second half of November, everything in this itinerary is two to three times busier, and the early-morning rule stops being an optimisation and becomes the only way it works. Aim to be at the first site at opening and finished with it by nine.

Both seasons add evening illuminations at several temples, which are ticketed, crowded and genuinely worth doing once — and which give you something to do in the hours when the daytime sites are unpleasant.
The rest of the year, and especially the fresh green of late May and the quiet of January, the same three days are a completely different and much gentler trip.

sections.heading: What three days cannot include
paragraphs: Three days buys you one side of the city per day and a little slack. It does not buy the northern mountains — Ohara, Kurama and Kibune each want most of a day — and it does not buy Uji, which is where the tea and the Byodo-in phoenix hall are.
It also does not buy Nara, which is forty-five minutes away and deserves its own day rather than an afternoon. Attempting Nara on day three of a Kyoto trip produces a rushed version of both.
If you have a fourth day, spend it north rather than adding more temples in the centre. If you have a fifth, spend it in Nara. The marginal value of a seventh temple in Higashiyama is close to zero.

sections.heading: What to skip
paragraphs: Nijo Castle: historically interesting, architecturally significant (the nightingale floor squeaks deliberately to detect intruders), and fairly dry as a visitor experience compared to everything else Kyoto offers. Come if you have four or more days. Toei Kyoto Studio Park (a movie set theme park): enthusiastically recommended by some and entirely optional for everyone who isn't specifically interested in period samurai dramas. Philosopher's Path during peak cherry blossom season: beautiful, but the crowd density removes the contemplative quality that is the entire point.

title: The Unwritten Rules of Japanese Trains — Read This Before You Board
excerpt: Japan’s trains run on time to the minute and operate on a set of social rules that nobody posts on a sign. Here’s what they are.
heroImageAlt: The interior of a Tokyo commuter train with passengers sitting quietly
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Silent mode means silent
paragraphs: The first thing operators ask is that you set your phone to manner mode. That means no ringtone, no notification sounds, no audio of any kind. It does not mean vibrate — in a quiet carriage a buzzing phone on a hard surface is clearly audible to the six people nearest you.
Put it fully silent. It takes two seconds and prevents one of the more uncomfortable social experiences available to a visitor.
Headphones count too. Audio leaking from earbuds is one of the standard announcements on Japanese trains, and it carries further than the wearer ever believes.

sections.heading: Phone calls are not done
paragraphs: Taking a call on a commuter train is a social violation roughly equivalent to eating a sandwich in a library. The standard approach is to let it go to voicemail, or answer, say quietly that you are on a train, and end the call immediately.
On long-distance Shinkansen, calls are acceptable in the vestibule between carriages, and that is where everyone goes to make them. In the carriage itself the same rules apply.
Texting, reading, gaming and watching things silently are all completely normal. It is the voice that is the problem, not the phone.

sections.heading: Priority seats and offering a seat
paragraphs: The seats marked near the doors, usually in a different colour, are for elderly passengers, pregnant women, people with young children and anyone with an injury or disability. On a crowded train they fill like any other; on an empty one the norm is to leave them free.

The nuance is time of day. At eleven on a Friday night nobody is enforcing anything. At eight on a Monday morning, a healthy young person sitting in a priority seat while an elderly passenger stands is making a choice that the carriage notices.

Offering your seat is less common here than visitors expect, and offers are frequently declined — refusing is a way of not being treated as old or frail. If you offer and are turned down, sit back down without fuss; it is not a rejection of the gesture.
Pregnant passengers often carry a small pink maternity badge on their bag, which exists precisely because early pregnancy is not visible. It is worth recognising.

sections.heading: Platform queuing and boarding
paragraphs: Most platforms have markings on the ground showing where the doors will open and where to stand. You queue behind the lines in two columns, and you let everyone off before you board. Look at the floor, find the lines, stand in them.
This works entirely by social agreement and no barriers, which is why it collapses the moment a group of people who do not know the system arrives at the door.
Do not run for a closing door. The doors close hard and on time, another train is along in three minutes, and the sight of someone sprinting down a platform is genuinely unusual here.

sections.heading: Bags, backpacks and luggage
paragraphs: On a crowded train a backpack worn on the back takes up the space of another person and hits someone every time you turn. Take it off and hold it in front of you, or put it on the overhead rack. This is announced on trains constantly and is the visitor behaviour most likely to irritate a Japanese commuter.

Large suitcases go in the space at the end of the carriage, not in the aisle and not on a seat. On the Shinkansen, the overhead rack takes a surprising amount, and the space behind the last row of seats is the place for a big case — which is why booking that row is worth doing.

One rule with a penalty attached: on the Tokaido, Sanyo and Kyushu Shinkansen, baggage over 160cm in total dimensions requires an oversized baggage seat reservation, free in advance and ¥1,000 if you turn up without one.

sections.heading: Eating and drinking
paragraphs: Eating on local commuter trains is generally not done. Drinking from a closed container is fine.

On long-distance trains, eating is expected — the entire ekiben culture of station lunch boxes exists for it, and buying one before boarding the Shinkansen is part of the journey rather than a lapse. Beer with it is normal.

The distinction is between a ten-minute metro ride and a two-hour intercity journey. If nobody around you is eating, you probably should not be either. Strong-smelling food is the one thing to avoid even where eating is fine.

sections.heading: Rush hour, and women-only carriages
paragraphs: Peak-hour crowding in Tokyo is real and is unlike anything most visitors have experienced. Roughly 7:30 to 9:00 in the morning is the crush; if you can travel outside it, do. Pushing is normal, apologising is not expected, and the way out at your station is to say sumimasen and move.

Many operators run women-only carriages during morning peak, marked with pink signs on the platform and stickers on the doors, introduced in response to groping on crowded trains. The restriction usually applies only at certain hours and is printed on the sign. Men wandering into one by accident is a common visitor error and is met with pointing rather than anger.
If you are travelling with luggage, avoid peak hours entirely. A suitcase in a rush-hour carriage is genuinely difficult for everyone including you.

sections.heading: Gates, fares and small things
paragraphs: Tap your IC card flat on the reader on the way in and out; the gates close fast on anyone who hesitates. If the gate rejects you on exit — usually an insufficient balance — do not force it; use the fare adjustment machine before the gates, or the window at the side.
Sleeping on trains is completely normal and nobody thinks anything of it, including people asleep on a stranger's shoulder. Setting an alarm for your stop is sensible.
Each station has its own departure melody, which regular commuters recognise before they look up. It is one of the small pleasures of the system.

sections.heading: Why these rules matter
paragraphs: Japan's rail network carries millions of people daily with near-zero conflict. The reason is not enforcement — there are no transit police watching for phone calls or checking priority seats.

The reason is that everyone in the carriage has implicitly agreed to the same rules, and the rules work because they are followed consistently. A visitor who does not know them is not being judged harshly; they are simply outside the system.
Knowing them before you board means you spend the journey looking at the city rather than at an awkward situation.

title: How to Visit a Japanese Temple or Shrine Without Being Accidentally Rude
excerpt: Temples and shrines have different rules, different purposes, and different gods. Getting them confused is the starting mistake. Everything else follows from there.
heroImageAlt: A stone torii gate leading to a Shinto shrine path lined with lanterns
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Temple or shrine, and why it matters
paragraphs: Temples are Buddhist. Shrines are Shinto. The buildings differ, the rituals differ, and the correct behaviour differs slightly at each.

The fastest test: if there is a torii — the distinctive gate, usually vermilion or stone — you are at a shrine. If there is a large incense burner and a hall with Buddhist statuary, you are at a temple. Shrine names often end in -jinja, -jingu or -taisha; temple names in -ji, -dera or -in.

Many famous sites have both on the same grounds, particularly in Kyoto and Nara, because the two coexisted and intermingled for over a thousand years before being forcibly separated by the Meiji government. Where you find both, nobody minds which set of manners you use.

sections.heading: The torii and the approach
paragraphs: Walking through a torii marks the transition from the ordinary world into sacred space. Walk through it rather than around it, and a small bow before passing under is the conventional gesture — you will see people do it without breaking stride.
The centre of the approach path is considered the route of the deity, so many people walk slightly to one side. This is not required of visitors and is the kind of thing worth knowing exists.

At temples, the equivalent is the main gate, often with guardian figures in alcoves on either side. Same principle: pass through it rather than around, and look up at the statues, which are frequently the best thing on the site.

sections.heading: The purification fountain
paragraphs: Near the entrance there is a temizuya — a stone basin with ladles. The sequence: take a ladle in your right hand and pour water over your left; swap hands and pour over your right; pour a little into your left palm, rinse your mouth and spit to the side onto the ground, never into the basin; then tip the ladle upright so the remaining water runs down the handle, and replace it face down.
One ladleful covers all of it, which is the part people get wrong. You are not meant to refill.

Since the pandemic many basins have had their ladles removed and run as a simple flowing spout instead, in which case rinsing your hands is the whole ritual. Most foreign visitors skip this entirely and it is not obligatory, but doing it correctly is a straightforward gesture of respect.

sections.heading: How to pray at a shrine
paragraphs: Approach the main hall. Toss a coin into the offering box — a five-yen coin is traditional because go-en also means a good connection or good fortune. Ring the bell if there is a rope. Bow deeply twice, clap twice, hold the moment, then bow once more.
Two bows, two claps, one bow is the standard sequence at most shrines, though a few famous ones use a different count and will have a sign saying so.
You do not need to remember all of it. Two deep bows and two claps gets you most of the way and nobody will correct you. Coins are thrown gently, not lobbed, and the box is not a wishing well.

sections.heading: How to pray at a temple
paragraphs: Buddhist temples do not involve clapping, and this is the single most common visible error visitors make. Place a coin in the box, put your hands together, bow, hold the moment. That is all of it.

The large incense burner in front of the main hall is for purification: light a stick, place it in the sand, and waft the smoke towards yourself — commonly towards a part of the body that hurts. Buy the incense at the counter rather than taking from someone else's bundle, and light it from the burner rather than from another person's stick.
Many halls require shoes off at the threshold. There will be a step and either a rack or plastic bags. Photography inside is often prohibited and there will usually be a sign.

sections.heading: Omamori, ema and omikuji
paragraphs: Omamori are cloth amulets sold for specific purposes — safe travel, health, study, childbirth, road safety. They are not souvenirs exactly; they are meant to be carried, replaced annually, and returned to a shrine to be burned rather than thrown away. Do not open them to see what is inside.
