Ema are the small wooden plaques you see hung in racks by the hundred. Buy one, write your wish on the back, hang it. English is fine. The wish is between you and whatever you have chosen to address.

Omikuji are paper fortunes, drawn at random for a hundred yen or so, ranked from great blessing down to great curse. The convention is to keep a good one and tie a bad one to the rack or the tree provided, leaving the misfortune behind at the shrine rather than carrying it home.

sections.heading: The stamp book
paragraphs: Goshuin are hand-brushed calligraphic stamps, written for you in ink on the spot by a priest or attendant, recording your visit. They are collected in a dedicated concertina book — a goshuincho — sold at most shrines and temples for a couple of thousand yen, and each stamp costs a few hundred.
This is the best souvenir in Japan and very few visitors know about it. Each one is drawn while you wait, and a full book from a two-week trip is an object nobody else has.

The etiquette: use a proper goshuincho rather than a notebook, hand it over open at the page you want, do not talk while the calligrapher is working, and do not treat it as an autograph collection to be rushed around for. Many places will not stamp a book that already contains stamps from the other religion, so some collectors keep two.

sections.heading: General conduct
paragraphs: These are working religious sites, not museums. Services happen, funerals happen, and people are praying beside you. Keep your voice down, do not photograph anyone mid-prayer, and step aside rather than through if someone is at the offering box.
Dress is not formally regulated and nobody will refuse you entry over shorts, but the general standard of dress in Japan is neat and matching it is easy. Remove hats inside halls.

Most sites are free; some charge a few hundred yen for a garden or a treasure hall, which is nearly always worth paying. Opening hours are shorter than you expect — many close by four or five, and the last admission can be half an hour before that.

If you want to go further, some temples run shukubo, temple lodging, where you stay overnight, eat the vegetarian temple cuisine and can join the morning service. Koyasan is the best-known place to do it and it is a genuinely different experience from any hotel.

title: Why You Should Never Tip in Japan — and What to Do Instead
excerpt: In Japan, the service is built into the price. Adding a tip doesn’t reward the server — it creates an awkward situation for both of you.
heroImageAlt: A server at a traditional Japanese restaurant carefully placing dishes on a low table
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The rule
paragraphs: Do not tip in Japan. Not at restaurants, not in taxis, not at the ryokan, not at the hotel. The rule applies everywhere, with essentially no exceptions.
This is not a matter of the tip being too small or the service not meriting it. Tipping is simply not part of the service culture, and attempting it creates confusion rather than goodwill.

sections.heading: Why tipping is not done
paragraphs: Service in Japan is understood as part of what you already paid for. The waiter refilling your water, the taxi driver operating the door from the front seat, the ryokan attendant laying out your futon — all are doing the job to a high standard because that is the expectation, not because a financial incentive is available for exceeding it.
Tipping implies the service was beyond what was expected, which implies the expectation was low. That is not the message most people intend to send.

There is a structural reason too: hospitality staff here are paid a wage rather than being expected to make it up in gratuities, so the tip is not filling a gap in anyone's income. The practice has no function to perform.

sections.heading: What happens if you try
paragraphs: If you leave cash on a restaurant table, staff will frequently chase you down the street to return it, assuming you forgot it. If you hand money to a server directly, it will usually be declined, sometimes with visible discomfort.

The genuinely awkward version is at a small owner-run place, where refusing costs the owner face and accepting costs them something else. You have created a problem for someone who was having a perfectly good evening.
None of these outcomes is the one you were hoping for. The generous act here is to pay the bill and say thank you.

sections.heading: Charges that are not tips
paragraphs: Two things on Japanese bills get mistaken for tipping and neither is.

Otoshi, at an izakaya, is a small dish that arrives unordered at the start along with a per-person charge of a few hundred yen. It is a seating and cover charge and it is not optional, not a scam, and not something to send back. If you are surprised by an extra ¥500 a head on an izakaya bill, this is what it was.

A service charge — sabisu-ryo, often ten per cent — appears at high-end restaurants, hotel restaurants and ryokan, and is stated on the menu or the tariff. Where it appears it is already in the total. It is not a tip and it does not mean you should add one.
Consumption tax is separate again and is now generally shown included in the displayed price, so the number on the menu is the number you pay.

sections.heading: The ryokan exception, properly named
paragraphs: There is one traditional practice that resembles a tip, and it is worth naming correctly: kokorozuke. It is a small amount given to the room attendant at a ryokan, on arrival rather than departure, as a gesture of thanks for the personal service through the stay. The typical amount is ¥1,000–3,000.

The form matters more than the sum. It goes in a small envelope — the plain ones sold at any convenience store or stationery shop are correct — and it is presented with both hands. Loose cash is not kokorozuke; it is just money on a table.

It is optional, increasingly rare, and never expected of foreign guests. Plenty of ryokan will politely decline it. If the whole idea makes you uneasy, skip it; nothing about your stay will be different.
The same logic applies to a private guide or a driver you have hired for a day, where a small envelope at the end is accepted more readily than a handful of notes.

sections.heading: In taxis, bars and hotels
paragraphs: Taxi fare is metered. You pay the meter, you do not round up, and the driver will produce exact change and expect you to take it. Saying 'keep it' lands as strange rather than generous.

Bars work the same way, including the ones where a bartender spends four minutes making one drink. Hotel porters and housekeeping are not tipped. Nor are hairdressers, delivery drivers or anyone else.
The one place money changes hands unusually is a hostess bar or similar, where the pricing structure is its own subject and has nothing to do with gratuity.

sections.heading: What to do instead
paragraphs: What the culture does value in place of a tip is acknowledgement. 'Gochisousama deshita' on leaving a restaurant thanks the kitchen for the meal and is the single most effective thing you can say — far more so than money, and it costs nothing but the effort of learning six syllables.
'Arigatou gozaimashita' with a small bow works everywhere else. Saying it to the specific person who helped you, rather than to the room, is what makes it land.

Beyond words: returning to the same restaurant twice in a trip is understood as a compliment, and telling a chef which dish you liked is the kind of feedback small places rarely get from visitors. If you genuinely want to reward good service, a review or a recommendation reaches further than ¥1,000 ever would.

title: When to Take Your Shoes Off in Japan: The Complete Guide
excerpt: The shoe rule in Japan is not arbitrary. It reflects a clear line between outside space and inside space that structures daily life. Here is where that line is drawn.
heroImageAlt: A row of shoes neatly arranged in a traditional Japanese entryway genkan
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The genkan
paragraphs: Traditional Japanese homes, ryokan and many older buildings have a genkan — an entrance area slightly lower than the rest of the floor, designed specifically for removing shoes. You step into the genkan, take off your shoes, and step up into the interior in socks or bare feet.

The step is the entire logic. The lower level is outside, conceptually, even though it is indoors; the raised level is inside. Once you understand that the floor height is doing the work, every situation in this article becomes readable without anyone explaining it.

The directional convention is that shoes are turned to point back toward the door once you have stepped up, ready to put on when you leave. This is not required of guests and it is what you will observe everyone doing. Doing it yourself takes two seconds and is noticed.

sections.heading: At ryokan
paragraphs: Shoes come off at the main entrance and you are given slippers. The slippers go everywhere inside the building except tatami rooms, where you go in socks or bare feet, and the toilet, which has its own dedicated pair.

The slippers-off-at-tatami rule catches most visitors at least once. Look at the floor: if it is woven straw matting, your slippers stay at the edge of it. The reason is practical as much as ceremonial — tatami marks and wears under hard soles.

Your outdoor shoes will usually be taken and stored for you, and produced again when you check out. You do not need to keep track of them, and you should not go and retrieve them yourself from the rack.

sections.heading: At restaurants and bars
paragraphs: Traditional restaurants — particularly those with tatami seating, private rooms or a raised platform — will have a designated shoe removal area near the entrance. The signal is usually a step, a row of slippers, or a member of staff making the gesture. Western-style restaurants do not require it.

There is often a wooden shoe locker with a wooden key, or a numbered cubby. Take the key with you. Some izakaya have a sunken floor under the table so you can sit at a low table with your legs down — shoes still come off.
If you are unsure, look at what the people ahead of you are doing, or simply pause at the threshold. Staff will tell you within about a second, because they watch for exactly this.

sections.heading: At temples, and everywhere else
paragraphs: Certain temple halls require shoes off before entering. There will be a step at the entrance and either a rack or plastic bags to carry your shoes with you, which is the better option in a busy place where racks overflow. This varies by temple — outdoor grounds and paths never require it, interiors often do.

The list of other places that follow the rule is longer than visitors expect: some clinics and hospitals, most schools, many small museums and galleries, traditional craft workshops, some public halls, fitting rooms in clothes shops when you step onto a raised platform, and any home you are invited into.
Modern hotels, convenience stores, department stores, offices and Western-style restaurants do not. If there is no step, there is no rule.

sections.heading: The toilet slipper trap
paragraphs: The most reliable mistake visitors make is walking out of the toilet still wearing the toilet slippers. At ryokan and traditional homes there is a dedicated pair inside the toilet room. You put them on to enter and take them off when you leave.
Walking back through the inn in them is the equivalent of carrying the toilet brush into the dining room. It happens to almost everyone once, and it is met with amusement rather than horror.
The correction is mechanical: look at your feet before you open the door. That is the whole technique.

sections.heading: What this means for what you pack
paragraphs: This is the single most consequential packing decision for a trip to Japan and most people get it wrong. Bring shoes you can remove and put back on while standing, without sitting down and without untying anything. Slip-ons, loafers, or laced shoes you can leave loose. Knee-high boots are a genuine mistake here.

Socks matter, because they will be seen constantly and often at close range. Bring more pairs than you think and check them for holes before you leave home. This sounds trivial and it is the thing people report being most embarrassed by.

Two more practical notes. Guest slippers are sized for Japanese feet and stop somewhere around a men's UK 9 or US 10; larger feet should expect to walk on their heels or go in socks, and nobody minds. And if you are visiting a home in winter, thick socks are welcome — floors are cold and central heating is rare.

sections.heading: Reading the signal
paragraphs: The consistent indicator is a change in floor level at the entrance. When you see a step, assume shoes off until there is evidence otherwise. A row of slippers waiting, a shoe rack, a wooden cubby, or a floor that changes from concrete to wood or tatami all point the same way.
When there is no step and no slippers, the rule does not apply. That covers the overwhelming majority of places you will go.

Getting it wrong is a small, common and forgivable error, and the correction is always a polite gesture rather than a rebuke. Watch the threshold, follow the person in front, and you will be right nearly every time.

title: How to Behave in Public in Japan: The Unwritten Rules
excerpt: Japanese public spaces operate on a set of unspoken rules that make them exceptionally pleasant. Most visitors don’t know them. All of them are learnable in ten minutes.
heroImageAlt: A busy pedestrian crossing in Tokyo with people moving in orderly streams
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Don't eat while walking
paragraphs: Eating while walking is generally not done. The exception is festival food from stalls at a matsuri, where the context is explicit and everyone is doing it. Otherwise you finish your convenience store onigiri standing outside the shop, not while walking down the street.
Street food vendors at tourist sites have started providing small standing areas specifically because this norm exists and visitors do not know it. Use them — they are there for you.
The same applies to drinking, though less strictly: a closed bottle carried and sipped is unremarkable, an open cup of coffee while walking is mildly conspicuous.

sections.heading: Queuing is not optional
paragraphs: Japan queues. At ATMs, at crossings, at train doors, at ramen shops, at lifts, at bus stops. Cutting in is an extremely unwelcome behaviour.

If there is no visible queue but a crowd, look for the end of it and join there. Lines here are orderly and self-policing — nobody will say anything if you push in, but everybody will notice, and the social discomfort this produces is immediate and real.

Queues also form in places you might not expect one: at the platform door markings, at the escalator, at the single working ticket machine. When in doubt, assume the loose cluster of people is a line.

sections.heading: Noise levels
paragraphs: Japan is quieter than most countries in public. Not silent — Shinjuku at six in the evening is genuinely loud — but the background noise comes from the environment rather than from individual conversations.

Speaking at a volume that carries beyond your table, laughing in a way that commands the room, or holding a speakerphone conversation in a shop are all behaviours that will cause people to move away from you. That movement is the feedback system; nobody will say anything.

The single most common complaint from Japanese people about foreign visitors is volume, and it is almost always unintentional. A group of four talking normally in a language nobody around them speaks is louder in effect than the same group at home.

sections.heading: Escalators, lifts and pavements
paragraphs: On escalators the standing side is the left and the right is for walking, in Tokyo. Osaka reverses it — stand right, walk left — and the boundary between the two conventions falls somewhere around Kyoto, producing visible confusion. When in doubt, follow the person in front.
Worth knowing: rail operators have spent years asking people to stand on both sides for safety reasons, and the campaign has largely failed. Follow the crowd rather than the poster.

On pavements and in corridors, keep left in most of the country. In lifts, the person nearest the buttons operates them for everyone and holds the door, which is a small job you may find yourself doing.

sections.heading: There are no rubbish bins
paragraphs: Public bins were largely removed after the 1995 sarin attack on the Tokyo subway and never came back. In most streets, parks and platforms there is nowhere to put anything.

You carry your rubbish with you until you reach a convenience store, which has bins by the entrance or the till, or your accommodation. Vending machines have a bin beside them for that machine's own containers. Stations have some, usually past the ticket gates.
Carry a small bag for it. This is less inconvenient than it sounds once you accept that the rubbish is coming with you, and it is a large part of why Japanese streets look the way they do.

sections.heading: Smoking, which works backwards
paragraphs: The rule is close to the inverse of what most visitors expect. Smoking on the street is banned in many central wards and enforced with fines, and there are designated smoking areas — glass boxes, marked corners — where smokers congregate.

Indoors, smoking survives in a way it does not in most of Europe. Rules have tightened considerably, but small bars and some restaurants can still permit it, and a smoking room or a smoking floor in a hotel is normal.
If you smoke, use the designated areas and carry a portable ashtray, which is sold everywhere. If you do not, be aware that a bar you walk into may be smoky and that this is legal.

sections.heading: Small body things that read differently
paragraphs: Blowing your nose in public is considered unpleasant; the convention is to sniff, or to step away and do it discreetly. This genuinely surprises people from countries where the reverse is true.

Pointing at people is impolite — the gesture is an open hand. Beckoning is done palm down with the fingers waving towards yourself, which to Western eyes looks like a shooing motion. Counting on fingers starts with the thumb.

Wearing a mask when you have a cold is normal, unremarkable and appreciated, and has been long before recent years. And physical contact between strangers is minimal: no back-slapping, no hugging, no hand on the shoulder.

sections.heading: Umbrellas, and drinking outdoors
paragraphs: It rains, and there is an entire small infrastructure for it. Shops and museums have umbrella stands at the door, some with locks and keys, and you leave yours there rather than dripping through the building. Many have plastic sleeve dispensers instead. Take the umbrella when you leave; cheap ones do get taken by mistake, which is why you can buy a new one for a few hundred yen at any convenience store.

Drinking alcohol in public is legal and unremarkable in Japan, which surprises visitors from countries where it is not. A beer in a park during hanami, on a bench, or on a long-distance train is entirely normal.
What is not tolerated is being loudly drunk in a way that affects other people. The line is not the drinking; it is the volume and the mess.

sections.heading: Photography of strangers
paragraphs: The norms are broadly those of most countries, with one specific and well-documented problem: the geisha districts of Kyoto, where years of visitors photographing maiko and geiko at close range has led to restrictions, closed private lanes and fines.

Photographing someone in traditional dress without asking, following them for a shot, or blocking a path for a photograph are behaviours that have prompted legal responses in some areas. This is not a general hostility to cameras; it is a response to specific, repeated conduct.
Everywhere else: use judgement, ask when in doubt, and take no for an answer. 'Shashin, ii desu ka' is enough, and the answer is yes more often than not.

title: Japan Still Runs on Cash — Here’s How Much to Bring and Where to Get It
excerpt: Cards are increasingly accepted in Japan, but ‘increasingly’ is not the same as ‘reliably.’ Plan for cash and treat the card acceptance as a bonus.
heroImageAlt: A hand holding Japanese yen banknotes in front of a temple market
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why Japan still uses cash
paragraphs: Japan's cash culture is not technological backwardness. It reflects a combination of historical distrust of consumer credit, very low crime rates that make carrying cash safe, a retail infrastructure built around cash transactions, and a cultural preference for exact, visible payment. The ¥100, ¥500 and ¥1,000 denominations handle most daily transactions efficiently.

The safety point is not a throwaway. Losing a wallet in Tokyo has a genuinely high probability of it being handed in to a police box with the money still in it, and that fact underwrites the whole system. In a country where cash is not at meaningful risk, the case for cards is weaker than it is elsewhere.
There is also a merchant reason. Card processing fees are a real cost for a six-seat restaurant with thin margins, and plenty of small businesses have concluded that cash is simply cheaper to accept.

sections.heading: Is it changing
paragraphs: Yes, slowly. Card acceptance has expanded significantly in recent years — the convenience store chains, department stores, chain restaurants and supermarkets almost universally take Visa and Mastercard now, and contactless is normal in cities.

But neighbourhood restaurants, small temple admission counters, some bus routes, onsen entrance fees, market stalls and many rural businesses remain cash-only. You will encounter cash-only situations, and whether to carry cash is not really a decision.

Two acceptance details worth knowing. American Express and Diners are accepted far less widely than Visa and Mastercard, so do not travel with only an Amex. And QR payment apps — PayPay and its competitors, which is what you will see locals using — generally require a Japanese bank account or phone number and are not a practical option for a visitor.

sections.heading: How much to bring
paragraphs: A reasonable daily cash budget for someone eating well and visiting paid attractions is ¥5,000–8,000 per day. For a one-week trip to Tokyo and Kyoto, ¥50,000–60,000 in cash is a workable target, supplemented by card use where available.

Carry ¥10,000–20,000 on you at any given time — enough for a day with a buffer. More than ¥30,000 in a wallet is unnecessary given how dense the ATM network is; you are never far from a convenience store.

Bring a small amount of yen from home for the first few hours if it is convenient, but do not exchange large sums before you travel. Home-country exchange rates are almost always worse than withdrawing from a Japanese ATM, and the airport exchange counters in Japan are worse still.

sections.heading: The convenience store ATM
paragraphs: The most reliable cash source for foreign visitors is the ATM inside a 7-Eleven. These accept almost all international cards, have English and several other language menus, charge a flat fee of a couple of hundred yen, and run around the clock. Japan Post ATMs in post offices and AEON bank ATMs are the other dependable options.
Traditional Japanese bank ATMs — Mizuho, MUFG, SMBC — frequently do not accept foreign cards at all, or accept them only during banking hours, which defeats the purpose. Do not waste time on them.

Two practical points. Withdraw larger amounts less often, because the fee is flat and your home bank probably adds its own. And tell your bank you are travelling before you go; a Japanese ATM withdrawal is a classic fraud trigger and a blocked card at 9pm in a country where you are relying on cash is a genuinely bad evening.

sections.heading: The money itself
paragraphs: Notes come in ¥1,000, ¥5,000 and ¥10,000. A new series was issued in 2024 — different portraits, different security features — and both old and new circulate together as legal tender. Occasionally an older vending machine or ticket machine will reject the new notes; if that happens, it is the machine, not the money, and a convenience store will break it for you.

Coins run ¥1, ¥5, ¥10, ¥50, ¥100 and ¥500. The ¥500 is a substantial coin worth about three or four dollars, which takes some adjustment for visitors used to treating coins as small change. The ¥5 and ¥50 are the ones with holes in the middle.

You will accumulate coins at a startling rate, because cash payment plus consumption tax produces awkward totals constantly. The fix is to load them onto your IC card at any station machine, which accepts coins and turns them into train fare and convenience store purchases.

sections.heading: Where cards work and where they do not
paragraphs: Cards work reliably at hotel check-in, department stores and shopping centres, chain restaurants, supermarkets, convenience stores, pharmacy chains, Shinkansen ticket machines and major-city attractions.

Cards work unreliably or not at all at local izakaya, neighbourhood restaurants, temples and shrines, market stalls, some local buses, small guesthouses, coin lockers of the older type, and anything describable as family-run. Festival food stalls are universally cash. So are most admission boxes at small temples, which frequently amount to a wooden slot and an honesty system.

The reliable test is to look before you order. If there are no payment logos on the door, the window or the till, assume cash — and if you are unsure, kaado, tsukaemasu ka settles it in three words before you have committed to a meal.

sections.heading: The IC card exception
paragraphs: The IC card — Suica, ICOCA and their regional equivalents — sits between cash and card and is worth treating separately. It is a prepaid tap card accepted on trains and buses nationwide, at convenience stores, at vending machines, in many shops and at a lot of coin lockers.

Load it with cash at any station machine and keep a couple of thousand yen on it. The combination of an IC card and a modest cash reserve handles the overwhelming majority of daily transactions without friction, and it removes the fumbling for coins that slows everything down.

Recent iPhones and many Android phones can hold a Suica in the wallet app and top it up from an overseas card, which sidesteps the physical card entirely. If that works on your handset it is the single best small preparation you can make before arriving.

sections.heading: Etiquette, and one thing not to do
paragraphs: Money is passed on the small tray by the till, not hand to hand. Put your notes in the tray; change and receipt come back the same way. It is universal and it is not a formality you can skip without the cashier being briefly stuck.

There is no tipping anywhere in Japan — not in restaurants, taxis, hotels or bars. Leaving money on a table will result in someone chasing you down the street to return it. If you want to express appreciation, say gochisousama deshita on the way out; it lands better than money would.

Finally, count your change and take your receipt. Not because anyone is trying anything — the accuracy here is absolute — but because the receipt is what you need for tax-free processing, and the tax-free counter will not help you without it.

title: SIM Card vs Pocket Wi-Fi in Japan: What Nobody Tells You Before You Choose
excerpt: Both work. One is significantly more convenient. The answer has changed in the last three years and most travel articles haven’t caught up.
heroImageAlt: A person holding a phone with a Japan map open in a busy train station
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why you need internet
paragraphs: Navigation in Japan without internet access is not impossible — the signage in major train stations is multilingual and the numbered exit system on the Tokyo Metro is excellent — but it is significantly harder. Google Maps with Japanese transit data is the most useful single tool available to a visitor, and it needs a live connection to be worth much.

It is not only maps. Restaurant booking, train times, translating a sign, the taxi apps, contacting your accommodation, and increasingly the ticket for whatever you have booked all assume you are online. Sort this before you arrive rather than at the airport.

sections.heading: eSIM is now the default answer
paragraphs: If your phone supports eSIM — most released after 2020 do — a Japanese eSIM is the cleanest solution and the reason most older advice on this question is out of date.

You buy it online before you travel, install the profile over your home wifi, and switch it on when you land. Your original SIM stays active for calls and texts from home while data runs over a Japanese network. No physical swap, no spare device, no counter to queue at, and nothing to return. Providers including Ubigi, Airalo and several Japanese operators sell Japan plans in the region of $15–25 for a week to a month.

Two things to check before you buy. That your phone is carrier-unlocked, which is the usual reason an eSIM fails to activate. And which network the plan actually uses — Japan has three, and coverage in the mountains and on rural rail lines differs between them, though all are fine in cities.

sections.heading: Pocket Wi-Fi: the case for
paragraphs: A pocket Wi-Fi is a small device that creates a personal hotspot on a Japanese network. It connects several devices at once, which is the real argument for it: a family or a group of four sharing one rental is cheaper per head than four eSIMs, and a tablet or a laptop gets online without tethering.

It also requires no changes to your phone at all, which matters if your handset is locked, old, or issued by an employer. Airport rental desks are efficient and the return is a prepaid envelope you drop in a postbox.

sections.heading: Pocket Wi-Fi: the case against
paragraphs: It is one more thing to carry, charge and remember. The battery typically lasts eight to ten hours under real use, which is not a full travel day, so you are also carrying a power bank for it.

If you leave it at the hotel, the whole group has no internet until someone goes back. If you split up for the afternoon, only one of you is online. This is the failure mode that gets people, and it happens on nearly every trip where a couple shares one device.

Data may be throttled after a few gigabytes a day depending on the plan, and the cheapest rentals are the most aggressive about it. And there is a deposit and a return obligation — losing the unit is expensive.

sections.heading: Physical SIM cards
paragraphs: A Japanese tourist SIM replaces your existing SIM and gives you a local data connection. Data-only cards run roughly ¥3,000–5,000 for fifteen to thirty days with five to ten gigabytes; voice-capable cards cost more and most visitors do not need one.

The advantages are the same as an eSIM: nothing extra to carry, your phone's own battery life, always connected. The disadvantages are physical. You have to swap the card, which means storing your original somewhere it will not be lost — the ejector-pin trick of taping it inside your passport cover works. And you may need to set the APN manually, which takes five minutes and a look at the provider's instructions.
This is the right answer for a phone that does not do eSIM, and it is easy to buy on arrival.

sections.heading: What about free wifi and roaming
paragraphs: Free wifi exists and is not a plan. Convenience stores, major stations, most cafés and many trains have it, but the coverage is patchy, several networks require a registration form and an email confirmation, and sessions time out. As a fallback when your data runs out it is fine; as the primary way of navigating a country you do not know, it is not.

Roaming from your home carrier is the zero-effort option and it has got much cheaper. Some plans include Japan at no extra cost, and a daily-rate roaming pass at a few pounds or dollars a day is competitive for a short trip. For a week or less, check what your own carrier charges before buying anything — it may already be sorted.
The one thing not to do is arrive with nothing and decide at the airport. That is how people end up on the most expensive counter rental available at eleven at night.

sections.heading: How much data you actually need
paragraphs: Less than the plans imply. Maps, messaging, translation, searching and email run at well under a gigabyte a day for most travellers — call it 500MB to 1GB. A 10GB plan comfortably covers two weeks of that.

What consumes data is video: streaming on the Shinkansen, uploading photos and clips at full resolution, and video calls home. If you intend to do those, buy a larger allowance or set your phone to upload only on wifi, which is the simpler fix.
Unlimited plans are usually not worth the premium and frequently are not unlimited — read the fair-use clause, which typically throttles after a daily threshold anyway.

sections.heading: Where to get them, and the short answer
paragraphs: eSIMs are bought online before departure and activated on landing. Pocket Wi-Fi rental counters are at Narita, Haneda, Kansai and most other major airports, and booking online in advance is meaningfully cheaper than walking up. Physical SIMs are sold at airport shops and at the big electronics retailers, Bic Camera and Yodobashi, in every city.

The short answer for most people: one or two travellers on a phone from the last five years should buy an eSIM before leaving home. A group of three or more, or anyone with a locked or older handset, should rent a pocket Wi-Fi and book it in advance. Anyone staying under a week should check their home roaming rate first, because it may already be the cheapest option.

title: The Only Japanese Phrases You Actually Need
excerpt: Japanese is difficult. A handful of phrases isn’t. The ten expressions below will handle the majority of situations a visitor encounters, and they take about 20 minutes to learn.
heroImageAlt: A Japanese menu board with handwritten chalk specials at a small restaurant
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why bother
paragraphs: English in Japan is available, patchily. Major chain restaurants have English or picture menus. Train stations in Tokyo and Kyoto are multilingual. Hotel staff at international properties speak English. Beyond these contexts — at the neighbourhood izakaya, the market stall, the onsen town's local restaurant — Japanese is what you have.

A few phrases, used with reasonable pronunciation and a willingness to repeat them, will get you through almost everything. Nobody expects fluency. They do notice the attempt, and the shift in warmth when a visitor opens with sumimasen rather than 'excuse me' is immediate and consistent.

There is also a practical point. Many Japanese people studied English for years and can read it far better than they can speak it, and the barrier is often confidence rather than vocabulary. Slowing down, using short sentences and writing things down unlocks a surprising amount.

sections.heading: The four daily essentials
paragraphs: Sumimasen — excuse me, sorry to bother you. The Swiss Army knife of Japanese phrases. Use it to get attention in a restaurant, to apologise for bumping into someone, to start a question, to ask for help. If you learn one word, learn this one.

Arigatou gozaimasu — thank you very much. The full form; the bare arigatou is casual and slightly abrupt to a stranger. Hai — yes, and also a general acknowledgement that you have heard and are following. Iie — no, softer than it sounds, though in practice Japanese speakers avoid a flat no and so can you.

Add onegaishimasu — please, in the sense of 'if you would' — and you have five. It attaches to almost any request and makes it polite: point at a menu item and say onegaishimasu and the transaction is complete.
These, repeated calmly and clearly, handle a remarkable proportion of daily interaction.

sections.heading: At restaurants
paragraphs: Kore wo kudasai — this please. Point at the menu item. Three words, works everywhere. Hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu — one, two, three, for quantities. O-kaikei kudasai — the bill please; you can also trace a rectangle in the air with both index fingers and everyone understands.

Two more are worth having because they are social rather than transactional. Itadakimasu is said before eating, to no one in particular, and gochisousama deshita is said on leaving — it thanks the kitchen for the meal and it is the single phrase most likely to get a genuine reaction from a small restaurant. Oishii, delicious, used mid-meal, does the same job.
For a bar: nama hitotsu onegaishimasu gets you a draught beer, and osusume wa nan desu ka asks what they recommend, which is usually the right question in a place with a handwritten menu.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: [Destination] wa doko desu ka — where is [destination]. Fill in the place name, show it written down or on a map, and you will receive directions, usually very thorough directions, occasionally with an escort who walks you there.

Chotto matte kudasai — please wait a moment, for when someone is talking faster than you can process. Mou ichido onegaishimasu — once more please. Yukkuri onegaishimasu — slowly please. Those last two do more work than any amount of extra vocabulary.
For taxis, the useful sentence is not a sentence: show the address in Japanese, or better, read out the destination's phone number, which Japanese car navigation systems search on directly.

sections.heading: Shopping
paragraphs: Ikura desu ka — how much is it. Most shops will type the figure on a calculator or point at the tag, but the question opens the interaction correctly. Kore wa nan desu ka — what is this, for market stalls and menus where the item is unidentifiable. Expect a demonstration rather than an explanation.
Two that save real trouble: kore, arimasu ka — do you have this — while showing a photograph, and kaado, tsukaemasu ka — can I use a card, which is worth asking before you order rather than after.
When a shop assistant greets you with irasshaimase, no response is required. It is an announcement, not a question, and visitors often stall trying to answer it.

sections.heading: Declining, and getting help
paragraphs: Daijoubu desu is the most useful phrase nobody teaches. It means roughly 'it's fine' and functions as a soft no — to a bag at the till, to another drink, to an offer of help you do not need. Kekkou desu is the firmer version.

Wakarimasen — I don't understand. Nihongo ga wakarimasen — I don't understand Japanese. Eigo ga hanaseru hito wa imasu ka — is there someone who speaks English. That last one is more useful than asking an individual whether they speak English, because it lets them fetch a colleague rather than decline.
And the one to know and hopefully not use: tasukete kudasai, please help. For anything official, koban means a police box, and there is one near every major station.

sections.heading: Pronunciation
paragraphs: Japanese vowels are consistent: A is 'ah', I is 'ee', U is 'oo', E is 'eh', O is 'oh'. They do not shift the way English vowels do. Arigatou is ah-ree-gah-toh, not ah-rig-uh-toe. Getting the vowels right matters more than anything else and takes five minutes of practice.

Two more adjustments. Japanese is flat in stress — English speakers instinctively stress a syllable and it is the main thing that makes a simple word unrecognisable. And the u at the end of words is often barely voiced: desu is closer to 'dess', and gozaimasu ends 'mahss'.
Japanese people will meet you much more than halfway as long as the vowels are approximately correct. Speaking slowly and evenly beats speaking accurately and fast.

sections.heading: The mistakes worth avoiding
paragraphs: Sayonara is not 'bye'. It carries a sense of parting for a long time, and using it when leaving a shop is odd. Use arigatou gozaimasu, or shitsurei shimasu when leaving somewhere formal.

Do not attach -san to your own name; it is a title you give other people. Do not use anata for 'you' — it reads as distant or intimate depending on context and neither is what you want; use the person's surname plus -san. And you do not need watashi wa at the start of every sentence, because Japanese drops the subject when it is obvious.
Konnichiwa is daytime only. Ohayou gozaimasu in the morning, konbanwa in the evening. Getting this wrong is harmless and mildly funny, which is a reasonable description of most beginner errors here.

sections.heading: The characters worth recognising
paragraphs: You do not need to read Japanese, but eight or ten characters will save you real time. 入口 is entrance and 出口 is exit. 押 is push and 引 is pull, on every door. 男 is men and 女 is women, on every lavatory and every onsen curtain, and confusing those two is the one error with genuine consequences.
営業中 means open for business and 準備中 means preparing, which is the sign on a restaurant that will open in an hour. 無料 is free of charge. 円 is yen. 予約 is a reservation. 禁煙 is no smoking.
On a menu, 大 is large and 小 is small, and 定食 means a set meal with rice and soup — which is usually the thing to order.

sections.heading: Translation apps, and where they fail
paragraphs: The camera translation in Google Translate handles printed menus and signs well enough to be genuinely useful, and downloading the Japanese pack before you arrive means it works without a connection. Conversation mode works for simple exchanges if you hand the phone over rather than pointing it at someone.

Where it fails is handwriting, which is most of the menus in the restaurants worth eating in, and the compressed shorthand used on signs. It also renders dish names into nonsense with confidence — a machine translation promising 'burnt bird' is yakitori.
The best use of a phone is not translation but display: a photograph of the dish, a map pin, the destination written in Japanese, the item you want. Showing beats saying, nearly every time.

title: The Tokyo Subway: How to Navigate It Without Getting Lost
excerpt: Tokyo’s train network is the most complex urban rail system in the world. It is also, once you understand the basics, extremely easy to use.
heroImageAlt: The platform at Shinjuku Station during morning rush hour with commuters boarding a train
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: It is not two networks, it is about a dozen
paragraphs: The Tokyo Metro has thirteen lines and the Toei Subway has four, and between them they are what most people mean by the subway. But JR East runs the surface network on top of it, and half a dozen private railways — Tokyu, Odakyu, Keio, Seibu, Tobu, Keikyu, Keisei — run the lines out to the suburbs.

They are separate companies with separate fares, and transferring between them costs more than staying on one. An IC card handles all of this invisibly, which is the main practical reason to have one.

The complication that catches people is through-service: a Tokyo Metro train frequently continues past the end of its own line onto a private railway and keeps going under a different name. You have not made a mistake and you do not need to change; but you may have left the network your ticket covers, which is another reason for the card.

sections.heading: The Yamanote Line is your backbone
paragraphs: The Yamanote is not a subway — it is a JR surface loop around central Tokyo connecting Shinjuku, Shibuya, Harajuku, Ebisu, Shinagawa, Tokyo, Akihabara, Ueno, Nippori and Ikebukuro, and back around. A full circuit takes about an hour and trains run every few minutes.
Think of it as the outer ring. To move between major neighbourhoods you generally go out to the loop, round it, and back in. Almost everything a visitor wants is inside it or on it.

Two lines cut across the middle and are worth knowing for that reason: the Chuo, which runs straight through from Tokyo to Shinjuku and out west, and the Ginza and Hanzomon metro lines, which cross the centre diagonally.

sections.heading: The numbering system means you never read kanji
paragraphs: Every line has a letter and a colour, and every station on it has a number: Ginza on the Ginza Line is G09, Shibuya on the same line is G01. The codes are printed on every platform sign, every map and every carriage display.
This means you can navigate entirely on letters and numbers. If you need to get from G09 to G01, you are on the right line and going the right way if the numbers are counting down.

Inside the carriages, digital displays cycle through the next stations in Japanese, English, Chinese and Korean, and show which side the doors will open and where the transfers are. Free multilingual maps are at every station office.

sections.heading: Exits are the actual difficulty
paragraphs: The trains are the easy part. The stations are where visitors lose time. Shinjuku has upwards of two hundred exits and Shibuya, Tokyo and Ikebukuro are not far behind, and coming out of the wrong one can leave you fifteen minutes and one large building away from where you meant to be.
Exits are numbered and lettered, and Google Maps will tell you which one you want. Note it before you go underground, because there is often no signal down there.

Follow the yellow signs for exits and the coloured line symbols for transfers. Transfers within a station can be genuine ten-minute walks, and the journey planner accounts for that; if it says the change takes eight minutes, it means eight minutes of walking.

sections.heading: IC card, and the passes that are not worth it
paragraphs: Buy an IC card at any ticket machine and load ¥2,000–3,000. Tap in, tap out, the fare is deducted, and you never calculate anything. A paper ticket requires selecting the correct fare from a map that is sometimes only in Japanese, and there is no situation where it is preferable.

Day passes exist — Tokyo Metro sells 24, 48 and 72-hour tourist tickets, and there is a combined Metro and Toei version. They only pay off if you are making a lot of separate journeys, since a typical fare is ¥180–320. Four or five rides a day is roughly the break-even.
For most itineraries the card is simpler and cheaper. Passes are worth it on a day of deliberate criss-crossing, and not much else.

sections.heading: Google Maps is the right tool
paragraphs: Transit directions for Tokyo are accurate and reliable: the correct line, the platform, the number of stops, the transfer, the fare and often the specific carriage to board for the fastest exit.
The specialist Japanese apps are more detailed for Shinkansen and long-distance planning and add nothing for basic subway navigation.
One habit worth adopting: screenshot the route before you go underground. Coverage in stations is generally good and it fails at the worst moments.

sections.heading: Rush hour and the last train
paragraphs: Peak crowding, roughly half seven to nine in the morning, is real. If you are carrying luggage, avoid it entirely; a suitcase in a rush-hour carriage is difficult for everyone including you. Coin lockers at major stations solve this, and they take IC cards.
Many lines run women-only carriages during the morning peak, marked in pink on the platform. Men wandering into one is a common visitor error.

Trains stop around midnight and do not run again until about five. This is not London or New York with a reduced overnight service — they simply stop. Taxis are expensive and scarce at that hour on a Friday. Check your last train before you settle in somewhere, and note that the last train on your line may be considerably earlier than the last train out of Shibuya.

title: What You Can and Cannot Photograph in Japan
excerpt: Japan is exceptionally photogenic. It also has specific places and situations where photography is restricted, disrespectful, or now actively prohibited. Knowing the difference matters.
heroImageAlt: A photographer framing a traditional Japanese street scene at dawn with no other people visible
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The general principle
paragraphs: In most outdoor public spaces in Japan, photography is unrestricted. Streets, parks, temple grounds, shrine pathways, market areas, train stations — all are freely photographable. The restrictions apply inside specific buildings, in areas where signage prohibits it, and in situations where the photography causes problems for other people or for the place itself. Read the signs, watch what other people are doing, and when in doubt, ask.

The prohibition sign is consistent and easy to learn: a camera icon inside a red circle with a diagonal bar, usually beside the characters 撮影禁止 (satsuei kinshi, photography forbidden). A second common sign shows a camera with a lightning bolt crossed out, which restricts flash only and leaves ordinary photography fine.
The most reliable instrument is the room itself. If nobody else has a phone out, there is a reason, and it is generally a better guide than any sign you did or did not spot on the way in.

sections.heading: Inside temples and shrines
paragraphs: Interior photography inside the main hall of a temple or shrine is usually prohibited. The sign will typically show a camera with a red line through it. Some places allow photography inside with a fee; some famous main halls are not accessible at all. Gardens attached to temples are generally freely photographable. Detailed garden photography is expected — it's one of the primary reasons people visit.

There are reasons behind the rule beyond crowd control. Many interiors hold designated cultural properties whose pigments and gold leaf are genuinely damaged by repeated flash. Others contain objects that are religious rather than exhibited — a statue in a working temple is an object of worship, not a display item, and photographing it is closer to photographing a person praying than photographing a museum piece.

Watch for funerals and memorial services, which happen in working temples constantly and are not always obvious to a visitor. Black formal clothing and a gathering near a side hall is your signal to put the camera away entirely.

sections.heading: At onsen and public baths
paragraphs: Photography is prohibited at onsen and sento (public baths), including in the changing rooms. This is absolute and enforced. Phones are not permitted in the bathing areas of most facilities, and taking your phone into a bathing area is both a rule violation and a privacy invasion of every other person present. Leave the phone in the locker.

This is one of the few photography rules in Japan with real legal weight behind it rather than social pressure. Prefectural nuisance ordinances cover surreptitious photography, and an onsen changing room is exactly the situation they exist for. Staff will remove you, and depending on circumstances they will call the police.
The exception people ask about is a private open-air bath attached to a room in a ryokan, where you are the only person present. That is your own space and there is nobody to photograph but yourself.

sections.heading: Photographing strangers
paragraphs: Japan doesn't have a specific law against street photography, but the social norms around photographing strangers are similar to those in most countries: pointing a camera directly at someone's face without consent, following someone for a photograph, or photographing children without parental consent all cross reasonable lines. Most Japanese people will not object verbally, but this reflects a cultural reluctance to confront rather than permission.

There is a recognised legal concept — shozoken, the right to one's own likeness — developed through court decisions rather than a single statute. In practice it is rarely invoked against tourists, but it means that publishing a recognisable photograph of someone who did not consent is not automatically safe just because you took it in the street.

The usable rule: a person incidental to a scene is fine, a person who is the subject of the scene needs consent. If you would feel obliged to explain yourself were they to notice, ask first. 'Shashin, ii desu ka?' — is a photo all right? — is enough, and the answer is yes more often than you would expect.

sections.heading: In Gion, Kyoto
paragraphs: Gion and the surrounding geisha districts of Kyoto are a specific and documented problem. Years of tourists surrounding and following maiko and geiko for photographs has led to complaints from residents, businesses, and the performers themselves. Some streets now carry photography restriction signs, and the private lanes off Hanamikoji have been closed to tourists altogether, with fines attached.

Note the distinction the signs are making: the public streets remain open, the private alleys are private property. The alleys are where people live, and the complaints that closed them were about tourists blocking doorways and pulling at sleeves, not about photography in the abstract.

More simply: if you see a maiko walking quickly with her head down, she is late for an appointment in a costume that costs more than a car and takes hours to put on. She is not a photo opportunity. She is a person doing her job. If you want the photograph, book a formal appointment — several teahouses and studios arrange them, and everyone involved has agreed to be there.

sections.heading: On trains
paragraphs: Photography on trains is not explicitly prohibited but is not commonly practiced for good reason: photographing other passengers without consent in an enclosed space they cannot leave is uncomfortable regardless of country. Photographing the view from the window is universally fine. Photographing your own group is fine. Pointing a camera at strangers in a carriage is not.

Platforms are a different matter and photographing trains is a substantial hobby in Japan, with its own etiquette. Stay behind the yellow tactile line, never use flash toward a cab, and do not set up where you block the flow of people. Station staff will move you promptly if you do.

sections.heading: Shops, restaurants and museums
paragraphs: Retail is the restriction visitors trip over most, because it is the least expected. A great many shops prohibit photography of their goods and displays, particularly department stores, confectioners, bookshops and anywhere selling designs that can be copied. There is often a small sign, and often there is not.

Restaurants vary. Photographing your own food is normal and nobody minds. Photographing the interior, the staff, or an open kitchen requires asking. Sushi counters and small chef-run places are the sensitive case: the chef is working a metre away, and a phone raised toward them without a word is intrusive in a way it is not at a chain restaurant.

Museums usually permit photography in permanent collections without flash and forbid it in special exhibitions, where the works are on loan under conditions the museum does not control. The signage for this is normally at the entrance to each room rather than the building.

sections.heading: The shutter sound you cannot switch off
paragraphs: Phones sold in Japan make an audible shutter noise that cannot be silenced, even on mute. This is not a legal requirement but an industry convention adopted decades ago in response to surreptitious photography, and every domestic manufacturer follows it.

A foreign phone on roaming will normally stay silent, which produces an odd asymmetry: you can take a quieter photograph than any local can. Treat that as a reason for more care rather than less. The noise exists so people know when they are being photographed, and its absence does not change what they are entitled to expect.

sections.heading: Drones and tripods
paragraphs: Drones are heavily restricted. Flying is prohibited over densely populated areas — which covers essentially all of Tokyo and Osaka — near airports, and in most national parks, and requires registration and permission that is not realistically obtainable for a short visit. Assume you cannot fly, and confirm the exception rather than the rule. Penalties are substantial.

Tripods are banned far more widely than people expect: most temple gardens, most museums, many station concourses, and effectively every crowded viewpoint during cherry blossom and autumn foliage season. The reasoning is congestion rather than image rights. A compact travel tripod used somewhere empty is rarely an issue; the same tripod at Kiyomizu-dera in November will get you moved on.

title: Your First Ryokan: What to Expect, What to Do, and What Not to Wear
excerpt: A traditional Japanese inn is not a hotel. The sooner you accept that, the better the stay.
heroImageAlt: A traditional ryokan room with tatami floor, low table, and garden view
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What you are actually booking
paragraphs: A ryokan is not a hotel with tatami. It is a package: a room, a bath, dinner and breakfast, staffed by people whose job is to move you through an evening in a particular order. The price is quoted per person including both meals, not per room, which is the first thing that confuses visitors comparing it against hotel rates.

There is a hierarchy of names worth knowing. A ryokan is the full version. A minshuku is the family-run, simpler equivalent — think bed-and-breakfast, shared bathroom, home cooking, considerably cheaper. An onsen hotel is a large modern building with hot springs and buffet meals, which is what a lot of Japanese families actually book and is a different, less formal experience.
Cancellation policies are strict, because the kitchen buys for you specifically. Expect meaningful charges from a week out and full charge within a day or two.

sections.heading: Check-in, checkout, and why timing matters
paragraphs: Check-in is usually 3pm and checkout is 10am. These are not suggestions. Your room is being transformed twice a day — futon laid out during dinner, rolled away before breakfast — and that choreography is coordinated with the bath and meal schedule.

Arriving at 6pm and expecting the room to be ready the way a hotel room is always ready will produce confusion on both sides, and if dinner is set for 6:30 it will produce a genuine problem. Tell them your arrival time when you book, and call if you are running late.

The early checkout catches people too. Breakfast at 7:30 and out by 10 is a short morning, and it is deliberate — the staff need the room. Plan the following day accordingly rather than expecting a slow start.

sections.heading: Shoes, slippers, and one rule about the toilet
paragraphs: You remove your shoes at the entrance and switch into slippers. The slippers go everywhere except tatami rooms — on tatami you go barefoot or in socks, never in slippers.

There will be a separate pair of toilet slippers in the bathroom. Put them on to enter, take them off to leave. Forgetting and wandering the hallway in toilet slippers is the ryokan equivalent of walking through a dinner party in a life jacket, and it happens to almost everyone once.
Your shoes will be put away for you and produced again when you leave. This is normal and you do not need to keep track of them.

sections.heading: Your room, and the yukata
paragraphs: Your room will have a low table, zabuton cushions, a tokonoma alcove with a seasonal arrangement, a yukata folded somewhere, and a kettle with tea and a small sweet. There will be no bed visible, because it is in the cupboard.

The yukata is your uniform. Wear it to the bath, to dinner if the place is traditional, back to your room, and to bed. It is a cotton robe, not a costume, and in an onsen town it is also correct outdoor wear for walking to the other bathhouses. Left side over right — right over left is how the dead are dressed.

There is usually a heavier jacket called a tanzen to go over it in winter, and wooden geta at the entrance. Amenities are comprehensive: toothbrush, razor, towels, often skincare. You need to bring very little.

sections.heading: The onsen
paragraphs: The bath operates on a schedule — typically gender-segregated, sometimes with the men's and women's baths swapping over during the night so that everyone gets both. The rules: wash thoroughly at the seated shower station before entering the communal water, and enter clean.

Do not put the towel in the bath. The small hand towel goes on your head or on the side. Do not swim, do not splash, keep long hair tied up, and do not get in if you have been drinking heavily — people faint, and it is a problem for everyone.

Two things worth checking before you book. Tattoos are still refused at a proportion of traditional baths, though this is easing; ryokan with private baths attached to rooms, or with bookable family baths, sidestep the issue entirely. And if the water is a strong sulphur spring it will tarnish silver jewellery, so leave it in the room.

sections.heading: Kaiseki dinner
paragraphs: Dinner is kaiseki — a multi-course meal built around seasonal and local ingredients, arriving in a sequence you do not choose and cannot rush. It takes ninety minutes to two hours, the plates are small, and you will briefly feel you are not getting enough food. You are getting enough food.

Do not ask for the menu in advance and do not request variations casually. But do declare genuine allergies and dietary restrictions at the time of booking, not on arrival — the kitchen plans and shops for each guest, and a vegetarian request made at 6pm cannot be accommodated. Made three weeks earlier, it usually can.

It is often served in your room by an attendant, which is part of what you are paying for. In larger ryokan it is in a dining room at a set time. Either way the time is fixed when you check in, and being late is a real inconvenience to a kitchen cooking to the minute.

sections.heading: Breakfast, and the evening in between
paragraphs: Breakfast follows the same logic: rice, miso soup, pickled vegetables, grilled fish, tofu, a small egg dish, arriving at a fixed time between roughly 7:30 and 9. It is also among the best breakfasts in the world.

The evening between dinner and sleep is the part first-timers underuse. In an onsen town, this is when you put on the yukata and geta and walk — to the other bathhouses, to a bar, to a shrine, clattering along in wooden sandals with everyone else doing the same. In an isolated mountain ryokan it is a second bath and a book.

There is no tipping in Japan and a ryokan is no exception. There is an old custom of kokorozuke, a small amount in an envelope to the room attendant, which is optional, increasingly rare, and never expected of a foreign guest. Do not leave cash on a tray.

sections.heading: What it costs
paragraphs: Prices run from around ¥8,000 per person at a decent mid-range place with a bath and breakfast, to ¥80,000 and well beyond at the top with full kaiseki and a private open-air bath.

The sweet spot is ¥15,000–25,000 per person, particularly in onsen towns without the premium attached to Hakone or Kyoto — Kinosaki in Hyogo, Gero in Gifu, and a long list of places in Tohoku that are genuinely excellent and cost half what the famous names do.

Winter is materially cheaper than autumn for the same room, and midweek cheaper than weekends by a wide margin. One night is enough to understand it; two nights in the same ryokan is when it becomes restful rather than novel.

sections.heading: On language
paragraphs: The staff may not speak much English, and that is genuinely fine. The experience requires very little language to work, because the sequence is fixed and everyone knows what happens next.

Arigatou gozaimasu and oishii will handle most of it. The rest comes from gestures, patience, and the fact that people who run a ryokan have been doing this for decades and know how to communicate without words. If anything, the places with no English are the ones worth seeking out.

title: Why January Is the Best Month to Visit Japan (Yes, Really)
excerpt: No cherry blossoms. No 38-degree humidity. No crowds. January is when Japan stops performing for tourists and just exists.
heroImageAlt: Snow-dusted temple grounds in Kyoto in winter
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why even consider January
paragraphs: Summer in Japan is spectacular and exhausting. Cherry blossom season is magical and so crowded that the famous spots feel like theme parks. Autumn foliage is genuinely among the most beautiful things in the natural world and is also, by November, completely overrun. January has none of these problems, because January has a reputation for cold and grey that is only partly deserved.

The reputation comes from the wrong side of the country. Japan's winter splits down the middle: the Sea of Japan coast gets enormous snowfall, and the Pacific side — where Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka are — gets cold, dry, sunny weather. Both are winter. Only one of them is what people picture.

sections.heading: The actual weather
paragraphs: Tokyo in January sits between about 4°C and 10°C during the day, with clear skies more often than you would expect, occasional rain and rare snow. It is not harsh. A good coat and a scarf are enough, and the sunshine hours are among the highest of any month.

Kyoto is a couple of degrees colder and gets occasional snow, which on temple grounds with grey stone and winter moss looks exactly like the photograph you have seen your whole life, except there are almost no other people in it. When Kinkaku-ji has snow on the roof, half of Japan tries to get there — but it lasts a day or two a year and the rest of January is simply quiet.

The genuine trade-offs: daylight is short, with dark falling around five, and some mountain roads and high routes are closed for the season. Dress for indoors as well as out, because trains, shops and restaurants are heated hard and you will be removing layers constantly.

sections.heading: Where the crowds went
paragraphs: The tourist surge disappears after New Year, when domestic travellers return home and the holiday-season international visitors leave. From around January 5th onwards you can visit the famous temples at human scale — the Arashiyama bamboo grove with nobody in your frame is not an exaggeration, it is a cold Tuesday.

The effect on the practical side of a trip is just as large. Restaurants with long waiting lists have tables. The ryokan in Hakone with no rooms in November has rooms, often at a meaningfully lower rate. Flights and hotels both cost less than in October or April.
It is the one month where you can plan a Japan trip loosely and have it work.

sections.heading: New Year, and the first week
paragraphs: The rituals of New Year give early January a purposefulness that ordinary months do not have. Hatsumode, the first shrine visit of the year, fills the major shrines from the 1st to the 3rd and keeps them festive through the first week. Senso-ji in Asakusa at six in the morning on January 2nd is one of the better crowds in the world to be part of.

The complication is closure. A great many restaurants, small shops and museums shut from around December 29 to January 3, and in smaller towns the shutdown is close to total. Convenience stores, department stores and chain restaurants stay open, and the shrine visit is worth doing, but this is not the week for a food-led itinerary.
If you can choose, arrive on about January 4th. You get the tail of the festivity and none of the closures.

sections.heading: Onsen towns are the point
paragraphs: Onsen towns are at their best in winter and this is not a small thing. The specific pleasure of sitting in an outdoor rotenburo with snow falling and steam rising is not available in July. The baths feel hotter, the air is colder, and the meal afterwards is twice as satisfying.

Hakone from Tokyo, Kinosaki from Kyoto, Beppu and Yufuin in Kyushu, Nyuto in Akita for the properly remote version. Kinosaki is the one to know: seven public bathhouses in a small canal town, and the local custom is to walk between them in the yukata and wooden geta your inn provides, which is an entire evening's entertainment.
Book the ryokan first and build the trip around it. This is the month when that is affordable.

sections.heading: Snow country
paragraphs: The Sea of Japan side gets some of the heaviest snowfall of any inhabited place on earth, and it is worth going to see. Shirakawa-go's thatched farmhouses under two metres of snow, lit for a handful of evenings each winter, is the image; the village is reachable by bus from Takayama or Kanazawa and the illumination nights are ticketed and book out months ahead.

The Ginzan Onsen street in Yamagata, gas-lit with snow on the wooden inn facades, is the other one people travel for. Both are extremely popular for a small number of days and empty either side of them.

For skiing, Hokkaido has some of the best powder in the world — Niseko, Furano, Rusutsu — and January is peak season. Hakuba and the Nagano resorts are closer to Tokyo and nearly as good. If skiing is relevant to your trip at all, this is not a consolation prize, it is the main event.

sections.heading: Winter food
paragraphs: Japanese cooking is more seasonal than most, and winter is when the best of it happens. Nabe — a communal hotpot cooked at the table — is the centre of it, in a dozen regional forms. Oden, the simmered pot of daikon, egg and fishcake sold everywhere including convenience stores, is a winter food and tastes like it.

This is also crab season on the Sea of Japan coast, and the entire Hokuriku region reorganises around it from November. A crab kaiseki at a ryokan in Kanazawa or the Tango peninsula is expensive and is one of the great meals available in Japan.

Smaller pleasures: hot canned coffee from a vending machine on a freezing platform, roasted sweet potato sold from a truck, amazake at a shrine, and the fact that every convenience store has a heated cabinet by the till from November.

sections.heading: What winter reveals
paragraphs: What Japan offers in winter that it cannot offer in spring or autumn is something closer to daily life. When a place is over-visited it optimises for visitors; when it is not being watched, it relaxes. January Japan is commuters and schoolchildren and the ramen shop that opens at half past six for the early shift.

February keeps most of the advantages and adds the Sapporo Snow Festival in the first week and, towards the end of the month, the plum blossom — which flowers on bare branches in the cold, gets a fraction of the attention cherry blossom does, and is arguably the more beautiful of the two.
That Japan is worth seeing, and it is more accessible than people think.

title: The Convenience Store Is Japan's Greatest Culinary Achievement
excerpt: Seven-Eleven in Japan is not Seven-Eleven anywhere else. This distinction matters and deserves your full attention.
heroImageAlt: Onigiri and sandwiches at a Japanese convenience store counter
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: This is not convenience store food
paragraphs: The first thing to understand about konbini is that the food is genuinely good. Not good for a convenience store. Just good. The onigiri is made fresh and delivered several times a day. The sandwiches are produced to specifications refined over decades. The hot food meets a standard most fast-casual restaurants elsewhere do not.

The reason is competition and turnover. Three national chains fight over the same corners, products are dropped if they underperform for a few weeks, and stores take deliveries around the clock, so almost nothing sits. The result is a supply chain that behaves like a restaurant kitchen operating at national scale.

sections.heading: The three chains are not the same
paragraphs: 7-Eleven is generally reckoned the strongest on food overall, and its egg sandwich and onigiri are the ones people write about. Its ATMs are also the most reliable for foreign cards.

Lawson runs a premium bakery line and the Natural Lawson variant aimed at healthier eating, and its fried chicken is a genuine rival to the others. Family Mart's fried chicken has been the subject of national argument, and its own-brand clothing — plain socks and t-shirts in a distinctive colourway — became an unexpected fashion item.
The differences are small and real, and the practical advice is to try the same category at all three in the first week and pick a side. Everyone in Japan has one.

sections.heading: What to eat
paragraphs: Onigiri: rice with a filling — tuna mayonnaise, pickled plum, salmon, kombu — wrapped in a three-panel system that keeps the seaweed crisp until you open it. The opening sequence is printed on the wrapper with numbered arrows. Follow them. Attempting it another way produces rice everywhere and no dignified explanation.

The egg salad sandwich has developed a following that crosses borders: thick-cut egg, slightly sweet, in the particular soft white bread that Japan does and nowhere else quite manages. Buy one on the first morning and the question of why people travel here for food starts to answer itself.

Hot food lives by the register. Oden in winter — a simmering pot of daikon, fishcake, egg and tofu, chosen with tongs and counted onto your bill. Steamed buns in the heated case. Fried chicken on a stick. In summer the same case sells cold noodles instead.

Also reliable: the pasta and bento in the chilled cabinet, the sweets — the chains take dessert seriously and the seasonal ones are genuinely good — and the fruit sandwiches, which sound wrong and are not.

sections.heading: Drinks
paragraphs: Canned coffee is a category of human achievement. Around ¥130 a can, cold or hot depending on the season, developed through research cycles most car companies would find excessive. The hot can on a November morning is one of those sensory memories travel writers try to describe and never manage.

The tea wall is the other thing to understand: unsweetened green tea, barley tea and oolong in every size, which is why nobody here carries a water bottle. If you want something sweet you have to look for it.

Alcohol is sold in every store, cold, at any hour the licence allows — beer, chuhai in a hundred fruit flavours, small bottles of sake and whisky. Drinking in public is legal, which makes the konbini beer on a park bench an entirely normal evening.

sections.heading: The services are the real point
paragraphs: Konbini are infrastructure. The 7-Bank ATMs take foreign cards, run around the clock and have English menus, and they are the single best place to withdraw cash in Japan.

The multifunction copier does more than it looks: it prints documents from a USB stick or your phone, scans, and sells tickets to concerts, football and some attractions. The counter ships luggage nationwide through the courier services, sells stamps, takes parcel returns and pays utility bills.

They also sell almost anything you have forgotten — chargers, umbrellas, shirts, ties, underwear, phone cables, plasters, batteries. At eleven at night this is the thing you will be most grateful for.
Larger branches offer tax-free above the usual threshold, and most have a lavatory that they will let you use without buying anything.

sections.heading: How to actually order
paragraphs: Budget ¥500–800 for a full meal. Pay at the register, where two questions will be asked. 'Atatamemasu ka' — shall I warm this up — and yes is nearly always the answer for anything from the chilled cabinet. And whether you want a bag, which now costs a few yen; 'fukuro wa irimasen' declines it.
Chopsticks, spoons and straws are handed over as needed and you will be asked how many. Wet wipes come with hot food.

Do not eat inside the store. There is usually a small counter with stools, or a space outside, and if there is not, eat by the entrance rather than walking away with it. The bins by the door are for things bought there, and they are one of the few public bins in the country.

sections.heading: The seasonal calendar
paragraphs: The shelves change with the year in a way that is worth noticing. Sakura-flavoured everything in March. Cold noodles and shaved ice in July and August. Chestnut and sweet potato from September. Oden and steamed buns from November. Christmas cake and fried chicken in late December, then New Year osechi boxes ordered in advance.
Regional exclusives exist and are worth checking wherever you are — chains stock local flavours that do not travel, and it is the cheapest way to eat something specific to a prefecture.
Limited-edition items are genuinely limited, often a few weeks. If you like something, buy it again the next day rather than assuming it will be there at the end of the trip.

title: Tokyo's Kissaten: The Coffee Shops That Refuse to Change
excerpt: Somewhere between the third-wave cafés and the chain stores, Tokyo's old coffee shops have been quietly waiting.
heroImageAlt: A dimly lit kissaten coffee shop interior with wooden counters and vintage cups
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What kissaten means
paragraphs: The word has no clean English translation. A coffee shop, technically — but that misses it. A kissaten is a room where time moves differently: the owner has been making the same blend since 1978, the cups are heavier than they need to be, nobody is on a laptop, and the ashtrays are still on the tables even if nobody uses them any more.

The legal distinction is a piece of trivia that explains a lot: a kissaten licence historically permitted the sale of coffee and light food but not alcohol, which is why these places serve toast and pudding rather than wine, and why they have a completely different atmosphere from a bar.
They emerged in the post-war decades as public living rooms, in a city where flats were small and there was nowhere else to sit down. That function is still what they are for.

sections.heading: Why they are invisible to visitors
paragraphs: Tokyo has thousands. Most are invisible because they do not appear on social media, rarely have English menus, and are frequently up a staircase or down into a basement with almost no signage.
This is not an accident. Kissaten are not trying to attract new customers. They already have their customers, and those customers have been coming in for decades.
The threshold feels forbidding and is not. Push the door, say nothing in particular, and sit down. Nobody will be surprised to see you.

sections.heading: The specialised kinds
paragraphs: Several subgenres are worth knowing because they are entire subcultures with a coffee shop attached. A jazz kissa is a listening bar built around a record collection and a very expensive pair of speakers, where conversation is discouraged and the volume is high — you go to listen, not to talk. Some have been running since the 1950s.

A meikyoku kissa does the same with classical music, often with requests written on slips of paper. A manga kissa is the modern descendant and a different animal entirely: a warren of booths with thousands of comic volumes, free drinks and overnight rates, used as much for cheap accommodation as for reading.
If you like records, the jazz kissa is one of the genuinely unrepeatable Tokyo experiences. The rule is simple: order, sit, do not talk over the music, and do not photograph the room.

sections.heading: Where to find them
paragraphs: The ones worth finding are in older neighbourhoods — Koenji, Shimokitazawa, Yanaka, Jimbocho, the parts of Shinjuku that have not been redeveloped. They cluster around stations that are not on the tourist circuit.
