The strategy is to walk until you see a menu in the window that was laminated in approximately 1990, or a display case of plastic parfaits that have faded in the sun. Both are reliable signals.

Nagoya and Osaka have their own strong traditions, and Nagoya in particular is where the free breakfast-with-coffee custom comes from. If your trip goes through either, the kissaten there are as good as Tokyo's and cheaper.

sections.heading: What you are drinking
paragraphs: Blend coffee: filter or drip made with a proprietary blend the owner has been refining for decades. This is not specialty coffee in the third-wave sense. It is not trying to taste of blueberries. It tastes of coffee, deeply and darkly, without fuss, and it is served black with a small jug of cream beside it.

The brewing method is often visible and is part of the appeal — a glass siphon over a spirit burner, or nel drip, where the coffee is filtered through a cloth sock the owner has been seasoning for years. Both are slow, which is the point.

The other things on the menu are a fixed cast: cream soda in improbable green, a firm custard pudding with dark caramel, napolitan spaghetti in ketchup, and a very thick slice of toast. None of it is fashionable and all of it is exactly what it should be.

sections.heading: The morning set
paragraphs: Food at a kissaten tends to be one of two things: a morning set or toast. The morning set, usually available until eleven, is coffee plus a thick slice of buttered toast, sometimes a boiled egg, sometimes a small salad, for a few hundred yen — and in the Nagoya tradition the food is thrown in free with the coffee.
It is one of the great underrated breakfasts in the world and it appears on no list of Tokyo's best breakfasts.
Expect to pay ¥500–900 for a coffee, which is more than a chain and buys you the table for as long as you want it. That is the actual transaction.

sections.heading: How to sit properly
paragraphs: You do not order at a counter. Sit down, wait for the owner to come to you, order quietly. Then wait. The coffee takes longer to arrive than you expect and you will feel briefly uncomfortable with the silence. That feeling passes, and its passing is the point.

Do not photograph the room without asking, do not take a call, and do not spread out a laptop and work — several places have signs asking you not to. One person, one seat, one drink, one book is the format.
Smoking is still permitted in some of them, which is part of the atmosphere and worth knowing if it matters to you.

sections.heading: What they represent
paragraphs: A few worth knowing in Tokyo: Café de l'Ambre in Ginza, roasting since 1948 and specialising in aged beans; Chatei Hatou in Shibuya, precise and serious; Kayaba Coffee in Yanaka, in a building from 1938. Do not try to do all of them. Pick one, sit down properly, stay an hour.

The number of kissaten has been falling for decades as owners retire and nobody takes the shop on, and each closure takes a room that cannot be rebuilt. Going to one is not nostalgia tourism; it is the only way they continue.

What they represent is a way of organising time that has largely been optimised away. Nobody is tracking you, nobody cares about table turnover, you ordered a coffee and you are welcome to stay all morning. That this feels unusual is its own commentary.

title: Kanazawa: The City Most Japan Itineraries Skip — and Shouldn't
excerpt: Three hours from Tokyo by bullet train. A fraction of Kyoto's crowds. Arguably better seafood. There is no good reason it's on so few itineraries.
heroImageAlt: Higashi Chaya geisha district in Kanazawa, wooden ochaya buildings lining a quiet street
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why Kanazawa is overlooked
paragraphs: Kanazawa is on the wrong side of Japan. That appears to be the only explanation for why it receives a fraction of Kyoto's visitors while having a castle, two preserved geisha districts, one of the country's three great landscape gardens, and what a lot of serious food people consider the best seafood market outside Tokyo.

It was never bombed in the war and never had a major earthquake, which is why the old districts are genuinely old rather than reconstructed. Under the Maeda clan it was the wealthiest domain in Japan after the shogunate itself, and the money went into crafts rather than fortification. The city is still living on that.

sections.heading: Getting there
paragraphs: The Hokuriku Shinkansen from Tokyo takes about two and a half hours. From Kyoto it is two and a half to three with a change, and from Osaka similar.

The obstacle is psychological rather than practical: most visitors arrive with a Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka triangle already built, and Kanazawa sits outside it. The natural way to absorb it is on the way between Tokyo and Kyoto rather than as a there-and-back detour, and the Hokuriku Arch Pass exists precisely for that routing.

The station itself is worth two minutes of attention: the enormous wooden Tsuzumi gate and glass dome out front regularly appear on lists of the world's most beautiful stations, which is a strange thing for a provincial city to have.

sections.heading: Kenroku-en and the castle
paragraphs: Kenroku-en is one of Japan's three great gardens, developed over two centuries by the Maeda and covering about eleven hectares. In cherry blossom season it is crowded. In late November, when the pines are wrapped in rope cones against the snow in a technique called yukizuri, it is extraordinary and very nearly empty.
It opens early — before the ticket office in some seasons, when entry is free for the first hour or so. That hour is the best time to be in it by a wide margin.

Across the road, Kanazawa Castle is a careful timber reconstruction using traditional joinery rather than the usual concrete, and the grounds are large and free to walk. Gyokusen'inmaru, the small restored garden inside them, is lit in the evenings and almost nobody goes.

sections.heading: The old districts
paragraphs: Higashi Chaya is the best-preserved geisha quarter, smaller and less managed than Gion, with wooden lattice fronts that have not changed structurally since the early nineteenth century. Some of the teahouses still operate. Two are open to visitors, including one with a gold-leaf tea room upstairs. Come early morning or at dusk and the street is effectively yours.
Kazue-machi, along the river below it, is the quieter second district and is arguably the better walk. Nishi Chaya on the other side of town is the third and sees almost nobody.

Nagamachi is the samurai quarter: earth walls, narrow lanes and water channels, with one restored residence open and a garden inside it. And Myoryu-ji — universally called the ninja temple, though it has nothing to do with ninja — is a defensive building full of hidden staircases, trapdoors and a concealed well. It can only be seen on a guided tour in Japanese, and it must be booked in advance.

sections.heading: The food
paragraphs: Kanazawa sits on the Sea of Japan and receives fish from waters that do not reach the Pacific side in the same condition. Omicho Market, a covered market the size of a small neighbourhood, has been running since the eighteenth century and is where the city actually shops.

In winter: crab, specifically the male snow crab, which arrives in November and is the reason a lot of Japanese people come here at all. In spring: firefly squid and sweet shrimp. Year round, a sashimi set from a mid-range place near the market will beat most of what you would eat in a Tokyo tourist district at half the price.

The local cuisine has its own name, Kaga ryori, and its signature dish is jibuni — duck dusted in flour and simmered with wheat gluten in a thickened broth. It is not what anyone expects from Japanese food and it is very good.

sections.heading: Crafts, and the modern half
paragraphs: Gold leaf has been made here since the Edo period and effectively all of Japan's supply still comes from Kanazawa workshops. You can beat your own sheet at several studios, and the city sells gold-leaf ice cream, which is ridiculous and photographs well and tastes exactly like ice cream.
Kutani porcelain, with its heavy overglaze colours, and Kaga yuzen silk dyeing are the other two traditions, and both have museums and working shops rather than only displays.

The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, a circular glass building by SANAA, is one of the better contemporary museums in Japan and draws a local crowd rather than only tourists. Leandro Erlich's swimming pool — which you can appear to stand at the bottom of — is the piece everyone comes for and is worth booking ahead.

sections.heading: Where to stay, and how long
paragraphs: The centre is small enough that almost anywhere is walkable, and the loop bus covers the rest. Katamachi is convenient and has the restaurant density; the area around the station is cheaper and duller.

Two nights minimum. The city rewards an unhurried second day in a way a single overnight cannot capture, and it is also the base for Shirakawa-go, the thatched village about ninety minutes away by bus.
Bring an umbrella regardless of the forecast. There is a local saying that you should not forget your lunch but you should never forget your umbrella, and the weather here justifies it.

sections.heading: What Kanazawa has that Kyoto lost
paragraphs: The feeling of visiting somewhere people actually live. The geisha quarter is not a theme park, the old town is genuinely old and genuinely in use, and the market is a market rather than a food court.
If that is what you are looking for — and increasingly it is what travellers say they want — Kanazawa is close to the correct answer.

title: Tsukiji Outer Market: Where to Actually Eat (and What to Skip)
excerpt: The inner market moved to Toyosu in 2018. The outer market never moved and never needed to.
heroImageAlt: Fresh seafood stalls at Tsukiji outer market at early morning
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What stayed and what moved
paragraphs: In 2018 the wholesale fish market at Tsukiji relocated to Toyosu, a reclaimed island further east, and travel writers immediately began writing elegies for Tsukiji. What they missed is that the part most visitors cared about — the outer market, several hundred shops selling seafood, street food, knives and tamagoyaki — never moved and shows no sign of moving.
What went to Toyosu was the business end: the auction floor, the wholesalers, the pre-dawn tuna trade. What stayed was the retail and restaurant street that grew up around it over eighty years.

If you want the auction, Toyosu has a viewing deck above the tuna floor, which requires being there before about half past five in the morning and watching through glass. It is interesting and it is not the same as walking through a market. Most people want the outer market, and the outer market is still here.

sections.heading: When to arrive
paragraphs: The outer market opens early. Most stalls are running by six, and the target window is between seven and ten, when the selection is widest and the food is freshest. By noon the best places have sold out of the things worth eating and many are closing.
Come for breakfast. This is the single piece of advice on this page that is not negotiable.

Check the day before you go. The market largely closes on Sundays and public holidays, and many shops also shut on Wednesdays — the schedule follows the old wholesale market's calendar and it is published online. Turning up on a closed day is the most common way to waste the trip.

sections.heading: Sushi first
paragraphs: Sushi from one of the small counters in the side streets off the main lane. Eight seats, a glass case in front, no ceremony. Point, sit, eat immediately. The fish came from Toyosu this morning.

A ¥1,500–3,000 set here will be among the best sushi you have eaten, and the gap between it and a ¥20,000 counter in Ginza is far narrower than the price gap. Some of these places have queues by eight; the ones down the narrower lanes usually do not.
The alternative is kaisendon — a bowl of rice under an arrangement of raw fish, roe and urchin — which is the market's other signature and is easier to eat standing up.

sections.heading: Tamagoyaki, ikura and uni
paragraphs: Tamagoyaki, the thick rolled sweet omelette, is a Tsukiji speciality and several stalls sell slices on wooden skewers for a couple of hundred yen. The outside is slightly caramelised, the inside is custard-soft, and you will want two.
Ikura — salmon roe — on rice, from any stall making it fresh. The roe should be bright and translucent, and the texture is unlike anything from a jar. A small bowl runs ¥500–1,000.

Uni, sea urchin, is the market's luxury item and the place to find out whether you like it, since it is served here fresh enough to taste sweet rather than metallic. Buy one tray from a stall with turnover rather than a cheap one that has been sitting.
Also worth stopping for: grilled scallops and oysters in season, dashi-maki, and the dried goods shops selling katsuobushi and kombu, which pack flat and make far better souvenirs than they sound.

sections.heading: What to skip, and how to behave
paragraphs: Skip the photogenic seafood-on-a-stick vendors near the main entrance that have been optimised for social media. The scallops are fine and the prices are for tourists, and the queue is people taking the same photograph. Walk past, turn into a side street, and find the stalls where nobody has a phone out.

Eating while walking is discouraged here specifically, and several shops have signs asking you not to. Most have a small standing counter or a designated area beside the stall — eat there, then move on.

This is a working market and the narrow lanes carry delivery carts and staff who are in a hurry. Do not stop in the middle of a lane to photograph, do not touch produce, and do not block a shopfront. Most stalls are cash only.

sections.heading: The knife shops
paragraphs: Tsukiji has one of the highest concentrations of professional knife dealers outside the forging towns, and it is a genuinely good place to buy. Prices run from a few thousand yen for a competent home santoku to well over ¥50,000 for a hand-forged single-bevel blade.

Buy in person, after handling several. Ask whether the blade is single or double bevel, what steel it is, and whether they will sharpen it before you leave. Most will engrave a name in Japanese characters at no charge, which takes a few minutes and turns it into a gift.
Pack it in checked luggage, never in hand baggage. This catches somebody at Haneda security every single day.

sections.heading: Getting there, and the alternatives
paragraphs: Subway to Tsukijishijo on the Oedo Line or Tsukiji on the Hibiya Line. Allow two hours, three if the knives are part of the plan.

While you are there, the Namiyoke Shrine at the market's edge has been the fish traders' shrine for three hundred years and has monuments donated by the sushi and egg trades. It takes five minutes and it explains the neighbourhood.

If you are travelling beyond Tokyo, the same morning is available elsewhere: Nishiki in Kyoto for prepared foods and pickles, Kuromon in Osaka for grilled seafood eaten standing, and Omicho in Kanazawa, which is the best of the three and the least visited.

title: How to Eat at an Izakaya Without Looking Completely Lost
excerpt: The curtain over the door. The laminated menu with pictures on maybe two pages. The small charge you didn't order. You'll be fine.
heroImageAlt: Inside a Tokyo izakaya with warm lighting, wooden tables and yakitori on the grill
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What an izakaya is
paragraphs: An izakaya is a Japanese pub — not a restaurant, not a bar, but what happens when the two are combined without either winning. You drink and eat in roughly equal measure, the food comes in small plates meant to be shared, and nobody orders a main course.
The lighting is low, the room is loud, and you will probably be sharing it with people who have loosened their ties, which is always a good sign.

There are three broad kinds. Chains, which are cheap, reliable, have picture menus and are a completely reasonable first visit. Independents, which are where the good food is. And tachinomi, standing bars, which are tiny, cheap, fast and the most fun of the three once you have the confidence.

sections.heading: Getting in and sitting down
paragraphs: Look for the noren, the short split curtain over the door — if it is hanging, the place is open, and it is taken in at closing. Push through it and someone will shout irasshaimase, which requires no reply.

You will be asked how many people. Holding up fingers works; 'futari desu' is two, 'sannin desu' is three. You may also be asked whether you want a table or the counter — the counter is better on your own or as a pair, and it is where you can see what other people are eating.
Popular independents fill up by seven and many do not take reservations for small groups. Going early, at half past five, is the reliable move and is when locals go anyway.

sections.heading: Otoshi: the charge you did not order
paragraphs: A small charge appears on the bill without explanation. It is called otoshi, it runs ¥200–600 a head, and in return a small dish arrives that you did not order — pickled vegetables, a little salad, sometimes something genuinely excellent.
It is a seating and cover charge, it is standard almost everywhere, it is not a scam, and it is not optional. Sending the dish back does not remove the charge.
Knowing this in advance removes the single most common moment of suspicion foreign visitors have about Japanese restaurants. The bill is correct.

sections.heading: The opening round
paragraphs: The convention is that everyone orders a drink first, together, and food follows. 'Toriaezu nama' — a draught beer for now — is close to a national catchphrase and is the correct thing to say while you look at the menu.

Then two or three small dishes to start. Edamame, karaage and potato salad are almost universally available and almost universally good. They are not exciting. They are correct. Order them while you work out the rest.
Order in waves rather than all at once. Dishes arrive as they are cooked, in no particular order, and a table that orders everything at the start gets everything at the start.

sections.heading: What to order after that
paragraphs: Yakitori, grilled chicken on skewers — order a mixed set, and specify tare for the sweet soy glaze or shio for salt. Dashimaki tamago, a rolled omelette made with stock, soft and savoury. Sashimi, if the place looks like it takes fish seriously, which you can usually tell from whether the locals at the counter are eating it.
Beyond that: agedashi tofu, grilled fish, motsuni for the adventurous, and whatever is on the handwritten paper stuck to the wall, which is the day's special and the best thing on offer.
'Osusume wa nan desu ka' — what do you recommend — solves any menu. Someone will point at something and whatever they point at will be good.

sections.heading: Shochu, chuhai and nomihodai
paragraphs: Shochu is probably what is in your cocktail. Distilled most often from sweet potato or barley, served over ice, with hot or cold water, or mixed with soda. It is gentler than whisky and goes with everything on the menu.
Chuhai is shochu with fruit soda — the izakaya equivalent of a spritz, and perfectly respectable. A highball is whisky and soda and is what a great many people drink all evening.

Nomihodai is all-you-can-drink for a fixed period, usually ninety or a hundred and twenty minutes, often bundled with a set food course. It is good value with a group and it is not a challenge; the time limit exists so the table turns over, and last orders are announced ten minutes before the end.

sections.heading: Paying and leaving
paragraphs: To get the bill, catch someone's eye and trace a rectangle in the air with your index fingers, or say 'o-kaikei onegaishimasu'. In many places you take the slip from your table to the register by the door and pay there rather than at the table.

Groups usually split evenly rather than itemising — this is warikan, and trying to calculate individual shares goes against the spirit of it. Cash is safest; plenty of independents still do not take cards.
There is no tipping. Say gochisousama deshita on the way out.

sections.heading: The golden rule
paragraphs: The more local and less translated the menu, the better the food. The izakaya in a residential neighbourhood near a station that is not on any tourist map will beat the one with an English sign near the temples every time.
Your hotel is on the tourist circuit. The izakaya should not be. Walk fifteen minutes in a direction with no sights in it and look for a lit noren and a bit of noise.
And if a small place is full and the owner waves you away, that is not rudeness — a six-seat counter with a queue cannot seat you, and there will be another one round the corner.

title: The IC Card Is the Best Thing in Japan. Here's How to Actually Use It.
excerpt: You can survive Tokyo's train network without one. You just won't want to.
heroImageAlt: Commuter tapping a Suica IC card at a Tokyo train station gate
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Get one before you leave the airport
paragraphs: Find a ticket machine and get an IC card. Do not deliberate, do not check whether you really need one. You need one.

It is a rechargeable transit card — the same basic idea as London's Oyster or Hong Kong's Octopus — except that in Japan it works on practically everything: trains, subways, buses, some ferries, taxis in major cities, convenience stores, vending machines, coin lockers, and the self-checkout at Don Quijote at two in the morning.

sections.heading: Which card, and does it matter
paragraphs: Suica is issued by JR East and covers Tokyo and eastern Japan; ICOCA is the JR West equivalent for Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe. There are ten major cards in total, including PASMO in Tokyo, TOICA, manaca, SUGOCA and others.

They are mutually interoperable for travel and shopping across almost the whole country, so the practical answer is to take whichever is sold where you land. A Suica works fine in Kyoto and an ICOCA works fine in Tokyo.

The exceptions are narrow but real: a handful of rural private railways and local buses take cash only, and refunds are only possible at the issuing company's offices — an ICOCA cannot be cashed in at a JR East window.

sections.heading: Getting hold of one
paragraphs: A physical card costs a ¥500 deposit on top of whatever you load. Availability of standard unregistered cards has been intermittent in recent years because of a semiconductor shortage, with sales suspended and then partially resumed, so check the current position rather than assuming.

The reliable fallback for visitors is the tourist version — Welcome Suica and its ICOCA equivalent — sold at airport counters and major stations, with no deposit and a validity of about 28 days. It works identically and any remaining balance is simply lost at the end, so do not over-load it.
The better answer if your phone supports it is a mobile card, which sidesteps the physical stock entirely.

sections.heading: Mobile Suica is the upgrade
paragraphs: Recent iPhones and many Android phones can hold a Suica in the wallet app, and on iPhone it can be created and topped up with an overseas card from your own sofa before you fly. Setup takes about ten minutes and the process is in English.

The advantage is not novelty. You top up from the app instead of finding a machine, you can see the balance without tapping, and you cannot leave it in a jacket pocket. It also removes the deposit and the refund question entirely.

One caution: the phone must have enough battery to work at the gate. Japanese phones use a mode that functions on reserve power for a short period; not all handsets do. A completely dead phone is a card you cannot use.

sections.heading: Loading and tapping
paragraphs: Load at any ticket machine: insert the card, press Charge — there is an English option on every machine — and add ¥1,000 to ¥10,000. Machines take cash, and most take only notes and coins rather than foreign cards. Keep at least ¥2,000 on it; the maximum balance is ¥20,000.

Tap flat on the reader going in, tap again going out. A double beep and a red light means insufficient balance: step aside and use the fare adjustment machine before the gates rather than holding up the queue.
Do not tap twice on entry, and do not put two IC cards in the same wallet — the reader sees both and rejects them. This is the single most common gate failure among visitors.

sections.heading: Everything else it does
paragraphs: Convenience stores, supermarkets, chain restaurants, many vending machines and most coin lockers take it, and paying this way is noticeably faster than cash. In practice a visitor can run most small daily spending off the card and keep cash for the places that take nothing else.
It is also the tidiest solution to the coin problem. Japan's cash economy generates handfuls of change constantly, and a station machine will swallow all of it onto the card in one go.

What it does not cover: Shinkansen and limited express reserved seats, which need a separate ticket or a registered mobile setup, and long-distance JR travel beyond regional boundaries. It is a local card, and crossing between company regions on one journey can fail even where both ends accept it.

sections.heading: When you leave
paragraphs: Keep it. Physical cards do not expire for ten years from last use, and having one ready for the next trip is genuinely convenient. Balances survive.

If you want the money back, a JR office of the issuing company will refund the balance and the deposit, minus a handling fee of a couple of hundred yen. If the balance is small, the fee eats most of it and keeping the card is the better call. Welcome Suica cards are not refundable at all.

The larger point is that the card removes an entire class of friction. You never read a fare table, never choose a destination on a machine, never work out which company's ticket you need at a station served by three of them. Get it at the airport, and everything else in Japanese transport gets easier.

title: Japanese Whisky: What's Worth Buying and What's Just Marketing
excerpt: The golden age is over but the whisky is still exceptional. You just need to know what you're actually looking at.
heroImageAlt: Japanese whisky bottles displayed at a specialist liquor shop in Tokyo
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The golden age and the scarcity
paragraphs: Somewhere around 2014, the world decided Japanese whisky was the best in the world. A Suntory expression won a prominent international award, whisky writers made pilgrimages to Nikka's distilleries, and within two years you could not find a bottle of Yamazaki single malt at anything resembling its old shelf price. By 2020 you frequently could not find it at all.

What happened is straightforward supply arithmetic. Japanese distilleries had been producing at a domestic-consumption pace for decades, and whisky takes twelve or eighteen years to become a twelve or eighteen year old. Global demand arrived instantly; the stock to meet it had needed to be laid down in the 1990s, when nobody was buying. The aged expressions ran dry and the secondary market went strange.

The distilleries kept working throughout, and the whisky filled in the boom years is now coming of age. Availability is slowly improving, age statements are creeping back onto labels, and the frenzy has cooled enough that ordinary shops have stock again. It is a better time to buy than any point in the last decade.

sections.heading: What actually makes it Japanese
paragraphs: The style descends directly from Scotch — the founders trained in Scotland — but the industry evolved differently in one structural way. Scottish distilleries trade casks with each other constantly, so a blender can source a hundred component whiskies. Japanese houses historically did not trade, so each had to produce every character it needed in-house. That forced single distilleries to install multiple still shapes, multiple yeast strains and multiple cask types, and it is why one Japanese distillery can taste like several.

The cask that gets talked about is mizunara, Japanese oak. It is difficult wood — porous, prone to leaking, awkward to coop — and it gives long-aged whisky a distinctive sandalwood and incense character. It is used sparingly and it is genuinely different from anything in Scotland.

The house style overall runs cleaner and more precise than most Scotch, with less emphasis on peat and more on balance. Whether that is better is a matter of taste; that it is a coherent style is not.

sections.heading: The labelling rule, and why it matters
paragraphs: Until recently, 'Japanese whisky' meant nothing legally. Some producers were importing bulk Scottish or Canadian spirit, blending and bottling it in Japan, and selling it with Mt. Fuji on the label. It was not illegal and it was not disclosed.

A labelling standard introduced in 2021 fixed this for members of the industry association: to be called Japanese whisky, the spirit must be fermented, distilled, matured for at least three years and bottled in Japan, using water sourced in Japan. Producers were given a transition period to sell through old stock, which has now passed.

In practice this means you should read two phrases carefully. 'Japanese Whisky' now means what it says. 'World Blended Whisky', or a label that avoids the phrase entirely while using Japanese imagery, generally indicates imported spirit in the blend. Some of those are perfectly good drinks. They are just not what most people think they are buying, and they should not cost what Japanese whisky costs.

sections.heading: What is genuinely worth buying
paragraphs: Nikka From The Barrel is the standing recommendation and has been for years: a blend bottled at high strength in a squat little bottle, sold for a few thousand yen, and better than a great deal of whisky at three times the price. If you buy one bottle, buy this one.

Suntory Kakubin — the yellow-label blend in the hatch-patterned bottle — is what Japan actually drinks, costs very little, and exists to be made into highballs. Suntory Toki is its slightly more refined sibling aimed at the same job. Neither is a sipping whisky and neither is pretending to be.

In the middle, Nikka's Coffey Grain and Coffey Malt are unusual and worth the money: distilled in a continuous still of a type almost nobody else uses for malt, giving a soft, sweet, almost pastry-like whisky. Above that, any Yamazaki, Hakushu, Yoichi or Miyagikyo expression at close to list price is worth taking, and the no-age-statement bottlings are far better value than the aged ones.

sections.heading: The craft distilleries are the interesting part
paragraphs: The more rewarding shopping now is below the two big houses. A wave of small distilleries has come of age in the last few years, and their whisky is arriving at drinkable maturity just as the giants remain constrained.

Chichibu, in Saitama, is the one that made the category's reputation — small, meticulous, and released under the Ichiro's Malt name at prices that reflect how sought-after it has become. Mars Shinshu, high in the Nagano mountains, releases Komagatake expressions that are not as famous as Yamazaki and are much closer in quality than the price gap suggests. Kanosuke in Kagoshima, Akkeshi in Hokkaido and Nagahama in Shiga are all worth a punt if a shop is pointing at them.

These bottles are the ones you cannot easily buy at home, which is the actual test of a souvenir. A Yamazaki 12 is available in any good bottle shop in London or New York. A single-cask release from a distillery with two stills is not.

sections.heading: The highball is the format
paragraphs: Japanese whisky culture is built around the highball — whisky over ice with soda, in a tall glass — and it is not a compromise. It is the default way whisky is drunk here, it is what Kakubin exists for, and it is the correct thing to order with fried food.

The technique is taken seriously, which is why a bar highball tastes better than yours. The glass and the whisky are chilled first, the ice is a single dense block or large cubes rather than small ones, the soda is poured down a bar spoon to preserve carbonation, and it is stirred once. Never more than once.
Order one at a decent bar before you commit to a bottle. It calibrates your sense of what you are buying better than any tasting note, and it costs the price of a beer.

sections.heading: Where to buy, and visiting
paragraphs: Department store basement floors and specialist liquor shops have the best selection and the fairest prices. Large discount chains sometimes turn up bargains on the standard blends. Airport duty free is convenient but the range has narrowed since the shortage and the prices are no longer obviously better.
Avoid hotel gift shops entirely, and be sceptical of any shop in a tourist district displaying rare bottles in a lit cabinet — that is secondary-market pricing aimed at people who will not check.

The distilleries themselves welcome visitors, and Yamazaki, Hakushu, Yoichi and Miyagikyo all run tours with tastings. All of them require booking well in advance, often months, and the distillery-only bottlings in their shops are among the few genuinely scarce things you can buy at a fair price. If you know your dates, book before you book anything else.

title: Naoshima Is Japan's Art Island — and Nobody Tells You How to Do It Right
excerpt: It's a real island with real people living on it. The art just happens to be everywhere.
heroImageAlt: A contemporary outdoor sculpture near the coast of Naoshima with the Seto Inland Sea behind
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What Naoshima is
paragraphs: Naoshima sits in the Seto Inland Sea between Okayama and Takamatsu, about an hour by ferry from either. It is small enough to cross on a bicycle in an afternoon and has a population of around three thousand.

In the 1980s and 90s the Benesse Corporation commissioned the architect Tadao Ando to build a museum on a largely depopulated island, and what followed over three decades was a collaboration between art, architecture and landscape that should not quite work and absolutely does. It has been widely imitated and nothing else is quite like it.

It is also a real island with real residents, most of whom are elderly and none of whom signed up to live in an attraction. That tension is worth carrying with you: the village streets are somebody's neighbourhood, not part of the exhibit.

sections.heading: The Chichu Art Museum
paragraphs: Chichu is underground, with no exterior visible from above and all its light arriving through openings cut in the ceilings. It contains exactly three artists: Monet, with five late Water Lilies in a room of white marble mosaic you enter barefoot; James Turrell, with light installations that take several minutes for your eyes to resolve; and Walter De Maria, with a granite sphere on a staircase.
That is the entire collection. The building is the fourth work and is arguably the best of them.

Tickets are timed and must be booked online in advance — this is the single most common way visitors get caught out, because turning up at the door does not work in the busy months. Book Chichu first and build the day around the slot you get.

sections.heading: The Art House Project
paragraphs: This is what separates Naoshima from every other art destination in Japan. Artists were given abandoned houses in Honmura village and told to do what they wanted.

James Turrell built a light piece into a farmhouse that you enter in complete darkness, sit in, and slowly begin to see. Hiroshi Sugimoto rebuilt a shrine with a staircase of optical glass running down into an underground chamber. Another is a room of water with LED counters flickering under the surface. These are not galleries with labels and benches; they are encounters, and several take a few minutes before anything happens.
A single ticket covers most of the houses and they are within a ten-minute walk of each other in the village. Allow half a day and do not rush between them.

sections.heading: Everything else on the island
paragraphs: Benesse House Museum, up the hill, is a hotel and a museum in the same Ando building, with works installed along corridors and outside on the shore. Guests can walk the galleries after closing, which is the strongest argument for staying there.

The Lee Ufan Museum and the small Ando Museum in the village are both worth an hour. Outside, Yayoi Kusama's yellow pumpkin on the pier at the Benesse end and the red one at Miyanoura port are the island's two most photographed objects, and both are free to stand next to.

If art on islands turns out to be your thing, Teshima and Inujima are the neighbours, each with a small number of extraordinary works and even fewer visitors. Teshima's art museum — a concrete shell with two openings and water rising through the floor — is the one people talk about afterwards.

sections.heading: Getting there and getting around
paragraphs: From Tokyo it is a half-day commitment: Shinkansen to Okayama, a local train to Uno port, then a twenty-minute ferry. From Takamatsu on Shikoku it is about an hour by ferry. That journey is the filter, and it is why the island still has the quality it has.

On the island, a bus loops between the port, the village and the museum area. Bicycles are the better option, but the island is hilly and summer here is severe — take an electric bike from one of the rental places by the port. It is not cheating.

The two things that catch people out: most museums close on Mondays, and the ferries stop in the early evening. Check the last sailing before you settle into anything, because there is no other way off.

sections.heading: Stay overnight if you can
paragraphs: After the day visitors leave on the last ferry, the island changes. The Art House buildings glow from inside, the grounds around Benesse House are quiet, and you are one of a small number of people who do not live there.
Accommodation is limited and books out well ahead, particularly during the Setouchi Triennale, the art festival that takes over these islands every three years and multiplies visitor numbers.

Eating is the other thing to plan. There are few restaurants, several close early or on irregular days, and the island effectively shuts by nine. Buy something at the port shop if you are arriving late.

sections.heading: The right mindset
paragraphs: Naoshima rewards a willingness to be disoriented — to find things with no label, to sit with something that does not explain itself, to wait in a dark room for several minutes on the assumption that something is happening.
Photography is prohibited inside most of the works, which is deliberate and which visitors find harder than they expect. The pieces are about duration and adjustment, and neither survives a camera.
If that is what you came to Japan for, the island earns its reputation. If you want an informational plaque and a gift shop at every turn, this is not the place.

title: The JR Pass: Who It's For, Who It Isn't, and How to Not Overpay
excerpt: The JR Pass is one of Japan's most famous travel products. Since the 2023 price rise it is also, for most itineraries, a waste of money.

factsExpire.what: JR Pass fares rise to 53,000 / 84,000 / 105,000; drop the old prices once this has passed

heroImageAlt: Shinkansen bullet train at a Japanese station platform
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The cost, and why old advice is wrong
paragraphs: The 7-day JR Pass costs ¥50,000, and rises to ¥53,000 on 1 October 2026. The 14-day goes from ¥80,000 to ¥84,000 and the 21-day from ¥100,000 to ¥105,000 on the same date. For that price you get unlimited travel on most JR-operated trains, including the Shinkansen. If you are booking ahead and your dates allow, buying before the increase locks in the lower price. If your itinerary involves Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and Hiroshima in that sequence, the maths works. If your itinerary is mostly in one city with a few day trips, it almost certainly doesn't.

That qualifier matters more than it used to. In October 2023 the 7-day pass went from ¥29,650 to ¥50,000 — a 69% increase overnight. At the old price the pass was close to an automatic purchase for any first-time visitor; at the new one it is a calculation. Almost every blog post, forum answer and guidebook paragraph written before that date is describing a product that no longer exists, and a lot of it is still the first thing you find when you search. Check the date on any JR Pass advice before you trust it, including this page.

There is also a Green Car version, roughly 30–40% more, which buys you the first-class carriage: wider seats in a 2+2 layout instead of 2+3, more legroom, and a quieter car. On a two-hour ride in a full train it is pleasant. It is not a different train and it does not arrive earlier. Buy it if the comfort is worth the money to you, not because it sounds like the serious option.

sections.heading: Break-even: when the pass wins
paragraphs: The break-even calculation for the 7-day pass: a single Tokyo–Kyoto Shinkansen (Hikari) ticket is ¥13,870 each way. Two of those is ¥27,740. Add Kyoto–Osaka (¥1,420), Osaka–Hiroshima (¥5,720 each way), a couple of JR local trips, and you're somewhere near ¥60,000. The pass wins.

Now the itinerary most people actually have. Tokyo for four days, Kyoto for three, back to Tokyo to fly home. That is one round trip: ¥27,740 against a pass price of ¥50,000. You lose ¥22,260 — more than the round trip itself cost. Adding a day trip to Nara or Osaka moves the needle by a couple of thousand yen and changes nothing about the conclusion.

The version that flips it is the long west-bound run. Tokyo → Kyoto → Hiroshima → Osaka → Tokyo inside seven days clears ¥50,000 comfortably, and every JR local ride, airport express and side trip after that point is free. The general rule: the pass wins when you are covering long distances in one direction and coming back, and loses when you are basing yourself in one or two cities. Work out your actual route on a fare calculator before you buy. It takes ten minutes and the answer is frequently the opposite of what you assumed.

sections.heading: The Nozomi supplement changed the calculation
paragraphs: The JR Pass does not cover the Nozomi or Mizuho, the fastest services on the Tokaido–Sanyo line — only the Hikari and Kodama. Tokyo to Kyoto on a Hikari takes about 2h45m versus 2h15m on a Nozomi. This is not a big difference and most people don't notice it.

What did change in 2023: you can now pay a supplement to ride the Nozomi with a JR Pass, rather than being barred from it outright. This is less about the half hour and more about frequency. Nozomi services are the backbone of the timetable; Hikari runs perhaps two an hour, Kodama stops everywhere and takes close to four hours to Kyoto. If you arrive at the platform at an awkward time, the supplement buys you the next departure instead of a forty-minute wait for a train that is itself slower.
The trap is the Kodama. It appears on the same board, it is fully covered, and it is a genuinely slow train that stops at every station on the line. Read the service name, not just the destination.

sections.heading: What the pass covers that people miss
paragraphs: What the pass does cover that people underestimate: the Narita Express (N'EX) from the airport, the local JR lines within Tokyo (which serve some neighborhoods that subway doesn't), the JR Haruka from Kansai Airport into Kyoto, and most Shinkansen within Kyushu (on the Kyushu JR Pass). If you're starting from Narita, the N'EX alone is ¥3,070 to Shinjuku. Over seven days that's two trips or ¥6,140 saved before you board a Shinkansen.

Two more that regularly go unused. The JR ferry to Miyajima — the one that puts you in front of the floating torii — is a JR service and is included. And the Yamanote line, the loop that connects most of the places you will go in Tokyo, is JR. If you are holding an active pass, you do not need to touch your IC card inside Tokyo at all. People carry an activated pass around for a week and pay cash for the Yamanote out of habit.

sections.heading: Regional passes are usually the better buy
paragraphs: This is the part the national pass's fame obscures. JR is six separate regional companies, and each sells its own passes covering its own territory at a fraction of the national price. If your trip stays in one region — which most trips do — one of these is almost always the right answer.

The Kansai Area Pass covers Osaka, Kyoto, Nara, Kobe and Himeji for one to four days and costs a small fraction of the national pass. JR East sells area passes for the Tohoku and Nagano/Niigata directions, useful if you are going north rather than west. The Hokuriku Arch Pass covers Tokyo to Osaka via Kanazawa, which is a genuinely good route and a poor fit for the national pass. JR Kyushu and JR Hokkaido each sell their own.

Two practical notes. These passes are sold to foreign passport holders on a tourist entry, same as the national pass, and several of them can only be bought before you arrive or at specific station offices. And you can stack them across a trip — a regional pass for the week you are moving around and plain IC card travel for the week you are not is usually cheaper than one long national pass covering both.

sections.heading: Reserve your seats — it is free and unlimited
paragraphs: With a JR Pass, seat reservations cost nothing and you can make as many as you like. A surprising number of pass holders never do it, ride in the non-reserved cars, and stand from Tokyo to Nagoya during a busy period.

Reserve at any JR ticket office (Midori no Madoguchi) or a reserved-seat machine, in a few minutes, with the pass and your passport. Do it the evening before rather than on the platform. During Golden Week, Obon in mid-August and New Year, the reserved cars fill days ahead and the non-reserved cars become standing room from the moment the doors open — these are the three weeks of the year when the difference is not comfort but whether you sit down at all.
If you are travelling with luggage, ask for a seat in the last row of the carriage. The space behind it is the only place on a Shinkansen where a large suitcase fits without blocking an aisle.

sections.heading: The luggage rule that catches people
paragraphs: On the Tokaido, Sanyo and Kyushu Shinkansen — the Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka–Hiroshima line, which is to say the line most visitors use — a bag whose combined length, width and height exceeds 160cm requires an oversized baggage seat reservation. That reservation is free if you make it in advance. If you turn up with the bag and no reservation, you pay a ¥1,000 penalty and the staff will find you a place for it.

A large checked-size suitcase is often exactly at this threshold. Measure yours before you travel rather than discovering the rule at the gate, and make the reservation at the same time as your seat — it is the same counter and the same conversation.

The alternative most residents use is to not carry the bag at all. Takkyubin, the overnight luggage courier, moves a suitcase between hotels for roughly ¥2,000–3,000 and it is the single best-value service in Japanese travel. Hand it to your hotel's front desk before noon, collect it at the next hotel the following afternoon, and cross the country with a day bag.

sections.heading: Alternatives to the JR Pass
paragraphs: Alternatives to consider: IC cards (Suica) cover everything within cities. Individual Shinkansen tickets bought in advance can be slightly discounted through JR's Ekinet system. The Osaka Amazing Pass and the Kyoto Sightseeing Card cover local transit within those cities and don't require a JR Pass to function alongside them.

Two more worth knowing. Platt Kodama sells discounted Tokyo–Osaka seats on the slow Kodama service — if you have the time, it is materially cheaper than the standard fare. And the overnight highway bus, at roughly a quarter of the Shinkansen fare, is a real option that Japanese students and budget travellers use constantly; the modern three-across coaches are more comfortable than the idea sounds, and you save a night of accommodation.
Domestic budget airlines (Peach, Jetstar Japan, Skymark) beat the Shinkansen on price for the long hops — Tokyo to Fukuoka or Sapporo — where the train stops being competitive on time as well.

sections.heading: If you have decided to buy one
paragraphs: If you've already decided to buy the pass: buy it before leaving your home country. It used to be only available abroad, and while you can now buy it in Japan, the domestic price is roughly 10–20% higher. Get it from JR's official website or an authorized travel agent in your country. Activate it at a JR office in any major station, not at the airport machines.

Bring your passport to the exchange counter — the pass is sold only to visitors on a temporary visitor entry, and the staff will check the stamp. When you activate it you choose the start date, and it does not have to be the day you collect it. If you are spending your first three days in Tokyo without leaving the city, start the pass on day four. People routinely burn two days of a seven-day pass riding the Yamanote line.

The pass is now issued digitally through the official site, which lets you make seat reservations online instead of queueing. The queues at the exchange counters in Tokyo Station and the airports are long, and they are longest at exactly the hour your flight lands.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Add up the long-distance legs you will actually take, at the real fares, and compare that to ¥50,000. If you are doing one city with day trips, skip it and use an IC card. If you are staying in one region, buy that region's pass. If you are crossing the country and coming back inside a week, buy the national pass and then use it for everything, including the airport train and the Yamanote line, because you have already paid for it.

title: Where to Stay in Tokyo: Honest Assessments of Each Neighborhood
excerpt: Every first-time visitor books Shinjuku because someone told them to. Some of those people are right.
heroImageAlt: Aerial view of Tokyo at dusk showing the city lights
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why neighborhood choice matters
paragraphs: Tokyo has 23 special wards and dozens of distinct neighbourhoods, each with a different character and a different argument for why you should sleep there. The decision matters more than most hotel comparison sites suggest. An hour on the Yamanote Line from Ueno to Shibuya is not the same as a ten-minute walk from wherever you are standing. Where you sleep shapes what you do in the morning and, more importantly, what you do at eleven at night.

The single most useful filter is the Yamanote Line, the loop that connects most of the places a visitor wants to go. Staying on it, or one stop from it, removes almost every transport problem. Staying twenty minutes outside it saves money and costs you an hour a day.
The second filter is the last train. Tokyo's network stops around midnight and restarts around five, and a neighbourhood you can walk back to changes how the evenings work.

sections.heading: Shinjuku
paragraphs: The right choice for first-timers who want maximum convenience. Shinjuku Station connects to almost everything, including the Narita Express and the airport buses. The west side has the skyscraper district and the bus terminal for day trips; the east side has Kabukicho, Golden Gai and Omoide Yokocho, which are three quite different things to do after dark.
Hotels run from capsules at a few thousand yen a night to the top of the market. The area is not charming and it does not pretend to be. It works.

The one warning is the station itself, which is the busiest in the world and has upwards of two hundred exits. Note which exit your hotel is near before you arrive, because the difference between the correct exit and the wrong one is fifteen minutes and a lot of stairs.

sections.heading: Asakusa and the east
paragraphs: Asakusa is the tourist district, with one of the city's best sightseeing densities within walking distance — Senso-ji, Nakamise, the Sumida River. It is also the best-value area for accommodation, with a concentration of well-run hostels and small hotels.

The downsides: it is quiet outside tourist hours, the transport options are thinner than in Shinjuku or Shibuya, and it does not have the restaurant and bar density of the west side. Good for concentrated sightseeing and a vaguely traditional atmosphere. Less good for eating late or getting to Shibuya quickly.
Nearby, Kuramae has become the quiet alternative — a former wholesale district now full of small coffee roasters and craft workshops, ten minutes from Asakusa and considerably calmer.

sections.heading: Shibuya and the west
paragraphs: Better for people on a second or third visit. The neighbourhood has been under continuous redevelopment for over a decade and will be for several more years, which means construction hoardings and changed walking routes.

The crossing is iconic and worth seeing once; it is not worth basing a week around. The real advantage is access to the private lines heading west — Shimokitazawa on the Inokashira Line, and Nakameguro and Daikanyama within walking distance, which are among the more pleasant parts of the city to spend an evening.
Ebisu, one stop south, is the version of this for people who would rather eat well than go clubbing: same access, better restaurants, considerably calmer.

sections.heading: Ginza, Tokyo Station and Nihonbashi
paragraphs: Ginza is expensive, convenient and quiet at night. If your priorities are ease of movement and you are not interested in nightlife, the business hotels here are excellent value relative to the address. It is walking distance to Tsukiji and one line from Shibuya. It can feel sterile, because it largely is.

Marunouchi, around Tokyo Station, is the choice if you are taking Shinkansen day trips or leaving from Narita by train — you are inside the station rather than travelling to it. It is a business district and it empties at the weekend, which some people find restful and others find eerie.
Nihonbashi sits between the two and is the underrated one: old merchant district, several centuries-old shops still trading, good access, and prices below Ginza for the same convenience.

sections.heading: Ueno, Yanaka and the old city
paragraphs: Ueno is the most practical choice for travellers arriving with luggage from the north, since the Shinkansen stops there. The area around the park is dense with museums and cheap restaurants, and Ameyoko market underneath the tracks is a genuine survivor of post-war Tokyo.

It has none of Shinjuku's energy and more neighbourhood character than Shinjuku has. Yanaka and Nezu are walkable from here, and they are among the most interesting surviving pieces of old Tokyo — low wooden houses, a large cemetery full of cherry trees, a shopping street that has not changed much in fifty years.
This is the area to choose if what you want from Tokyo is the version that is not on the postcards.

sections.heading: Ikebukuro, Akihabara, Roppongi, Shinagawa
paragraphs: Ikebukuro is Shinjuku with the prices reduced and the polish removed. Excellent transport, huge amount of cheap food, considerably less pretty. If budget is the binding constraint and you still want a Yamanote station, this is the answer.

Akihabara is a destination rather than a base unless electronics and anime are the point of your trip, in which case it is the obvious choice. Roppongi is where the international nightlife concentrates, along with two of the best art museums in the city; it is also the one area of Tokyo where visitors regularly report being hassled by touts, which is worth knowing.

Shinagawa is the pragmatic choice for a short trip flying into Haneda: fifteen minutes from the airport, on the Shinkansen, on the Yamanote. Nobody stays there for the atmosphere and nobody regrets it on a two-night stop.

sections.heading: What kind of room to book
paragraphs: The default is the business hotel: a small, clean, efficient room with everything working, priced per person rather than per room, and available everywhere. Expect it to be genuinely small — a double room of twelve square metres is normal and is not a mistake in the listing.

Capsule hotels are cheaper, better than they sound, and now frequently designed for tourists with separate floors by gender. Hostels in Tokyo are unusually good. At the other end, the international luxury hotels here are among the best in the world and priced accordingly.

Two practical warnings. Check-in is often 3pm or later and enforced, though nearly every hotel will store your bags from the morning. And short-term apartment rentals are regulated in Japan — a legal listing carries a registration number, and unlicensed ones do get shut down, occasionally while guests are booked in.

sections.heading: The general rule
paragraphs: Within the Yamanote loop, you are never more than about twenty minutes from anything important. The choice of neighbourhood is therefore not really about access; it is about what you walk outside into in the morning and what is still open when you come back at night.

Pick for the atmosphere you want at breakfast and at eleven at night, and trust the train system to handle the rest. And if you are in Tokyo for more than five nights, consider splitting between two neighbourhoods — it costs you one afternoon of moving and gives you two quite different cities.

title: Japan's Four Major Ramen Styles: What They Are and Where to Actually Eat Them
excerpt: Ramen in Japan is not one food. Depending on where you are, the word covers a range of things that share almost nothing except noodles.
heroImageAlt: A bowl of Hakata tonkotsu ramen with chashu pork and soft-boiled egg
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Four styles, not one
paragraphs: The four canonical regional ramen styles in Japan are Sapporo (miso), Hakata (tonkotsu), Tokyo (shoyu), and Kitakata (shoyu with flat noodles). This is a simplification. Within each region there are dozens of substyles, proprietary broths, and variations by shop. But the four regional types give you a framework that is more useful than 'ramen is ramen.'

The framework works because a bowl of ramen is really four separate decisions: the broth (what was simmered), the tare (the seasoning base — soy, salt or miso — that actually determines the flavour), the noodle (thin and straight, or thick and wavy), and the toppings. Regional styles are conventional combinations of those four. Once you can hear the four parts separately, a menu in a language you do not read becomes navigable.

One thing worth setting straight early: ramen is not ancient. It arrived from China around the turn of the twentieth century, spread through post-war street stalls, and became regionally distinct within living memory. It is a modern food that Japan made thoroughly its own, which is why it evolves so fast.

sections.heading: Hakata tonkotsu
paragraphs: Hakata ramen from Fukuoka is the style most likely to become your obsession. The broth is made from pork bones (tonkotsu) simmered for 12 to 18 hours until it turns milky white and rich enough to coat a spoon. The noodles are thin and straight, cooked harder than you'd expect. Shops around Hakata Station and the yatai stalls along the Naka River are where to eat it. Budget ¥700–1,000.

The small portion and the kaedama are the mechanism that makes the style work. Thin noodles go soft fast in a broth that heavy, so the bowl is built small deliberately: you eat the first portion at its correct texture, then call 'kaedama' and a second nest of noodles arrives in about ninety seconds to go into the remaining broth. Ordering one large bowl instead gets you a worse version of the same food.

Firmness is specified at the counter and the vocabulary is worth having: futsu (normal), katame (firm), barikata (very firm), harigane (wire — barely cooked). Start at katame. Barikata is not a test of character and locals order across the whole range.

The yatai — the open-air stalls that set up along the river at dusk — are the atmospheric version and cost a little more than a shop. Ten seats, a plastic sheet against the wind, strangers beside you. It is one of the few genuinely convivial ways to eat ramen, a food otherwise eaten fast and alone.

sections.heading: Tokyo shoyu
paragraphs: Tokyo shoyu ramen is the gentler style. Chicken or pork-based broth seasoned with soy sauce, usually clearer than Hakata broth, with medium wavy noodles. The toppings are what distinguish one Tokyo shop from another: chashu pork, a soft-boiled egg marinated in soy and mirin, bamboo shoots, nori.

This is the oldest of the four and the closest to the original Chinese-influenced bowl. It is also the one that rewards attention least dramatically and most durably — there is nothing overwhelming in it, so the quality of the stock and the tare has nowhere to hide. A great shoyu bowl tastes clean and deep at the same time, and a mediocre one just tastes like salty soup.

Tsukemen, where thick cold noodles are served beside a small bowl of concentrated dipping broth, is a Tokyo development worth trying once you have had the standard version. It is a different eating experience: the noodles stay firm throughout, and the broth is intense because it is never meant to be drunk on its own. Popular tsukemen shops have queues that form before opening.

sections.heading: Sapporo miso
paragraphs: Sapporo miso ramen is the winter version — a heavier broth with miso paste stirred in, often with butter, sweet corn, and bean sprouts on top. It makes sense in Hokkaido in November in a way it doesn't in Tokyo in August. The Susukino neighborhood in Sapporo has the highest concentration of shops worth trying. Expect to spend ¥900–1,200.

The technical detail that defines it: the vegetables and the miso are stir-fried in a wok before the broth goes in, so the bowl carries a slight caramelised edge that no amount of miso stirred into finished soup will reproduce. The noodles are thick, yellow and curly, which is a deliberate match — they hold a heavy broth without collapsing.

Hokkaido has two other bowls worth knowing if you are there. Hakodate is the home of shio (salt) ramen, the lightest of all the styles and almost transparent. Asahikawa uses a soy broth with a layer of lard on the surface that keeps it scalding in genuinely cold weather. Neither travels well to a Tokyo summer, which is rather the point of both.

sections.heading: Kitakata, the fourth one nobody orders
paragraphs: Kitakata is a small city in Fukushima with a population under fifty thousand and something in the region of a hundred ramen shops, which is the highest concentration per head in Japan. It is the fourth canonical style and the one visitors almost never eat, purely because it is not on the Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka line.

The bowl is a light soy broth, usually pork and dried sardine, and the distinguishing feature is the noodle: flat, broad, and visibly wavy, with a high water content that gives it a soft, slippery chew unlike anything in the other three styles. The topping is generally plain — chashu, spring onion, menma — because the noodle is the event.

The local habit is asa-ra: ramen for breakfast. Shops open at seven and are busy by half past. If you are travelling north to Aizu-Wakamatsu or through Fukushima at all, it is worth the detour, and it is a useful corrective to the idea that heavier always means better.

sections.heading: The styles that broke the map
paragraphs: The four-region framework describes ramen as it was around 1980. Several of the bowls you will actually be offered in Tokyo today belong to schools that postdate it.

Iekei, out of Yokohama, splits the difference between tonkotsu and shoyu — pork and chicken broth with a soy tare, thick straight noodles, spinach and a sheet of nori, and a bowl of rice on the side that you are expected to use to mop up. Jiro-style is the maximalist one: an enormous mound of boiled bean sprouts and cabbage over thick noodles and fatty pork, ordered with a shouted list of free toppings that intimidates newcomers on purpose. Abura soba has no broth at all — noodles, tare and oil in the bottom of the bowl, mixed vigorously before eating.
None of these is a tourist trap or a novelty. They are what a lot of people in Tokyo mean when they say they are going for ramen.

sections.heading: How to order
paragraphs: How to order at a ramen shop: most have ticket vending machines at the entrance. Put in your money, select your bowl, take the ticket, and hand it to staff when you sit. If you want a soft-boiled egg (ajitama), it's usually a separate button.

The machines are often Japanese-only, and the reliable move is to buy the top-left button. Japanese vending layouts put the shop's signature bowl there by convention, and it is what you want on a first visit anyway. Many machines now have an English toggle; a photo menu taped beside the machine is also common.

Do not over-specify at your first visit. Order the standard and learn what you're tasting before you start adjusting. Noodle firmness and broth richness can be specified at some shops, and doing so before you know the house version tells you nothing.

sections.heading: How to eat it
paragraphs: Fast. A bowl of ramen is engineered to be at its best for about eight minutes, after which the noodles have absorbed broth and gone soft. This is why ramen shops are quiet, why the seats are a counter facing a wall, and why nobody lingers. Eating it slowly while talking is not a relaxed approach to ramen, it is a worse bowl of ramen.

Slurping is real and it is functional — it cools the noodles on the way in and pulls broth along with them. Nobody is counting, but you will notice that the room is louder than any other restaurant in Japan and quieter in conversation.

Lift the bowl to drink the broth at the end if you want to; it is normal. Finishing all of it is a compliment and leaving some is not an insult. Put your chopsticks down across the bowl or on the rest, stack nothing, and leave. The seat behind you is usually spoken for.

sections.heading: What it costs and what to expect
paragraphs: A bowl runs roughly ¥800–1,200 nearly everywhere, including at shops with queues down the street. Ramen is not a food where price tracks quality closely, and a ¥2,000 bowl is unusual enough to be a warning rather than a promise.

Water is self-service from a jug at the counter, there is no table service to speak of, and there is no tipping. Many shops are cash-only and several of the famous ones seat fewer than twelve people. Solo dining is the default rather than the exception, and some shops have partitioned single booths precisely so that nobody has to interact with anyone.
Queues move faster than they look. A line of fifteen people outside a ten-seat shop is about a twenty-minute wait, because the turnover inside is ten minutes a head.

title: How to Watch a Sumo Tournament Without Watching It on TV
excerpt: Six tournaments a year, three of them in Tokyo. Tickets go on sale months in advance and sell out. Here's how to actually get in.
heroImageAlt: Two sumo wrestlers facing off in the dohyo ring at Ryogoku Kokugikan
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Tournament schedule and cities
paragraphs: Sumo holds six official tournaments (basho) per year, each lasting 15 days. The January, May, and September basho are in Tokyo at Ryogoku Kokugikan. The March basho is in Osaka, July in Nagoya, and November in Fukuoka. If you're planning a trip around attending a tournament, knowing this schedule is step one. January and September in Tokyo are typically the most accessible for international visitors because they don't overlap with Golden Week or summer school holidays.

Tournaments always start on a Sunday and end on a Sunday. The two weekends and the final few days are the hardest tickets; a Tuesday or Wednesday in the first week is the easiest, and the sumo is no worse. If your dates are flexible at all, aim mid-week and early.

Outside the six tournaments there is nothing to watch competitively, which catches people out — there is no weekly fixture list. If your trip falls between basho, the regional exhibition tours (jungyo) travel the country in the gaps, and morning practice at a stable is the other option.

sections.heading: Getting tickets
paragraphs: The Japan Sumo Association sells official tickets at Ticket Pia starting roughly two months before the tournament. The best seats (masu-seki, the box seats on the ground floor) sell out in days. What's available to visitors with short notice: elevated arena seats (isu-seki), which start around ¥3,800 for the upper tiers, and same-day door tickets (¥2,200 for the cheap seats) that go on sale at the venue from 8am. The door ticket strategy works — arrive at Ryogoku at 7:30am and you will get in.

The same-day tickets are the answer for most visitors and they are worth understanding properly. A limited number go on sale each morning, one per person, cash, at the box office on the east side of the building. On a quiet weekday you can turn up at 8am and walk in. On a final weekend, or if a popular wrestler is having a good tournament, the queue starts before dawn.

Resale sites carry tickets at multiple times face value. This is legal for some and not for others, and the Association actively discourages it. Given that a same-day seat costs ¥2,200 and the sumo is identical from every seat in the building, paying ¥15,000 to a reseller is a poor trade.

sections.heading: Which seat to actually buy
paragraphs: Masu-seki are the square boxes on the floor, sold as a unit for four people, and they are the iconic sumo seat: you sit on flat cushions in a railed-off square, with food and drink brought to you. They are also the least comfortable seat in the building for anyone not used to sitting on the floor for several hours, and the four-person pricing means a couple pays for two seats they will not use.

Isu-seki are ordinary chairs on the raised tiers above. They have backs, they have legroom, and the view of the ring is unobstructed and often better than the floor because you are looking down into it rather than across it. For a first tournament this is the correct purchase.

The front-row floor seats — tamari-seki, the ones directly against the ring where the audience sits in formal dress — are not generally sold to the public and come with a real hazard: wrestlers land in them regularly. This happens several times per tournament and is one reason the seats are what they are.

sections.heading: What you are watching
paragraphs: Sumo matches are short. The actual bout can last anywhere from two seconds to two minutes. The bulk of the time in a sumo tournament is ritual — the ring-entering ceremony (dohyo-iri) for the highest-ranked wrestlers, salt throwing, the slow psychological confrontation before the wrestlers crouch and charge. Understanding that the ceremony is the event, not the prelude to it, changes everything about how to watch.

Sumo is a Shinto practice as much as a sport, and the ring is treated as sacred ground. The salt is purification, thrown by the handful by the upper divisions and in visible quantity. The stamping is to drive out evil from the ring. The suspended roof above the dohyo is a shrine roof, and the four coloured tassels hanging from it represent the seasons and the compass directions.

The staring is not theatre either. The two wrestlers crouch, touch the ground, rise, retreat to their corners, and repeat this several times. They are timing each other. The charge (tachiai) is only legitimate when both men commit simultaneously and unprompted — there is no starting signal, and matching that instant is a genuine skill. A bout is frequently decided in the first half second of contact.

sections.heading: How a bout is won
paragraphs: The rules are simple enough to learn in a sentence: you lose if any part of your body other than the soles of your feet touches the ground, or if you step or are pushed out of the straw ring. That is the whole of it.

What is not simple is the vocabulary. There are eighty-odd recognised winning techniques (kimarite), and the announcer names the one used after each bout. Four cover most of what you will see: yorikiri (a forward drive out while gripping the belt), oshidashi (a push out with no grip), hatakikomi (a slap-down as the opponent lunges), and uwatenage (an over-arm throw). Recognising those four is enough to follow the day.

The belt — the mawashi — is the strategic centre of the sport. A wrestler who gets both hands on his opponent's belt in a favoured grip has usually already won, and much of the apparent stalemate in a longer bout is two men fighting over grip rather than position.

sections.heading: The ranks, and why the last day matters
paragraphs: The top division is makuuchi. Within it, from the top: yokozuna (grand champion), ozeki, sekiwake, komusubi, and then the numbered maegashira ranks. Below makuuchi sits juryo, and below that the unsalaried divisions whose wrestlers also serve as attendants to the ranked men.

Each wrestler in the top divisions fights fifteen bouts, one per day. Eight wins is kachikoshi — a winning record, which means promotion or at least safety. Seven or fewer is makekoshi and means demotion. This is why the final days carry so much weight: a large share of the field arrives at day 13 or 14 sitting on seven wins, with a career-relevant result riding on a bout lasting four seconds.

The rank list itself, the banzuke, is a calligraphed document published before each tournament, with name size scaling to rank. It is sold at the venue for a few hundred yen and is the best souvenir in the building.

sections.heading: When to arrive
paragraphs: The day begins at 8am with the lowest-ranked wrestlers, and the audience trickles in as the day progresses. The top-division matches (makuuchi) begin around 3pm and end around 6pm. Most visitors arrive around 2pm, which is correct. The atmosphere builds through the afternoon. The final few bouts of the day — particularly if a yokozuna or ozeki is involved in a high-stakes match — generate a noise level that is genuinely startling.

There is an argument for arriving much earlier at least once. In the morning the hall is nearly empty, you can sit close, the young wrestlers in the lower divisions fight with obvious desperation because their careers depend on it, and nothing is ceremonial because nobody is watching. It is a completely different event from the same building at five in the afternoon.

The two moments not to miss in the afternoon: the makuuchi dohyo-iri around 3:40pm, when the whole top division enters in embroidered ceremonial aprons, and the yokozuna's own entrance immediately after, performed alone with two attendants.

sections.heading: Food, drink, and the building
paragraphs: The basement of Kokugikan has chankonabe, the stew traditionally eaten by sumo wrestlers. It is not a gimmick. It's good stew, with chicken and vegetables in a clear dashi broth, and it costs around ¥1,000. There are also yakitori stalls and beer vendors. Food at the masu boxes is served in bento-style sets and can be ordered in advance with tickets.

The yakitori is worth a note of its own: it is made in a kitchen in the basement of the stadium itself, and it is genuinely good. Eating and drinking through the afternoon is entirely normal — this is not an event where the audience sits in silence.

There is also a small sumo museum on the ground floor, free with a ticket, and the souvenir shops sell everything from banzuke to hand towels printed with individual wrestlers' names. Arrive an hour before you plan to sit down and there is plenty to occupy it.

sections.heading: If you can't get a ticket: morning practice
paragraphs: Some sumo stables (heya) in the Ryogoku area allow visitors to watch morning training, and it is arguably a better experience than a tournament day. Practice starts around 6am, you sit on the floor a few metres from wrestlers colliding at full speed in a small room, and there is no crowd and no ceremony.

The conditions are strict and non-negotiable: absolute silence, no photography unless expressly permitted, no leaving mid-session, formal-ish clothing, and no talking to the wrestlers. You are in someone's home and workplace. Most stables require arrangement in advance, often through a hotel concierge or a specialist tour, and several no longer accept visitors at all.

Between tournaments this is the only sumo available, and even during a basho the stables train in the mornings. If your dates miss the basho entirely, this is the thing to arrange instead of writing sumo off.

sections.heading: What surprises you in person
paragraphs: The wrestlers are larger than you expect. The ring is smaller than you expect. The speed of the bouts is faster than you expect. These three surprises reliably improve the live experience over whatever you were imagining from television coverage.

The fourth is the noise. Between bouts the hall is unusually quiet for a sports venue, and the sound of two very large men colliding carries to the back row without amplification. Television compresses it into nothing. In the building it is the thing you remember.

title: The Onsen Rules Nobody Bothers to Tell You
excerpt: The water is shared. The silence is expected. The tattoo policy is more complicated than you've been told.
heroImageAlt: Outdoor rotenburo onsen with steam rising over a stone tub surrounded by bamboo
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The rule everyone needs to know
paragraphs: The fundamental rule of a Japanese onsen or public bath is that you wash before you enter the communal water. This is not optional and not a suggestion. There are shower stations around the perimeter — a low stool, a handheld showerhead, a bucket, shampoo and body wash in dispensers.

You sit on the stool, rinse thoroughly, wash properly, and rinse off every trace of soap before you get anywhere near the bath. The water in the tub is for soaking in, not for cleaning in, and it is shared by everyone in the room.
Sitting rather than standing matters, because a standing shower sprays the person on the next stool. Rinse the stool and the space when you finish, which is what the bucket beside you is for.

sections.heading: Naked is the format
paragraphs: There are no swimming costumes in an onsen. Bathing is done naked, in gender-separated rooms, and this is universal rather than a regional variation. A facility that permits swimwear is a water park, not an onsen.

This is the part that stops many first-time visitors, and it is worth saying plainly that it is far less uncomfortable than it sounds. Nobody looks at anybody. The social convention of not looking is absolute, and after about ninety seconds you stop thinking about it entirely.

The small towel you are given is the only concession. It is not for covering yourself in the water — it does not go in the water at all — but people carry it in front of them while walking between the changing room and the bath, and that is what it is doing.

sections.heading: What you bring in
