paragraphs: Essentially nothing. The large towel stays in the changing room. The small one comes in, and is folded on your head or set on the rim of the tub while you soak. Soap stays at the shower station.

Your phone does not come into the bathing area at all, and this is enforced seriously. Photography here is a privacy violation of every other person present, and it is one of the few rules in Japan that will get you removed rather than politely corrected.
Long hair goes up. It must not touch the water. Hair ties are usually available at the changing-room counter if you have forgotten one.

sections.heading: Tattoos, briefly
paragraphs: The official policy at most traditional onsen is no tattoos, a rule that dates to historical associations with organised crime. Enforcement varies enormously: large resort facilities tend to be stricter, small neighbourhood sento are often entirely pragmatic.
Private family baths, bookable by the hour at many ryokan and onsen hotels, have no policy because there are no other guests. Tattoo-friendly facilities exist and increase in number every year.

The workable approach is to ask before you book rather than discover the policy at the door. This is a large enough subject to have its own guide, and if you have tattoos it is worth reading before you plan an onsen trip.

sections.heading: Temperature, and how long
paragraphs: Onsen run hot. 40–42°C is standard and 44°C exists. The first immersion will feel excessive; give yourself thirty seconds to acclimatise before concluding you cannot manage it. Enter slowly, sit still, and breathe steadily, and you will be fine within a minute.

Ten to fifteen minutes at a time is plenty. If you feel dizzy, lightheaded or your heart is racing, get out and sit down — that is the heat, not a weakness, and fainting in a bathroom full of hot water and hard surfaces is the actual risk here.

Drink water before and after. Do not go in drunk, do not go in immediately after a large meal, and if you are pregnant or have heart or blood-pressure conditions, check before you soak — most facilities post the standard warnings at the entrance.

sections.heading: Working the room
paragraphs: Most onsen have several baths: an indoor main pool, an outdoor rotenburo, sometimes a cold plunge, a sauna, a carbonated or mineral bath. The protocol is to move between them over thirty to sixty minutes rather than sitting in one until you have cooked.
The cold plunge after a hot soak is optional and converts most people the first time they try it. The contrast is the point, and the sensation afterwards is out of proportion to the effort involved.

The rotenburo is the one to hold until last if the weather is cold. Sitting outdoors in hot water with snow coming down is the single best thing about winter in Japan, and it is worth planning an evening around.

sections.heading: The room is quiet
paragraphs: Conversation happens, quietly, between people who came together. What does not happen is loud talking, laughing across the room, splashing, swimming, or anything that carries. The acoustics in a tiled room are unforgiving and the expectation is close to library volume.

Children are present and are held to a looser standard, as everywhere. Groups of visitors talking at normal outdoor volume are the most common complaint that onsen staff have about foreign guests, and it is an easy one to avoid.
Do not put your head under. Do not wring the towel out into the bath. Do not shave at the bath edge.

sections.heading: Onsen, sento, and what the water is
paragraphs: An onsen is a bath fed by natural geothermal spring water, legally defined by mineral content and temperature at source. A sento is a public bathhouse using ordinary heated water — cheaper, urban, often architecturally wonderful, and a genuine piece of neighbourhood life. A super sento is the large suburban leisure version with several baths, a restaurant and massage chairs.

The water itself varies more than visitors expect. Sulphur springs smell of eggs and are milky; iron-rich springs run brown and stain towels; some are strongly alkaline and leave your skin slippery. The composition is posted on a board at the entrance, usually with a list of the ailments it is traditionally held to help.

Whether to rinse off afterwards depends on the water. For strongly mineral springs the local advice is generally not to, so the minerals stay on the skin, unless the water is acidic enough to irritate. If in doubt, do what the people around you do.

sections.heading: After the bath
paragraphs: Dry off in the washing area before you walk back into the changing room, using the small towel, so you are not dripping across the floor other people are standing on. The large towel and your clothes are waiting there.

The post-onsen state — warm, slightly light-headed, skin oddly soft — is best enjoyed horizontally for a quarter of an hour. Drink something cold. Most ryokan leave water or barley tea in the changing room for exactly this, and many sento sell bottled milk from a fridge, which is a tradition with no justification beyond being correct.
An evening onsen followed by eight hours of sleep in a cool room is, empirically, the best sleep you will have all year.

title: Don Quijote: What to Buy, What to Skip, and How to Survive the Store
excerpt: Don Quijote is five floors of everything at prices that make no sense. The key is knowing what you came for before you walk in.

factsExpire.what: Tax-free becomes refund-at-departure; the sealed bag and the consumable split end

heroImageAlt: A colorful Japanese discount store exterior at night with bright signs in Tokyo
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What Don Quijote is
paragraphs: Don Quijote — called Donki by everyone who shops there — is a discount variety store that operates on the principle that if you put enough products in a small enough space at a low enough price, people will buy things they didn't know they needed. This works. The stores are open until 5am or around the clock. The in-store jingle plays on loop. The lighting is aggressive. It is not a relaxing shopping experience. It is an effective one.

The chaos is engineered. The merchandising strategy has a name — atsuryoku chinretsu, compression display — and it is a deliberate policy of stacking goods floor to ceiling in narrow aisles so that customers slow down, look around, and find things by accident. The handwritten signs shouting prices in three colours are part of the same design. Nothing here is disorganised; it is organised to feel that way.

The chain has been running since 1989 and now has hundreds of branches, including larger MEGA Donki formats in the suburbs that lean more towards groceries. The city-centre branches are the ones visitors want, and several of them have added tourist floors with tax-free counters and souvenir sections in the last few years.

sections.heading: Skincare and cosmetics
paragraphs: Donki carries Japanese drugstore brands — Hada Labo, Kose, Shiseido, Biore — and some Korean imports at prices below almost anywhere else in Japan. The Hada Labo Gokujyun hyaluronic lotion is the specific item that beauty writers have been recommending for years, and the Donki price is genuinely competitive with anything in Tokyo.

Two things worth knowing before you fill a basket. Sunscreen is the category where Japan is furthest ahead and the prices are lowest — the Biore UV and Anessa lines cost a fraction of what the same bottles fetch abroad. And sheet masks sold in bulk packs of thirty are the highest value-per-suitcase-kilo item in the store.

Check dates on cosmetics. Donki's model involves buying up surplus and end-of-line stock, which is where some of the discount comes from, and occasionally that means an older batch. It is not a problem for most things and it is worth a glance on anything you plan to keep for a year.

sections.heading: Snacks, and the tax-free rule that catches people
paragraphs: The food section has Kit Kat flavours, Pocky, regional crisps and gift-packaged snack sets. If you're buying snacks to take home, this is more convenient than tracking down a specialty shop and often cheaper.

The tax-free counter is worth using — bring your physical passport, and the threshold is ¥5,000 or more in a day at the same store. How it works depends on when you travel. Until 31 October 2026 the tax is deducted at the register, and food, drink, cosmetics and medicines are sealed into a transparent bag you are not supposed to open before leaving the country — so if you were planning to eat the snacks on the trip, buy those separately and pay the tax. From 1 November 2026 the system changes: you pay the tax-inclusive price in the shop and claim the refund at the airport after Customs confirms you are taking the goods out. The sealed bag and the split between consumables and everything else both disappear, which makes the whole thing simpler at the till and slower at departure.

Consumables and general goods are also counted separately toward the threshold, which occasionally means a basket that looks like it qualifies does not. The staff at the counter will sort it out; it just takes longer than you expect at 2am.

sections.heading: Electronics, and what not to buy
paragraphs: The electronics section has genuine deals on portable chargers, travel adapters, USB cables and small appliances. The accessories are fine and the prices are good.

Do not buy anything complex. Rice cookers, cameras, and appliances sold for the domestic market run on 100V, carry Japanese-language menus that often cannot be switched, and come with warranties valid only in Japan. Voltage is the practical problem: 100V equipment on a 230V supply fails immediately and sometimes dramatically. Some branches stock export models specifically for visitors, and those are clearly labelled — if it is not labelled, assume domestic.

Skip the branded luxury goods in the glass cases near the registers. They are legitimate, but the selection is thin and the prices are not the bargain the rest of the store is. For whisky, sake or shochu worth buying, go to a dedicated liquor shop.

sections.heading: The things Donki is actually best at
paragraphs: Beyond cosmetics, three categories justify the trip. Costume and party goods — Donki is where Tokyo buys its Halloween outfits, and the year-round selection is enormous. Kitchen gadgets: single-purpose Japanese tools, egg moulds, onigiri presses, vegetable cutters, all cheap and all flat enough to pack.

And the own-brand line, Jonetsu Kakaku, which covers everything from socks to electric fans at prices that undercut everyone. The quality is variable and the packaging is loud, which is rather the point.

It is also the most reliable place in Japan to buy something you forgot at eleven at night — an umbrella, a charger, a shirt, a suitcase to hold everything else you bought. That utility is a large part of why locals actually shop there.

sections.heading: Navigation and which branch
paragraphs: The store layout is deliberately non-intuitive, and products are stacked floor-to-ceiling in a way that turns navigation into something between a maze and an archaeological dig. Accept this. Give yourself at least 90 minutes for your first visit, go with a list of categories rather than products, and let the store find you things.

The Shibuya and Shinjuku branches are the largest and most complete in Tokyo. Akihabara is useful if you want the electronics without the full experience. The Dotonbori branch in Osaka has a Ferris wheel attached to the building, which tells you most of what you need to know about the chain's sense of restraint.

Go late. The stores are busiest in the early evening and pleasantly empty after eleven, the tax-free queue is shortest around then, and Donki at one in the morning under those lights is an experience in its own right.

title: Hiroshima Is More Than the Peace Park — And the Peace Park Is More Than You Think
excerpt: People visit Hiroshima for one reason. Most leave having found three or four others.
heroImageAlt: The Genbaku Dome atomic bomb memorial in Hiroshima beside the river
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The Peace Memorial Museum
paragraphs: The Peace Memorial Park and Museum is why most people come to Hiroshima, and it should be. The museum documents what happened on August 6, 1945 with a directness and specificity that other memorial museums often avoid — personal objects, shadows burned into stone, recorded testimony. Budget two to three hours, not one.

The main building was rebuilt and rehung in 2019, and the sequence now leads with the human consequences before the historical and political context rather than after it. The effect is deliberate and it works. The objects carry it: a tricycle, a lunchbox with its contents carbonised, a school uniform, each with the name and age of the child it belonged to and a short account of where they were found.

It is a difficult two hours and you should plan the day around that rather than scheduling something cheerful immediately afterwards. Go in the morning while you have the energy for it. There are benches outside along the river, and taking half an hour there before doing anything else is the normal response, not an overreaction.

sections.heading: The rest of the park
paragraphs: The park is not only the museum, and the individual monuments repay knowing about in advance. The Genbaku Dome — the former Industrial Promotion Hall, left in exactly the state the blast left it — is the one image everyone knows. It stands almost directly under the detonation point, which is why any of it survived: the force came near-vertically down onto it rather than sideways.

The Children's Peace Monument commemorates Sadako Sasaki, who developed leukaemia at eleven and folded paper cranes toward a thousand in the belief that it would make her well. The glass cases around the monument hold cranes sent by schools from all over the world, and they are replaced constantly because the volume never stops.

The Cenotaph is worth standing in front of properly. It is a saddle-shaped arch holding the register of every named victim, and it is aligned so that looking through it frames the Flame of Peace and the Genbaku Dome behind it in a single line. The flame has burned since 1964 and is intended to be extinguished when the last nuclear weapon on earth is gone.

The hypocentre itself is not in the park. It is a small marker on an ordinary side street about 300 metres east, outside a clinic, with traffic going past. Finding it is a stranger experience than the park is.

sections.heading: Hiroshima beyond the park
paragraphs: Hiroshima has one of Japan's most interesting covered shotengai (shopping arcade) districts, centered around Hondori and its side streets. It's genuinely local — not a tourist market, but the arcade where people in Hiroshima buy clothes and eat lunch. The okonomiyaki restaurants here are a reason to visit Hiroshima independent of the memorial.

The thing that takes visitors a moment to absorb is that Hiroshima is a completely normal, busy, cheerful Japanese city of over a million people. It is not a memorial with a town attached. Spending the afternoon shopping and eating after spending the morning in the museum is not disrespectful; it is more or less the point the city has spent eighty years making.

sections.heading: Hiroshima okonomiyaki
paragraphs: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is different from Osaka okonomiyaki. The Osaka version mixes everything together; the Hiroshima version layers ingredients — batter, bean sprouts, cabbage, noodles (yes, noodles), pork, egg — in sequence on a flat griddle. The result is denser and more substantial than the Osaka style. Budget ¥1,000–1,400.

The specific place for it is Okonomimura, a three-floor building near the Hondori arcade with around 25 individual shops each making their version. Pick one that looks busy. The shops are nearly identical in menu and differ in the cook, so the crowd is the only signal you have and it is a good one.

Sit at the counter, not a table. The dish is built on the griddle in front of you over about ten minutes, served onto the hot metal directly rather than a plate, and eaten from there with a small metal spatula. Choose soba or udon for the noodle layer; soba is the default. Adding oysters is worth it between November and February, when Hiroshima Bay is producing most of Japan's supply.

sections.heading: Miyajima Island
paragraphs: Miyajima Island: a 10-minute ferry from Miyajimaguchi (covered by the JR Pass, as it is a JR service). The vermilion torii gate of Itsukushima Shrine, standing in the sea at high tide, is one of those images that is on every Japan poster and still manages to be more striking in person than in photographs.

Check the tide table before you go, because the island is effectively two different destinations. At high tide the gate and the shrine stand in water and the shrine's boardwalks appear to float. At low tide the water withdraws entirely and you can walk out across the sand to stand underneath the gate. Both are worth seeing and neither is a substitute for the other — the tide tables are published online and by the ferry operators.

Walk past the shrine to the hills. Daishoin Temple, on the slope above, is a working Shingon temple with a covered stairway lined with metal prayer wheels and a cave hall lit by hundreds of lanterns, and it is largely empty because most day-trippers stop at the shrine. Beyond it, Mt. Misen can be climbed in about two hours or reached by ropeway to a point twenty minutes' walk below the summit. The view from the top takes in the whole Seto Inland Sea.
The island also has deer, which are smaller and less aggressive than Nara's but will absolutely eat your map. There are no crackers sold here and feeding them is discouraged.

sections.heading: The castle, the garden, and the trams
paragraphs: Hiroshima Castle was flattened in 1945 and rebuilt in 1958. The keep is a concrete reconstruction housing a decent museum on the city's history as a castle town, and the grounds are pleasant. What is genuinely affecting is a eucalyptus and a willow inside the grounds that survived the blast and are still growing, marked as such.

Shukkeien is a formal garden dating from 1620, laid out around a central pond with a compressed miniature landscape of bridges, islands and tea houses. It was destroyed and became a refuge for the wounded in 1945; many died in it, and there is a memorial. It has been fully restored and is now simply a beautiful garden, half an hour's slow walk from end to end.

Get around by streetcar. Hiroshima kept its tram network when most Japanese cities scrapped theirs, and it is the easiest way to cross the city at a flat fare. Several cars still in service are pre-war, and a few of those were running on the morning of August 6 and were repaired and put back to work within days. They are marked, and riding one is a curious way to spend fifteen minutes.

sections.heading: How long to stay
paragraphs: Hiroshima is a half-day to full-day stop on the standard Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka route (Shinkansen from Shin-Osaka takes about 85 minutes). A full day allows the museum, Hondori, lunch, and a Miyajima trip, though it will be a compressed day and Miyajima will get the short end of it.

Staying overnight is the better call if you can. It gives Miyajima a proper half day rather than a rushed afternoon, and it gives you the city in the evening, when the riverbanks around the Motoyasu-gawa fill up and the Dome is lit. A night here also breaks up what is otherwise a long stretch of Kansai for most itineraries.

If you have two nights, stay one of them on Miyajima itself. The last ferry takes the day-trippers off around dusk, the island empties, and the shrine at night with nobody on the boardwalk is the version of the place that people who have been twice will tell you about.

title: Autumn Leaves in Japan: Where to Go and When the Timing Actually Works
excerpt: Koyo — autumn foliage — is not a fixed event. It starts in Hokkaido in September and ends in Kyushu in December. The timing requires a decision.
heroImageAlt: Maple trees in full autumn colour reflected in a garden pond in Kyoto
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: When koyo happens where
paragraphs: Japan's autumn colour season moves southward and downhill from September through late November. Hokkaido peaks first — late September to mid-October — while central Honshu peaks in early to mid-November. Kyushu and the warmer lowlands finish last, sometimes into December. 'When is the best time for autumn leaves?' depends entirely on where you're going, and the answer shifts by two to four weeks depending on whether you're in the mountains or at sea level.

Altitude moves faster than latitude. A mountain at 2,000 metres in Nagano turns weeks before the valley floor below it, which means a single day trip can take you from bare branches through peak colour to still-green trees. If your dates are fixed and the colour has not arrived where you are, going up is usually quicker than going north.

What triggers it is the cold: the leaves turn when night temperatures drop reliably below about 8°C, and the best years are those with warm days, cold nights and enough rain. A mild autumn delays everything by a week or more, which is why last year's dates are a weak guide to this year's.

sections.heading: How to check the forecast
paragraphs: Japan tracks the autumn colour front the same way it tracks the cherry blossom front, and the forecasts are published, updated weekly through the season, and free. The private weather companies run the most useful versions, with maps showing which locations are beginning to turn, at peak, and past it.

The vocabulary is worth learning because it appears on every site and most signs: mikoro means the colour has started, midokoro or migoro means it is at its best, and ochiba means the leaves are falling. Individual temples and parks publish their own status too, often with a photograph taken that morning, and that is the most reliable source of all.

Check three or four days out rather than three weeks. The front moves faster than long-range forecasts can track it, and a peak predicted in mid-October can shift a week either way by the time you get there.

sections.heading: Kyoto in November
paragraphs: Kyoto's season typically peaks in the second and third weeks of November. The problem: so does Kyoto's tourist density. Tenryu-ji in Arashiyama, Eikan-do near Nanzen-ji, the garden at Tofuku-ji — all spectacular, all packed. The answer is not to avoid them but to arrange your visit around timing. These gardens look different at 7:30am than at 11am. The light is better and the ratio of leaves to people is significantly higher.

Several temples open early specifically in November, and a handful run evening illuminations — Eikan-do and Kodai-ji are the well-known ones — where the maples are lit after dark and reflected in the ponds. The illuminations are crowded and they are also genuinely spectacular; buy tickets ahead where that is possible and go on a weekday.

The quieter alternative within Kyoto is to go north. Ohara, an hour out by bus, has Sanzen-in and a valley of maples with a fraction of the city's crowds. Kurama and Kibune, on the mountain railway, offer the same trade.

sections.heading: Nikko: the underrated option
paragraphs: Nikko, two hours by express from Asakusa or Ueno in Tokyo. The cryptomeria avenue leading to Tosho-gu, surrounded by beech and maple turning gold and orange, is one of the better koyo experiences in Japan and receives a fraction of Kyoto's November visitors.

The specific spot is the Irohazaka switchback road up to Lake Chuzenji — forty-eight hairpin bends, each labelled with a character of the old Japanese alphabet, through forest that turns completely. It is worth the drive if you have transport, or the bus if you don't, and the ropeway at the top opens the view across the whole valley.

One warning: Nikko peaks earlier than Kyoto, generally late October at altitude and early November lower down, and the Irohazaka traffic on an autumn weekend is legendarily bad. Go midweek and go early.

sections.heading: The Japanese Alps
paragraphs: For serious foliage, the high country peaks in October. Kamikochi, a river valley under the Hotaka range, is among the most beautiful places in Japan in autumn and closes for the winter in mid-November — the season is short and the reward is proportionate. The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route crosses the mountains by cable car, bus and ropeway through colour at several altitudes at once.

Shirakawa-go's thatched farmhouses surrounded by autumn maples is the kind of composition that doesn't require a good photographer; the scene does the work. It is also extremely popular, so the same early-morning rule applies.

These are mountain destinations with mountain weather. Snow at altitude in October is normal, roads and routes close without much notice, and the last buses run early. Check operating status before travelling, not after.

sections.heading: If you only have Tokyo
paragraphs: Tokyo turns late — the last week of November into early December — which is useful, because it means a trip that arrives after Kyoto has finished can still catch colour.

Rikugien and Koishikawa Korakuen are the two classic gardens, both compact, both with maples over water, and Rikugien runs an evening illumination. Meiji Jingu Gaien's ginkgo avenue is the other Tokyo image: three hundred metres of yellow trees in a straight line, peaking in early December and photographed by everybody.
Neither is a substitute for a mountain valley, and both are twenty minutes from a train station in the middle of a city of fourteen million, which is its own kind of remarkable.

sections.heading: What you are actually looking at
paragraphs: Two trees do most of the work and they are worth being able to tell apart, because signage names them. Momiji is the Japanese maple: small, deeply cut leaves, turning through yellow and orange to a deep red, and the tree that every temple garden is planted around. Icho is the ginkgo, fan-shaped leaves turning a uniform bright yellow, planted along city avenues rather than in gardens.

The distinction matters practically because they peak at different times — ginkgo runs one to two weeks behind maple in the same location. A city that has finished its maples may still have a fortnight of ginkgo ahead.
Ginkgo also drops fruit, which smells appalling. This is not a fault in your planning.

sections.heading: Rain and overcast days
paragraphs: What nobody says: rain makes autumn foliage better. The colours are more saturated, wet bark goes near-black and throws the leaves forward, and the light through wet maple leaves is different from the light through dry ones.

An overcast day in Kyoto in November is not a failed day; it is a different photograph and a quieter street. Bright midday sun is in fact the hardest light to work with, blowing out the reds and filling the gardens with people.

Adjust expectations and pack accordingly: a small umbrella, shoes that tolerate wet gravel, and a cloth for the lens. Temple gardens in the rain are among the best experiences available in Japan and most visitors sit them out in a café.

sections.heading: The practical window
paragraphs: If you have flexibility, aim for November 10 to 20 for central Honshu. Before that the colour is incomplete; after it, the leaves have begun to fall and you are watching the end of something.

Build in slack. A trip designed to hit peak colour on one specific day at one specific temple will fail about half the time, because the front is weather-driven and moves. A trip with three candidate locations at different altitudes over five days will succeed at one of them nearly always.
And book accommodation early. Kyoto in the third week of November is one of the two weeks of the year when the city genuinely runs out of rooms, and prices reflect it.

title: Beppu: The Onsen City That's Stranger and Better Than You Expect
excerpt: Beppu produces more geothermal steam per day than anywhere in Japan and possibly anywhere outside Iceland. The city treats this as completely normal.
heroImageAlt: Blue-green geothermal pool steaming at Umi Jigoku in Beppu
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What Beppu is
paragraphs: Beppu is on the north-east coast of Kyushu, about an hour and three quarters from Fukuoka by limited express. The city has eight distinct onsen districts, each with different mineral compositions and water colours — clear, milky white, reddish brown, and the vivid cobalt of the Kannawa area.

The steam rising off the streets on a cool morning makes it look as though the city is slowly cooking from below, which is more or less accurate. There are thousands of individual sources here, and the town produces more geothermal water per day than anywhere else in Japan.

The eight districts are collectively the Beppu Hatto, and they are genuinely different from each other. Beppu proper is the flat, slightly worn town centre by the station. Kannawa, up the hill, is the atmospheric one, full of steam vents and old bathhouses. Myoban is higher again and smells strongly of sulphur. Choosing which one to base yourself in matters more than choosing a hotel.

sections.heading: The Hell Tour
paragraphs: The Jigoku Meguri — the Hell Tour — is the headline attraction: seven pools of geothermally active water that cannot be bathed in because they are too hot, at close to boiling, or too acidic.

They are genuinely remarkable. Umi Jigoku, the Sea Hell, is a deep cobalt blue from dissolved iron sulphate. Chinoike Jigoku, the Blood Pond Hell, is exactly as red as it sounds, from iron oxide in the clay. Oniyama Jigoku keeps crocodiles, because the groundwater is warm enough to maintain tropical reptiles year-round, which is either delightful or dubious depending on your view.

A circuit ticket covers the set for around ¥2,200 and they are spread across two clusters, so allow half a day with a bus between them. It is unashamedly a tourist attraction and it is worth doing once — but it is not why you stay.

sections.heading: The baths are the actual reason
paragraphs: The bathing is why you stay overnight. Kannawa and the older neighbourhoods have small municipal baths — kyodo yokujo — for as little as ¥100–300. Coin-operated, simple tiled rooms, no facilities beyond a basket and a tap, and water that does things to your skin that a hotel bath does not replicate. Bring your own towel and soap; these places supply nothing.

Hyotan Onsen near Kannawa is the well-known larger option, with several pools including waterfall baths where hot water falls on your shoulders, and it stays open late. It holds a Michelin star for an onsen, which is a category most people do not know exists.

The water genuinely differs between districts. Myoban is sulphurous and milky and will tarnish silver; Kannawa is mineral-heavy; some of the coastal sources are salty. Bathing in three different districts in a day is the local sport and it is the correct way to spend one here.

sections.heading: Sand, steam and mud
paragraphs: Takegawara Onsen in the town centre is the famous sand bath: you lie in a shallow pit in a yukata and staff bury you in geothermally heated sand up to the neck. It sounds alarming and is instead comfortable in a way that is hard to convey. Ten to fifteen minutes is the standard session, and the weight of the sand is as much of the effect as the heat. The building itself dates from 1938 and is worth seeing regardless.

In Kannawa, the steam is used for cooking. Jigoku-mushi — hell steaming — means putting vegetables, eggs, seafood or meat into a stone box over a natural vent and letting the steam do it in ten minutes. Several places let you cook your own, and it is a genuinely good lunch as well as a novelty.

Myoban is where the yunohana huts are: thatched sheds where mineral crystals are harvested from the ground over months, a technique that has been going since the eighteenth century. You can buy the crystals to make onsen water at home, which is the best souvenir in the city.

sections.heading: Beppu or Yufuin
paragraphs: The two are half an hour apart and are constantly compared. Yufuin is the pretty one — a small town under a mountain, boutique inns, craft shops, art museums, and a main street that is essentially a promenade of gift shops. It is genuinely lovely and it is heavily curated.
Beppu is bigger, messier and considerably less polished, with a slightly faded seaside-resort quality and far more actual bathing. It is also much cheaper.
If you want a single elegant night, Yufuin. If you want to spend two days getting into as many different waters as possible, Beppu. Doing both is easy and is what most Japanese visitors do.

sections.heading: Tattoos, and the small baths
paragraphs: Beppu is unusually relaxed by Japanese standards, largely because so much of its bathing happens in tiny municipal baths run for local residents rather than in resort facilities. Many of the ¥100 baths have no staff at all.

That is not a guarantee. Larger facilities and hotel baths apply the standard policy, and the Hell circuit's associated baths are among the stricter. Ask, or book a room with a private bath, which is cheap here.
The private-bath option is genuinely inexpensive in Beppu — many ryokan have several family baths free to guests, which removes the question entirely.

sections.heading: Getting there and staying
paragraphs: The Sonic limited express from Hakata in Fukuoka takes around two hours and is covered by the JR Pass and by the Kyushu regional passes. From Osaka there is an overnight ferry, which is a slow and rather wonderful way to arrive.

The city is small enough that the main districts are reachable by local bus or a short taxi ride, and the bus day pass is worth buying on arrival. Kannawa is the best base for atmosphere, the station area for convenience and cheapness.

Ryokan here are genuinely affordable compared with Hakone — ¥10,000–15,000 per person including dinner and breakfast is achievable, and the food is Kyushu seafood. Beppu makes a strong case for being the most accessible serious onsen town in Japan.

One addition if you have a spare hour: Takasakiyama, just outside town, is a mountain with a resident population of well over a thousand wild macaques that come down to be fed twice a day. It is not an enclosure and the monkeys are entirely uninterested in you.

title: Japanese Stationery Is Worth the Suitcase Space
excerpt: Pens, notebooks, tape, paper clips. Japan has turned the mundane into an argument for why other countries aren't trying hard enough.
heroImageAlt: Rows of colorful washi tape rolls and stationery at a Japanese stationery shop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why this is worth half a day
paragraphs: The Pilot Hi-Tec-C is a 0.3mm gel pen that costs a couple of hundred yen at any stationery shop in Japan and writes with a precision that comparable pens elsewhere have not matched at any price. This is not enthusiasm. It is a statement about the difference between the Japanese stationery industry and everyone else's, and it is the reason to set aside half a day for stationery shopping.

The reason the gap exists is that paper never stopped being a serious consumer category here. Handwriting remains normal in Japanese offices and schools, the writing system rewards a fine, controlled line in a way the Latin alphabet does not, and a domestic market that cares produces manufacturers that compete on tenths of a millimetre. Pilot, Uni, Zebra, Pentel, Tombow and Sakura are all still fighting over the same pencil case.

sections.heading: Where to go
paragraphs: Itoya in Ginza is the institution — twelve floors, operating since 1904, with a whole floor given over to loose paper and another to fountain pens. It is for people who want to be deliberate and spend two hours doing it. Loft is the department-store format: wide selection, efficient, branches everywhere. Hands, formerly Tokyu Hands, has the broadest range if you want craft supplies alongside the stationery.

Two smaller places are worth the detour. Sekaido in Shinjuku is an art-supply store over several floors with prices well below the department stores, and it is where students actually shop. Kakimori in Kuramae builds custom notebooks — you choose the cover, the paper, the rings and the closure, and they assemble it while you wait, which is the single best stationery souvenir available in Tokyo.

Outside the specialists, the stationery aisle of any large supermarket or the ¥100 shops are both better than the best stationery shop in most countries. Daiso and Seria sell perfectly good notebooks, pens and desk accessories for a hundred yen, and for buying in bulk for other people they are unbeatable.

sections.heading: Notebooks and planners
paragraphs: The Hobonichi Techo is the cult object: an A6 daily planner with a page per day, published by the company Shigesato Itoi built, and sold in several formats including the larger Cousin and the slimmer Weeks. Its reputation rests on the paper, which is unusually thin and takes fountain pen ink without bleeding through. The edition year matters, and the covers are sold separately.

Midori's MD notebooks are the plainer, cheaper alternative and arguably the better everyday book: cream paper, exposed binding that lets the book lie flat, no branding on the cover at all. The A5 blank is a few hundred yen and it is the notebook to buy several of.

The Traveler's Notebook is the third of the big three — a leather cover holding replaceable paper inserts, designed to be beaten up and refilled for years. There is a dedicated shop at Nakameguro station. Kokuyo's Campus notebooks are what every Japanese student actually uses, cost almost nothing, and are excellent.

sections.heading: Pens worth buying
paragraphs: For everyday gel pens: the Uni-ball One in 0.38mm and 0.5mm, which has a denser black than anything in its price class, and the Pilot Juice line for colours. The Zebra Mildliner is the highlighter to buy — dual-tipped, in muted tones that do not glare off the page — and it is cheap enough to buy the full set.

Multi-pens are a Japanese speciality and underrated abroad. The Uni Jetstream 4&1 puts four ballpoint colours and a pencil in one barrel that actually writes well, which is not true of multi-pens generally. Bodies and refills are sold separately, so you can build one.

For fountain pens, the entry point is the Pilot Kakuno at around a thousand yen — a genuinely good nib in a plastic body with a smiling face stamped on it. Above that, Pilot, Sailor and Platinum all make serious pens at prices well below the European brands, and Pilot's Iroshizuku inks are the ones people bring home in quantity. Ask to try a nib before buying; every fountain pen counter expects it.

sections.heading: Tape, and the small stuff
paragraphs: Washi masking tape is the category Japan invented as a consumer product, and mt is the brand that did it — the manufacturer made industrial masking tape until a group of customers asked for colours. It comes in hundreds of patterns and widths at a few hundred yen a roll, removes cleanly, repositions, and takes ink. Department stores and the larger stationery shops carry deep selections, and limited regional designs turn up in station shops.

The unglamorous items are where the quality gap is most obvious. Tombow Mono erasers actually erase. Kokuyo's Harinacs staples paper without staples by punching and folding it. Correction tape here runs smooth and does not tear. Sakura's Pigma Micron pens are the archival drawing pens most illustrators outside Japan also use.

Also worth a look: the seal and sticker aisles, the letter sets and envelopes at Itoya, and the enormous range of pencil cases. None of this is expensive and all of it is better made than it needs to be.

sections.heading: The suitcase argument
paragraphs: Stationery is light and flat. A full day's shopping fits in a document bag. The pens weigh nothing, the Hobonichi is the size of a passport, and a stack of MD notebooks takes up less room than a pair of shoes.

This is the one gift category where there is no excuse not to buy for everyone you know, and where the ¥300 item is genuinely as good a present as the ¥3,000 one. A Mildliner set and two good pens costs under two thousand yen and will be used every day for a year, which is more than most souvenirs manage.

title: Eating at a Sushi Counter: What to Expect and How to Not Ruin It
excerpt: The sushi counter is not intimidating once you understand that there are three rules, they're easy, and the chef wants you to enjoy it.
heroImageAlt: A sushi chef preparing nigiri behind a counter with fresh fish displayed in a glass case
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Counter, conveyor, and standing
paragraphs: Counter sushi is different from kaiten in format, price and the nature of the relationship between you and the chef. At the counter there are usually eight to twelve seats and a glass case of today's fish. You either take a set omakase — chef's choice — or point at items and they are made in front of you. The fish was at the market this morning, the rice is slightly warm, and the whole operation is built around immediacy.

Kaiten, the conveyor belt, is not a lesser version so much as a different product: cheap, fast, family-friendly, and now mostly ordered from a touchscreen with the plates arriving on an express lane. It is genuinely fun and the good chains are far better than the format suggests.

The third category is tachigui, standing sushi bars, which serve counter-quality fish to people who eat six pieces in fifteen minutes and leave. They are the best value in the entire category and are worth seeking out.

sections.heading: The three rules
paragraphs: One: eat each piece as soon as it is placed in front of you. The rice is seasoned and tempered for eating now, not in three minutes. Sushi that sits changes, and at a counter the chef is timing each piece to the last.
Two: it is entirely acceptable to eat nigiri with your fingers, and this is the traditional method. Chopsticks work but risk the topping sliding off. Sashimi is always chopsticks.

Three: dip fish-side down, not rice-side down. Soy sauce in the rice makes the piece fall apart and oversalts the bite. Turn it over gently and touch the fish to the surface of the dish rather than soaking it.

sections.heading: How omakase actually works
paragraphs: Omakase means you have handed the decision to the chef, and the sequence is deliberate: lighter white fish first to calibrate the palate, then progressively richer, with the fatty tuna, the sea urchin and the eel later, and a rolled piece and tamago at the end.

You are not expected to say anything except at the start and the end. Tell them at the start if there is something you cannot eat — allergies, or you simply hate uni — and it will be quietly replaced. At a smaller counter, saying how hungry you are is useful information.

When the sequence has finished the chef will ask if you would like anything else. This is your moment to order a repeat of whatever you liked most, which is the correct and slightly flattering thing to do.

sections.heading: What to know about the fish
paragraphs: The tuna hierarchy is worth learning because it appears everywhere: akami is the lean red meat, chutoro the medium-fatty belly, otoro the fattiest. Otoro is the expensive one and it is overwhelming in quantity — chutoro is the piece most people actually enjoy more.

The words for the formats: nigiri is fish over a hand-pressed finger of rice, gunkan is the ones wrapped in a nori band to hold something loose like roe or urchin, maki is rolled, sashimi is fish alone with no rice at all.
Gunkan cannot be dipped without falling apart. The counter method is to use a slice of pickled ginger as a brush to paint soy sauce on top, which is what the ginger dish beside you is quietly for.
Fish is seasonal here in a way that is taken seriously. If the chef points at something and says it is in season now, order that.

sections.heading: Ginger, wasabi and tea
paragraphs: Ginger is a palate cleanser eaten between pieces, not a topping. Wasabi is already inside the piece at a proper counter, applied in the amount the chef judged right for that fish. Asking for extra is allowed and is a mild statement that you disagree with them; nobody minds.
Do not stir wasabi into your soy sauce at a counter. It is normal at a conveyor place and it is not done in front of a chef who put a measured amount into every piece.
The tea is called agari and it comes hot, strong and unlimited. It is deliberately astringent, to cut the fat between pieces.

sections.heading: Booking, cost and the lunch trick
paragraphs: The most common misconception is that counter sushi is prohibitively expensive. At a mid-range counter away from Ginza, ¥3,000–5,000 buys a satisfying meal of eight to ten pieces plus tea. The ¥20,000 experience exists and is extraordinary, but it is not the entry point.

Lunch is the trick. A great many serious sushi restaurants serve a lunch set using the same fish from the same case at a third to a half of the dinner price. Booking a famous counter for lunch instead of dinner is not a compromise.

The very top places are booked months ahead, often only through a hotel concierge or an existing customer, and some do not take foreign bookings directly. That is a real barrier and it is also irrelevant to having an excellent meal — the gap between a ¥5,000 counter and a ¥40,000 one is far smaller than the price difference implies.

sections.heading: The small courtesies
paragraphs: Do not wear strong perfume or aftershave to a sushi counter. You are sitting a metre from someone whose work depends on smelling fish, and this is a genuine request that good restaurants sometimes make explicitly.
Do not photograph the chef without asking; photographing your own plate is fine. Keep your phone off the counter — it is a work surface.
There is no tipping. Say gochisousama deshita on the way out, which at a counter reaches the person who made your food directly, and is worth more than money would be.

title: Nara Beyond the Deer: What to Do After the First Hour
excerpt: Yes, the deer are free-roaming and yes, they will bow to get crackers from you. This takes about 40 minutes. Nara has a full day's worth of things after that.
heroImageAlt: Sika deer roaming free in Nara Park with Todai-ji temple visible through the trees
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The deer
paragraphs: Nara Park has approximately 1,200 sika deer that have been designated national treasures and have, over generations of contact with tourists, learned that a particular bowing gesture triggers cracker-giving. You can buy shika-senbei (deer crackers) from vendors at ¥200 a pack. The deer will absolutely approach you. Some will grab your bag. One will probably bite you lightly on the jacket. This is fine and expected and takes under an hour before it becomes routine. The question is what you do with the rest of the day.

Two practical warnings. Do not tease them with the crackers — holding food above your head to draw out the bowing produces butting and nipping from animals that weigh fifty kilos, and the injury statistics are not zero. Buy a pack, hand it out promptly, show your empty hands, and they lose interest immediately.

And keep paper out of reach. They eat maps, tickets, and the corners of guidebooks with real enthusiasm. Anything in an outside pocket is fair game. The crackers themselves are made without any packaging for exactly this reason.

The deer are wild animals with legal protection rather than a managed attraction, which is why there are no fences and why they wander into the road, the shops and occasionally the train station. Autumn is rutting season and the males are genuinely unpredictable; the park cuts their antlers each October in a public ceremony that dates back to the 1600s.

sections.heading: Todai-ji
paragraphs: Todai-ji Temple: one of the largest wooden buildings in the world and home to a 15-meter bronze Buddha (the Nara Daibutsu) that has been sitting in approximately the same position since 752 AD. Entrance is ¥600. The scale is genuinely difficult to convey — the Buddha's nostril is the size of a small door, and there is a pillar inside the building with a hole at the base that's the same diameter as the nostril, which children (and optimistic adults) attempt to crawl through as a matter of ritual.

The building you are standing in is the third one. The first two burned in wars, in 1180 and 1567, and the current hall dates from 1709 — at which point the country could not afford the original width, so it was rebuilt at about two thirds of the earlier scale. That is worth pausing on, because it means the original was half again as wide as the enormous building in front of you.

Do not walk straight through the Nandaimon, the great gate on the approach. Set into its two sides are a pair of eight-metre guardian figures carved in 1203 by Unkei and Kaikei and their workshop, in a couple of months, out of thousands of pieces of joined wood. They are among the greatest sculptures in Japan and most visitors photograph the gate from outside and never look up into the alcoves.

sections.heading: Nigatsudo, the part people miss
paragraphs: Up the hill behind the Daibutsu hall, five minutes on a stone staircase, is Nigatsudo. It is free, it is open at all hours, and its wooden veranda looks out west over the whole of Nara with the temple roofs in the foreground. It is the best view in the city and it is nearly always quiet.

It is also the site of Omizutori, a fire and water ritual performed every year for over 1,250 years without interruption — through wars, fires and the pandemic. For two weeks in March, monks run along that veranda at night carrying six-metre burning cedar torches and shower sparks over the crowd below. If you are in Kansai in early March, reorganise your evening for it.
The lane between Todai-ji and Nigatsudo, walled and stone-paved, is the prettiest short walk in Nara and takes about eight minutes.

sections.heading: Kasuga Taisha
paragraphs: Kasuga Taisha: a Shinto shrine established in 768 AD, famous for its 3,000 stone and bronze lanterns that are lit twice a year (Setsubun in February and Obon in August). The path through the cedar forest to reach it is as good as the shrine itself — moss-covered stone lanterns lining the approach, deer wandering between the cedars. Entry to the outer grounds is free; the inner precinct is ¥500.

Pay the ¥500. The inner corridors are where the bronze lanterns hang in ranks under the eaves, and there is a dark room where a small number of them are kept lit permanently between mirrored walls, which gives you the lantern festival on any ordinary Tuesday.

The shrine was rebuilt to an identical design every twenty years for most of its history, in the same tradition as Ise, which is why a building founded in 768 looks new. The forest behind it has been protected from logging since the ninth century and is now primary woodland in the middle of a city — a genuinely rare thing.

sections.heading: Kofuku-ji and the National Museum
paragraphs: Kofuku-ji sits at the western edge of the park, closest to the stations, and its five-storey pagoda is the second tallest in Japan and the building most people photograph without knowing what it is. The grounds are open and free to walk through.

The reason to pay to go inside is the Ashura statue in the treasure hall: a 1,300-year-old dry-lacquer figure of a three-faced, six-armed guardian with the face of a teenager and an expression that is not the fierce one the form calls for but something closer to sorrow. It is one of the most famous objects in Japanese art and it is startlingly modern in feeling.

The Nara National Museum next door holds the country's best collection of Buddhist sculpture. For two weeks each autumn it also opens the Shosoin exhibition — objects from the eighth-century imperial treasure house, including Persian glass and Central Asian instruments that arrived along the Silk Road and have never been buried or excavated, only stored. If your visit coincides, prioritise it over everything else on this page.

sections.heading: Naramachi
paragraphs: Naramachi: the preserved merchant town directly south of Nara Park. Narrow alleys, machiya townhouses, textile shops, sake breweries, and craft cafés — the kind of neighborhood that was here 200 years ago and has been left largely intact. It's quieter than the park area and full of places to eat.

Nakatanidou, on the approach to the park, pounds mochi in public several times an hour — two men, one enormous wooden mallet, and a rhythm fast enough that it looks unsafe. A warm yomogi mochi rolled in kinako, eaten standing up, costs a couple of hundred yen and is one of the better small pleasures in Kansai.

Look for the small red cloth balls hanging outside the old houses. They are migawari-zaru, substitute monkeys, one for each member of the household, hung to take on misfortune in their place. Once you have noticed one you will see them on every street in the district.

sections.heading: Getting there and timing
paragraphs: Nara is 45 minutes from Kyoto by JR (¥730 or JR Pass) or about the same on the Kintetsu Line. It works as a half-day or full-day trip from either Kyoto or Osaka.

The choice of line matters more than it looks. Kintetsu Nara Station is a five-minute walk from the park. JR Nara Station is about twenty minutes away, or a short bus ride. If you are not using a JR Pass, Kintetsu is the better option; if you are, factor the walk in.

The main park and Todai-ji can be crowded in the morning; the deer and crowds thin significantly after 3pm. If you're coming on a weekday and can arrive at 8:30am, the park before the day-trippers show up is a genuinely different experience. Todai-ji opens at 7:30am for much of the year, which is early enough to have the Daibutsu almost to yourself.

sections.heading: A workable order for one day
paragraphs: Arrive early and go straight to Todai-ji before the coaches, then up to Nigatsudo for the view while it is still quiet. Walk the wooded path south to Kasuga Taisha, which puts you in the forest during the best light of the morning. That is the heavy half of the day and it is done by about noon.

Come down through the park to Kofuku-ji, eat in Naramachi, and spend the afternoon in the district at whatever pace you like. If the museum is showing something you want, put it after lunch. Head back to the station via Nakatanidou.

This leaves out Mt. Wakakusa, the grass hill on the eastern edge, which is worth an hour if you have it — a short steep climb, a ¥150 entry, and a view back over the temple roofs. It is burned to the ground every January in a festival nobody has a confirmed explanation for.

title: Golden Week: What It Is, Why It Will Destroy Your Trip, and When to Go Instead
excerpt: Golden Week runs from late April to early May. If your trip overlaps it — or Obon, or New Year — you have two options: embrace the chaos or reschedule.
heroImageAlt: Crowded hanami cherry blossom viewing in Ueno Park during Golden Week
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What Golden Week is
paragraphs: Golden Week is Japan's largest consecutive holiday period — a cluster of four national holidays between April 29 and May 5 that most companies treat as a full week off. Around 20 million Japanese people travel domestically during this window. International visitors add to this. The result is that every popular destination, every Shinkansen, every tourist attraction, and every hotel in Japan is at or near maximum capacity simultaneously.

The four are Showa Day on April 29, Constitution Memorial Day on May 3, Greenery Day on May 4 and Children's Day on May 5. How long the break actually runs depends on where those dates fall in the week: when they line up with a weekend the country gets nine or ten consecutive days off, and when they scatter across a Tuesday and a Thursday many people take the gaps as leave anyway.

Check the calendar for your specific year rather than assuming the dates. A Golden Week that produces a ten-day block is a materially different proposition from one that produces two separate four-day weekends, and hotels price accordingly.

sections.heading: The other two weeks nobody warns you about
paragraphs: Golden Week gets the attention because it has a name in English, but there are three periods of mass domestic travel in Japan and the other two catch visitors just as hard.

Obon, in mid-August, is when people return to their home towns to visit family graves. It is not a run of national holidays — only Mountain Day on August 11 is official — but the entire country moves at once for roughly a week around August 13 to 16. Trains and flights fill, rural accommodation books out, and city businesses close for several days. It is also the hottest and most humid part of the Japanese year, which makes it the worst of the three to be caught in.

New Year is the biggest of all, running roughly December 29 to January 3. This one is different in kind: the problem is not crowds at attractions but closure. Restaurants, small shops, museums and many businesses simply shut, sometimes for a week. Shrines, meanwhile, are extraordinarily busy with hatsumode, the first visit of the year, and the major ones handle millions of people over three days.

If your dates are fixed and they land on New Year, plan around what is open rather than what is crowded — department stores, chain restaurants and convenience stores keep running, and the shrine visit is genuinely worth doing once.

sections.heading: What actually happens
paragraphs: The Tokaido Shinkansen from Tokyo to Osaka sells out weeks in advance and runs extra services that also sell out. Popular ryokan are fully booked four to six months ahead. The queue for Fushimi Inari in Kyoto, normally manageable at 7am, is significant by 8am. Hakone accommodation triples in price. Narita arrivals and departures are maximally busy.

The traffic is the part people underestimate. Expressway congestion during Golden Week is reported in tens of kilometres, and a drive that takes three hours in October takes seven. If any part of your plan involves a rental car or a highway bus, assume it will not run to schedule.
None of this is impossible to navigate; it's just not the Japan trip most people imagine. The photographs that made you want to come were taken on a Tuesday in February.

sections.heading: If you are already booked
paragraphs: Lean into it. Go to places that are interesting specifically when full of Japanese people rather than tourists. City parks during Golden Week — Yoyogi in Tokyo, Maruyama in Kyoto — are excellent: families with picnic setups, food stalls, outdoor performances, a festive atmosphere that you don't get in October. The experience is genuinely different rather than categorically worse.

This is also the best week of the year for festivals, since they are scheduled to coincide with the holiday. Local matsuri run in most towns, and they are the version of Japan that is impossible to see on a quiet weekend in autumn.

The practical adjustments: stay in one city rather than moving between three, book restaurants ahead rather than walking in, start each day at opening time, and accept that the famous sites are a write-off between ten and four. Base yourself somewhere with good local transit and treat long-distance travel as the thing to avoid.

sections.heading: The booking timeline
paragraphs: Work backwards from the constraint that binds first. Ryokan and anything in Hakone, Kyoto or a hot-spring town: six months out, and the good ones go earlier. Domestic flights: as soon as the schedule opens, typically around two months. Shinkansen reserved seats: exactly one month before departure, which is when JR opens sales, and the popular departures go in the first hours.

If you have a JR Pass, reserved seats cost nothing and you can hold as many as you like, so reserve every leg the moment you activate. Non-reserved cars during Golden Week are standing room from Tokyo to Kyoto, and standing for two and a half hours with luggage is a specific kind of misery.
If you do not have a pass, buy through JR's Ekinet system or at any ticket office as far ahead as the rules allow. Same-day travel during these weeks is not a plan.

sections.heading: When to go instead
paragraphs: The weeks immediately after Golden Week ends — roughly May 10 to 25 — are among the best of the year. The weather is mild, the crowds have dispersed, hotel rates drop back to normal, and the new green on the maples is a genuinely underrated sight that gets no attention because everyone is looking at cherry blossom two months earlier.

Late October and early November give autumn colour with manageable crowds, though Kyoto in the third week of November is its own crush. Late September, after the summer humidity breaks and before the foliage crowds arrive, is quiet and pleasant. And January, once New Year is over, has the fewest tourists and the best value on onsen towns of any month.

One more to know about: the September holidays around Respect for the Aged Day and the autumn equinox occasionally align into a long run that the press calls Silver Week. It is nothing like Golden Week in scale, but in the years it lines up, domestic travel spikes for four or five days.

title: What to Buy When You Buy Japanese Sake
excerpt: Sake is rice wine in the same way that champagne is grape juice. The category is more complex than most people expect, and the range of quality is enormous.
heroImageAlt: Rows of sake bottles at a specialist sake shop in Japan
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The two main variables
paragraphs: Sake is fermented rice, water, yeast, and koji mold. The main variables: how much the rice has been polished before brewing (the seimaibuai, expressed as a percentage of the grain remaining), and whether distilled alcohol has been added. These two factors create the main classification categories that appear on labels and that are worth understanding before you buy anything.

Polishing matters because the outside of a rice grain holds the proteins and fats, and the centre is nearly pure starch. Milling away the outer layers gives a cleaner, more aromatic, more fragile sake — and throws away most of the grain, which is why a bottle polished to 40% costs what it does. It is not a quality score so much as a style dial: heavily polished sake is delicate and floral, lightly polished sake is savoury and full.

The added alcohol is misunderstood. A small measured addition late in the brew is a traditional technique that pulls out aroma compounds and lightens the body; it is not padding. Cheap bulk sake does use it to stretch volume, which is where the suspicion comes from, but a good honjozo is a deliberate style and often the better match for hot food.

sections.heading: Classifications that matter
paragraphs: Junmai: pure rice sake, no added alcohol. Honjozo: a small amount of distilled alcohol added, which lightens the sake and adds aroma. Ginjo: rice polished to at least 60% remaining, more aromatic. Daiginjo: polished to at least 50%, typically the most delicate and expensive. Combine these: Junmai Daiginjo is pure rice, top-tier polish. Futsushu is table sake — no premium designation, reasonable for everyday drinking.

Those eight combinations are the tokutei meishoshu, the special designations, and roughly a third of all sake made qualifies for one. Everything else is futsushu. A bottle carrying any of the eight names on the label has met a legal standard; a bottle covered in adjectives and carrying none of them has not.

Two further words appear constantly and change what you are buying more than the grade does. Namazake is unpasteurised — fresher, livelier, and requiring refrigeration from the brewery to your glass. Genshu is undiluted, arriving at 18–20% alcohol instead of the usual 15%, which is a different drink entirely and worth knowing before you pour a full cup of it.

sections.heading: Reading the rest of the label
paragraphs: Two numbers turn up on back labels and they are the closest thing to a taste description you will get. The nihonshudo, or sake meter value, runs from roughly -5 to +15: negative is sweeter, positive is drier, zero is neutral. The san-do, or acidity, sits around 1.0 to 2.0, and higher means more structure and a sharper finish.

They interact, which is why neither works alone. A +10 with high acidity is bracingly dry; a +10 with low acidity just tastes clean. If you liked something, photograph the back label and match the pair of numbers next time rather than the brewery name.
The rice variety is sometimes given too. Yamada Nishiki is the prestige grain, grown for brewing and prized for how well it mills; if a shop is pointing at it, they are pointing at a serious bottle.

sections.heading: What to actually buy
paragraphs: For a gift or something to drink on the trip: a Junmai Ginjo or Junmai Daiginjo from a mid-sized regional brewery priced between ¥2,000 and ¥5,000 for a 720ml bottle. The big names — Dassai, Kubota, Hakkaisan — are reliably good and widely available in department stores and specialist shops; they became famous because they're excellent. Dassai's numbers refer to the polish: Dassai 23 is milled to 23% remaining and priced accordingly, while Dassai 39 is similar in character for considerably less.

The more interesting purchase is a brewery you have never heard of from the region you are standing in. There are well over a thousand breweries in Japan, most of them small, and a great many never distribute beyond their own prefecture. A ¥2,500 junmai ginjo from a local kura is the bottle you cannot buy at home, and the shop staff will steer you if you say where you are from and what you like.

If you want to taste before committing, the sake tasting rooms attached to some stations and airports are the efficient route. The Ponshukan at Echigo-Yuzawa is the famous one — a wall of machines pouring small measures from around a hundred local breweries for a token each.

sections.heading: Nigori, sparkling, and aged
paragraphs: Nigori sake — unfiltered, cloudy, with rice sediment left in — is best drunk cold and fresh and doesn't travel as well. If you're drinking in Japan, try it; if you're buying to bring home, stick to clear filtered sake in sealed bottles.

Sparkling sake has grown into a real category rather than a novelty, usually around 8% alcohol, faintly sweet, and the single easiest bottle to hand someone who says they do not like sake. Most of it is meant to be drunk young and cold.

Koshu is aged sake, held for years until it turns amber and develops something closer to sherry or dried fruit. It divides people sharply and is worth a small glass somewhere before you buy a bottle of it.

sections.heading: Temperature, and the glass
paragraphs: Serving temperature is not a detail. Ginjo and daiginjo are aromatic and fragile, and heating them destroys precisely what you paid for — these are chilled drinks. Junmai and honjozo, which are fuller and more savoury, are the ones that reward warming, and warm sake is a genuinely different and underrated pleasure.

The vocabulary is worth a line: reishu is chilled, hiya is room temperature, nurukan is around 40°C, atsukan is hot. In an izakaya, ordering junmai nurukan in winter marks you out as someone who has thought about it.

Drink aromatic sake from a wine glass rather than the small ochoko cup. The cup is for pouring for other people, which is the actual social function; the wide bowl is what lets you smell a daiginjo. Serious sake bars will hand you a wine glass without being asked.

sections.heading: Where to buy
paragraphs: Department store basement floors have the best curated range and staff who can explain what they're selling. Specialist sake shops exist in most cities — Hasegawa Saketen has branches in and around Tokyo Station with English-speaking staff and a standing bar attached, which makes it the easiest single stop for a visitor.

Avoid convenience store sake for gifts; it's functional but unmemorable. The one exception worth making is cup sake — the small glass tumblers with foil lids, sold everywhere for a few hundred yen. They are the correct thing to drink on a long train journey and the printed cups make oddly good small souvenirs.

Look for a shop with a refrigerated section and stock in it. A sakaya that keeps its namazake and its ginjo cold is telling you it takes the stock seriously; a shop with premium bottles standing in a warm window in August is telling you the opposite.

sections.heading: Getting it home
paragraphs: Premium sake is best kept refrigerated and consumed within a few months of purchase. Nigori and namazake degrade fastest. Honjozo and futsushu are more forgiving. Buy what you can drink.

Practical transport notes: bottles cannot go in hand luggage, so anything you buy in the city must be packed and checked. The 720ml standard bottle is glass and heavy — two of them plus packaging is around three kilos. Wrap them in clothing in the middle of the case, or buy the padded bottle sleeves sold at the airport and most department stores.

Duty-free shops after security are the exception, since those bottles are sealed and can be carried on. Check your own country's allowance before you buy four bottles; the limits are lower than most people assume, and sake is taxed as a wine-strength product in most places.

title: Hokkaido in July: Japan's Best-Kept Summer Secret
excerpt: Tokyo in July is 35 degrees and 90% humidity. Hokkaido in July is 22 degrees and clear. These two facts explain a lot.
heroImageAlt: Lavender fields in full bloom at Farm Tomita in Furano, Hokkaido
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The climate case
paragraphs: Hokkaido is Japan's northernmost island and its least densely populated. The summer climate is a direct consequence of this geography: while central Honshu is enduring a summer that most temperate-climate visitors find difficult, Hokkaido is experiencing something close to a Northern European July. Average temperatures in Sapporo in July run 22–25°C, with lower humidity. It's possible to walk outside without immediately sweating through your clothes. For visitors arriving from humid climates, this discovery is approximately life-changing.

The other half of the case is the rainy season. Honshu, Kyushu and Shikoku spend roughly six weeks from early June under tsuyu, a near-continuous wet grey that ruins a lot of first trips to Japan. Hokkaido is the one region the front does not reach. June, which is a poor month almost everywhere else in the country, is one of the best months here.

Pack for it properly. Mornings and evenings drop into the low teens, and the high country is colder again — a summer day at Asahidake can sit around 10°C with wind. A light insulating layer and a waterproof shell are not optional, and visitors who packed for a Japanese summer are visibly cold by seven in the evening.

sections.heading: Lavender fields in Furano
paragraphs: The lavender fields of Furano are the most photographed image of Hokkaido summer: long rows of purple lavender against a backdrop of hills and clouds, peaking in early to mid-July. Farm Tomita in Furano is the most famous, and is legitimately beautiful despite being a tourist operation. Come early morning. The crowds arrive by 10am. The lavender at 7am with mist still on the hills is the real version of the photograph you've seen.

The bloom window is narrow — broadly the first three weeks of July, with the peak usually in the middle. Arrive in late June and you get green rows; arrive in August and the harvest has been cut. The farms publish bloom status, and building a trip around lavender without checking it is the most common way to be disappointed by Hokkaido.

Farm Tomita is free to enter and makes its money on lavender ice cream, soft drinks and cosmetics, which is a reasonable trade. If the crowds are too much, the smaller Choei Lavender Farm on the hillside above Nakafurano charges nothing, has a chairlift up through the rows, and is materially quieter for a nearly identical view.

sections.heading: Biei and the Panorama Road
paragraphs: Biei: a small town 20 kilometers north of Furano with rolling farmland — patchwork fields of potato, wheat, sunflower, and canola — that attracts photographers specifically for the quality of the light in summer. Renting a bicycle and spending the morning on the Panorama Road is the correct approach. No specific sight to reach; the road and the fields are the destination.

Take an electric bicycle rather than a standard one. The landscape photographs as gentle and rides as a continuous series of long climbs; rental shops by the station stock e-bikes for a modest premium and it is the difference between a pleasant morning and an ordeal.

There are named trees out here — the Ken and Mary Tree, the Seven Stars Tree, the Philosophy Tree — which became landmarks after appearing in cigarette and car advertisements decades ago. They are single trees in fields. Some visitors find the pilgrimage charming and others find it baffling; both reactions are correct. The Blue Pond a few kilometres away is the genuinely unusual sight: an artificial reservoir whose mineral content turns it an opaque cobalt with dead birch trunks standing in it.

One rule that matters here: the fields are working farms and not scenery. People walk into them for photographs every season, compact the soil, and destroy crops. Stay on the roads and the marked verges.

sections.heading: Sapporo
paragraphs: Sapporo: the capital and the city that functions as the base. The Odori Park beer garden runs all summer (July–August) — rows of tables under the elm trees with brewery stalls from Sapporo, Asahi, Kirin, and Suntory running simultaneously. This is worth a single evening on its own terms.

Soup curry, a Sapporo invention, is served in most restaurants here and is one of those regional dishes that makes no sense until you've eaten it: a thin spiced broth rather than a thick sauce, served with rice on the side and large pieces of vegetable and a chicken leg sitting in it. You choose a spice level and a rice size. It is the city's best cheap meal.

The other two things to eat are the seafood and the ramen. Nijo Market in the centre and the larger Curb Market near Nijujo Station do rice bowls piled with crab, sea urchin and salmon roe from around ¥2,000 — Hokkaido is where most of Japan's supply comes from, and the difference in a bowl eaten here is not subtle. For ramen, the miso version is the local style, and Susukino has the highest concentration of shops worth trying.

Sapporo is also unusually easy to navigate for a Japanese city. It was laid out on a grid in the 1870s with numbered blocks running north–south and east–west from a central point, so an address tells you exactly where a place is — which is not true anywhere else in the country.

sections.heading: Daisetsuzan National Park
paragraphs: The Daisetsuzan National Park: the largest national park in Japan, an alpine region accessible from multiple trailheads. The ropeway at Asahidake gives access to volcanic terrain above 1,500 meters where the hiking is excellent and the views extend across the island. A serious day-hike into the high terrain will not intersect with many other people and looks nothing like the rest of Japan.

The short version from the top of the ropeway is a marked loop of about an hour across a plateau of steaming vents, sulphur, and small alpine ponds. It requires no equipment beyond decent shoes and it is worth the trip on its own. The climb to the summit of Asahidake, Hokkaido's highest peak, is roughly two and a half hours up from the ropeway station and is a real mountain walk on loose volcanic scree.

Treat it as a mountain, not an attraction. Weather here changes fast and visibility can close in within twenty minutes; the ropeway suspends service in high wind, which can leave you walking down. Check the forecast, carry layers and water, and note that this is brown bear country — the population in Daisetsuzan is substantial. Carry a bell, make noise, and read the trailhead notices, which post recent sightings.
Snow lingers at altitude into July, and the alpine flowers come out immediately behind it. Mid-July to mid-August is the window where the high routes are reliably clear.

sections.heading: Getting there and getting around
paragraphs: Sapporo (New Chitose Airport) is 1h40m from Tokyo by air. Domestic flights are cheap — book at least three weeks in advance for ¥8,000–15,000 return. The route is one of the busiest air corridors in the world, which is why the fares stay low.

The Shinkansen does not reach Sapporo. It currently terminates at Shin-Hakodate-Hokuto in the south of the island, and the remaining leg is a further three and a half hours by limited express. Total journey time from Tokyo is eight hours or more. Unless you specifically want the ride, fly.

Once you're there, a rental car is the right choice for Furano and Biei; trains exist but the timing is inconvenient for covering multiple areas in a day. Distances are the thing visitors misjudge — Hokkaido is roughly the size of Austria with a fraction of the rail density, and two hours between places is normal. An international driving permit obtained before you leave home is required, and roads here are wide, well-surfaced and empty by Japanese standards.

If you would rather not drive, the Furano–Biei Norokko sightseeing train runs in summer between Asahikawa and Furano and stops at a temporary station beside the lavender farm, which covers the two headline sights without a car.

title: Koenji and Shimokitazawa: Tokyo for People Who've Already Done Harajuku
excerpt: Two stops on different lines. Two neighborhoods that run on thrift stores, live music, and a specific refusal to be improved.
heroImageAlt: Narrow street in Shimokitazawa lined with vintage clothing shops and cafes
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What these neighborhoods are
paragraphs: Harajuku is famous. Shimokitazawa is known. Koenji is where people who've lived in Tokyo for five years go when they want to be reminded what the city felt like before everything got expensive and curated. Both Koenji and Shimokitazawa deserve an afternoon each, and the fastest way to understand why is to walk from the station in either direction without a destination.

What they share is a history of being too awkward to redevelop. Both are dense grids of narrow streets around a small station, built up in the post-war decades with low rents that attracted students, musicians and people running one-room shops. Neither was flattened and rebuilt in the eighties, so the buildings are small, the rents stayed survivable longer than elsewhere, and the businesses in them are owner-operated rather than chains.
They are not preserved and they are not quaint. Both are ordinary places where people live, which is precisely the quality that makes them worth the trip after a week of Shibuya and Shinjuku.

sections.heading: Koenji: the vintage ecosystem
paragraphs: Koenji, on the Chuo Line, is Tokyo's vintage district — not vintage-as-aesthetic but vintage-as-ecosystem.
