The same line separates a genuinely worn floorboard from a factory-distressed one, and it is usually visible immediately. Real wear is uneven in ways that correspond to use: the threshold, the handle, the edge where hands go.

sections.heading: Impermanence is the load-bearing part
paragraphs: Underneath the aesthetics is a Buddhist observation that nothing lasts, including you. This is why the cherry blossom is the national flower rather than something more durable: it is admired specifically because it falls within a week.

Mono no aware, a related idea, names the particular sadness of being aware that a moment is passing while you are still inside it. Wabi-sabi is what that awareness looks like when applied to objects and rooms rather than to feelings.

Two neighbouring words fill out the vocabulary. Shibui describes restrained, understated good taste — the quality of something quiet that rewards long acquaintance. Iki is its urban cousin, a stylish, slightly sharp elegance that belongs to the merchant class of Edo rather than to the tea room. Neither is the same as wabi-sabi and both are frequently mistranslated as it.

sections.heading: Where to actually see it
paragraphs: It is easier to recognise than to define. A Raku tea bowl in a museum, hand-formed rather than thrown, thick-walled and irregular. A temple garden in Kyoto where the moss has been allowed to take the stones. An old wooden building where the timber has silvered and the floor has worn into a slight bowl at the threshold. A shop counter polished by sixty years of forearms.

If you want specific places: the subtemples of Daitoku-ji in Kyoto, several of which have small tea gardens and are far quieter than the famous sites; the dry garden at Ryoan-ji, early, before the coaches; and any municipal museum's ceramics room, where the labels will tell you which bowls were valued and why.

None of these were designed to be photogenic, which is a substantial part of why they are. And kintsugi — the repair of broken ceramics with gold — is the clearest single expression of the idea available, because it makes the argument literal.

sections.heading: Why it travels badly
paragraphs: Exported, wabi-sabi tends to become a shopping category: expensive rough ceramics, muted colours, linen, a particular kind of beige. That is a style, and styles are fine, but it inverts the original idea, which was about spending less attention on objects rather than more money on the right ones.

The book that carried the term into Western design in the 1990s did so by simplifying it, and the version that circulates now has passed through several more rounds of simplification since. This is not a scandal — ideas travel by being simplified — but it is worth knowing that the international version and the Japanese one are not the same object.
The useful version is not a palette. It is the habit of noticing that the chipped mug you have used every morning for nine years is more interesting than a new one, and declining to replace it.

sections.heading: What it offers now
paragraphs: The reason the idea keeps being rediscovered outside Japan is that it argues against two things modern life is heavily invested in: the pursuit of the flawless and the assumption that new is better.

Wabi-sabi proposes that wear is information, that incompleteness leaves room for attention, and that things reaching their end are not thereby diminished. Applied honestly it is closer to an argument for repairing and keeping than for buying anything at all.
You do not need to redecorate to take that on. It is mostly a change in what you are willing to find sufficient.

title: Kintsugi: The Art of Repairing Broken Things with Gold
excerpt: A 500-year-old technique for mending ceramics with lacquer and powdered gold has become a global metaphor for resilience. The craft itself is slower, stranger and far more demanding than the metaphor suggests.
heroImageAlt: A repaired ceramic kintsugi bowl with gold seams on an artisan worktable
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What it actually is
paragraphs: Kintsugi — golden joinery — repairs broken ceramics with urushi lacquer, then dusts the seams with powdered gold, silver or platinum. The result is a bowl whose fracture lines are the most conspicuous thing about it. The technique is usually dated to the fifteenth or sixteenth century, and the frequently repeated origin story involves a shogun sending a damaged tea bowl to China for repair and being dissatisfied with the metal staples that came back. Whether or not that particular account is reliable, the practice grew up alongside the tea ceremony and its taste for objects with history.

The essential move is that the repair is not disguised. Every other mending tradition tries to return an object to the state it was in before the accident, and judges itself by how invisible the work is. Kintsugi does the opposite: it draws the break in a precious metal so that the eye goes to it first. What you own afterwards is not a repaired bowl but a different bowl, and its value is generally higher than it was before it broke.

sections.heading: Lacquer is the real material
paragraphs: The gold gets the attention; the lacquer does the work. Urushi is sap from the lacquer tree, and it is both the adhesive and the structure of the repair. It cures through humidity rather than drying, so pieces spend days or weeks in a damp cabinet between stages, and each layer must harden before the next goes on.

Raw urushi is also a skin irritant closely related to poison ivy — the active compound, urushiol, is the same family — and reactions among apprentices are a normal part of learning the craft. This is one reason it has always been specialist work, and one reason most visitor workshops substitute something else.

Once cured, it is remarkable stuff: waterproof, acid-resistant, food-safe, and durable enough that lacquered objects survive from archaeological sites thousands of years old. The gold on a kintsugi seam is a few microns of decoration sitting on a structural repair that will outlast the person who made it.

sections.heading: The process, stage by stage
paragraphs: The pieces are first cleaned and dry-fitted, which is where the real skill sits: a bowl in eight fragments has an assembly order, and getting it wrong means the last piece will not go in. Then the edges are joined with mugi-urushi, a putty of raw lacquer and wheat flour, and the bowl is bound and left in the damp cabinet for one to two weeks.

Gaps, chips and missing areas are filled with sabi-urushi, lacquer mixed with a fine clay powder, built up in thin layers because a thick one will not cure through. Each layer is cured and then scraped and sanded flush. This filling and levelling stage is most of the labour and none of the glamour.

Only then does the decorative lacquer go on — a thin line of red or black urushi drawn along the seam with a fine brush. The gold powder is dusted onto that line while it is still tacky, using a cotton pad or a soft brush, and left to cure again before being burnished. A single bowl runs to a dozen or more separate operations spread over several weeks, and a complicated one takes months.

sections.heading: Three recognised styles
paragraphs: Practitioners distinguish between roughly three approaches. Crack kintsugi joins clean breaks with a thin gold seam. Piece-method kintsugi replaces a missing fragment with a solid area of lacquer and gold, so part of the wall of the bowl is metal-coloured rather than ceramic.

Joint-call kintsugi — yobitsugi — is the most striking: the gap is filled with a shard from a completely different vessel, so the finished bowl visibly contains two histories, often in clashing patterns and glazes. It makes the philosophy hardest to ignore, because the repair is not attempting to return the object to a previous state at all. It is making a third object out of the remains of two.
Which style a piece gets is a judgement about the break rather than a matter of taste. Clean breaks take a seam; missing material takes a fill; a hole too large to fill convincingly takes a shard.

sections.heading: Why the tea people wanted this
paragraphs: Kintsugi does not make sense outside the aesthetic that produced it. Sixteenth-century tea practice, under Sen no Rikyu and his successors, had turned decisively against the flawless imported Chinese wares that earlier collectors prized, in favour of rough domestic pots, uneven glazes and objects that showed the hand that made them and the time that had passed since.

In that setting a break is not a catastrophe to be hidden but the most interesting thing that has ever happened to the bowl — evidence of its life, and something no craftsman could have designed. A repaired tea bowl with a documented history of ownership and accident was, and is, worth more than the same bowl intact.

This is the same sensibility that produces wabi-sabi more generally: the preference for the weathered over the new, the incomplete over the finished, the particular over the perfect. Kintsugi is that idea applied with a brush and a few grams of gold.

sections.heading: Where to see it and where to try it
paragraphs: Kyoto is the centre for both. Museum collections hold repaired tea ware, and a number of workshops in the city and in Tokyo run short courses for visitors — typically half a day, usually using a synthetic substitute for urushi to avoid the curing time and the skin reaction.

That substitution is worth understanding before you book. A two-hour class produces something real and satisfying, but it is a demonstration of the aesthetic rather than the traditional technique, and the result is generally not food-safe. Ask which material a workshop uses if it matters to you; a genuine urushi course exists but requires returning across several sessions, which only works if you are staying a while.

If you want to see the real thing rather than make it, the Tokyo National Museum and the Kyoto National Museum both hold repaired tea ware, and temple treasure halls turn up examples regularly. Look for the seams before you look for the gold — on a good repair the line is thin, slightly irregular, and follows the break rather than correcting it.

sections.heading: Doing it at home
paragraphs: Kits are widely sold, both in Japan and online, and they fall into two categories that are frequently not distinguished on the box. Traditional kits contain real urushi and real gold or brass powder, take weeks, and require a humid box and a tolerance for possible skin reactions. Modern kits contain a two-part epoxy and a metallic powder, take an afternoon, and produce a convincing-looking result.

The epoxy version is a perfectly good craft project and there is no reason to be snobbish about it, with one hard limitation: it is not food-safe and it will not survive a dishwasher or boiling water. A bowl repaired this way is for display, dry goods, or the shelf. Repairing your favourite mug with an epoxy kit and then drinking tea out of it is the mistake to avoid.

If you want to bring a kit home as a souvenir, buy it in Japan rather than online — the traditional ones are cheaper here, and the instructions in the box are more likely to say honestly which material you have bought.

sections.heading: Buying repaired pieces
paragraphs: Antique shops and flea markets — the Toji temple market in Kyoto on the 21st of each month, Oedo in Tokyo — turn up kintsugi pieces regularly, at prices ranging from modest to serious.

Two things to check. Real gold seams are matte and slightly uneven under the light rather than uniformly bright, and genuine urushi repairs have a slight softness at the edge of the seam where the lacquer meets the glaze. A hard, glassy, perfectly even gold line usually means epoxy and brass.

Also ask whether a piece is food-safe; older repairs and some modern synthetic ones are not, and a bowl for display is a different purchase from a bowl for tea. And accept that price here tracks the pot rather than the repair — a fine repair on an ordinary bowl stays inexpensive, which is exactly where the good value is.

sections.heading: The metaphor, and its limits
paragraphs: Kintsugi has become globally popular as a metaphor for resilience: the break is part of the object, the repair is not concealed, the thing is more valuable for having been damaged. That reading is not a Western invention — it is close to what the tea masters were getting at.

It is worth adding the part that usually falls off in translation. Kintsugi is slow, expensive, requires a specialist, and cannot be done to every break. A bowl shattered into thirty fragments is not repaired, it is thrown away. The craftsman decides what is worth the weeks it will take, and a great deal is not.

The metaphor is more honest when it keeps the labour in. The bowl does not heal, and nothing about the process is automatic or free: somebody has to want the object enough to spend two months and a quantity of gold on it. That is a more demanding idea than the poster version, and a considerably more useful one.

title: Hanami 2026: Where to See Cherry Blossoms Like a Local
excerpt: Skip the crush at Maruyama Park and Ueno. The good hanami spots follow a pattern — canals, school grounds, old railway embankments — and once you know the pattern you can find them on any map before you leave the hotel.

factsExpire.what: Title names a year; refresh or retitle before the 2027 season

heroImageAlt: A peaceful riverside hanami picnic scene under cherry blossoms in Japan
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The forecast is a national institution
paragraphs: Cherry blossom timing is tracked and published every spring in considerable detail, with a front that moves roughly northwards from Kyushu in late March to Hokkaido in early May. Tokyo and Kyoto typically open in the last week of March and reach full bloom — mankai — around a week later.

The useful thing to understand is the shape rather than the dates: from first flowers to peak is about a week, peak lasts a few days, and a single day of rain or wind can end it. Check the forecast in the fortnight before you travel, and hold your plans loosely.

The vocabulary on the forecast maps is worth knowing. Kaika is the opening of the first flowers, mankai is full bloom, and the announcement of both is made from specific designated trees at specific shrines and parks — the same trees every year, watched by officials. It is a more formal exercise than the phrase 'blossom forecast' suggests.

sections.heading: Why the whole country blooms at once
paragraphs: Almost every cherry tree you will see is Somei Yoshino, a variety created in the nineteenth century and propagated entirely by grafting. That means the trees are not merely the same variety — they are clones, genetically identical, and they respond to temperature in lockstep.

This is why a whole city can go from bare to white in three days, and why the forecast works at all. It is also why the flowers arrive before the leaves: Somei Yoshino blooms on bare wood, which is what produces the effect of a cloud rather than a tree.

It has a melancholy footnote that Japanese writing about hanami returns to constantly. A monoculture of clones is fragile, the trees are not long-lived, and a great many of the ones lining Japanese rivers were planted in the same post-war decades and are ageing together.

sections.heading: Full bloom is not the best part
paragraphs: Two underrated windows sit either side of mankai. The days just before, when the trees are perhaps seventy per cent open, are quieter and the colour is stronger, because the flowers fade towards white as they age.

And the days just after, when the petals come down — hanafubuki, a blossom blizzard — are the ones people actually remember. Petals collecting on the surface of a canal, drifting against a kerb, blowing across a road: this is the part that appears in the poetry, and it happens after the crowds have decided the season is over.
If your dates are fixed and you miss the peak by a few days in either direction, you have not missed the thing. You have probably got a better version of it with fewer people.

sections.heading: Why the famous parks disappoint
paragraphs: Ueno and Maruyama are genuinely spectacular and genuinely unbearable. They operate less like parks than like festivals: tarpaulins claimed from early morning, food stalls, crowds moving at a shuffle, and in some cases a designated one-way route.

If that atmosphere is what you want, go, and go early — the ground-claiming starts before dawn and is often delegated to the most junior person in an office. It is a real and specific piece of Japanese social life and worth seeing once.
If what you pictured was standing under a tree, they will be a disappointment, and the alternative is not far away.

sections.heading: Look for water, schools and railways
paragraphs: The reliable rule is that cherry trees in Japan were planted along three kinds of edge: rivers and canals, school and public-building grounds, and old railway embankments. Any residential neighbourhood with a canal running through it will have a line of trees over the water and almost nobody looking at them.

In Tokyo, the smaller waterways in the east and the residential stretches of the Kanda and Meguro rivers away from their famous sections. In Kyoto, the canal paths north of the Philosopher's Path and the Kamo river banks well upstream of the centre. None of these need naming precisely — the pattern is the point, and you can find it on a map before you leave the hotel.

Temples and castle grounds are the third category, and they are the compromise: more crowded than a canal, far less crowded than Ueno, and the setting does a great deal of work. Many charge a small admission, which filters the crowd usefully.

sections.heading: Yozakura, the evening version
paragraphs: Many locations light the trees after dark, and blossom under artificial light against a black sky is a completely different object from blossom against a blue one. Castle grounds and temple gardens often run limited evening openings during the bloom, usually ticketed and usually only for a week or two.

It is also the version with the fewest daytime crowds, and the one where a phone camera struggles and a real camera earns its place. Bring a layer; late March evenings are colder than the afternoon suggests, and standing still under a tree is colder than walking.

sections.heading: How to actually do hanami
paragraphs: The practice is simple and social: a sheet on the ground, food from a convenience store or a department store basement, something to drink, and several hours of sitting under a tree talking. Shoes come off at the edge of the sheet.

The supplies are sold everywhere in season — the blue tarpaulin, the disposable cups, the bento boxes assembled specifically for this. Department store food halls put out hanami bento in the last week of March and they are considerably better than the park stalls.

Take everything away with you, including the bag. Bins are scarce and the expectation is total. Some parks prohibit alcohol and some prohibit sheets entirely, and the signs will say so. Do not shake branches for falling petals and do not climb or pull anything; this is the one behaviour that reliably annoys people. Beyond that there is no ceremony to get right — sitting down is the whole activity.

sections.heading: If you miss it entirely
paragraphs: The season is short and a lot of trips miss it. There are three fallbacks and all of them are good.

Go up, or go north. Higher elevations and the Tohoku region run one to three weeks behind Tokyo, and Hokkaido blooms in early May. Hirosaki castle in Aomori at the end of April is, by common agreement, one of the best hanami sites in the country and it happens after Kyoto has finished.

Or change tree. Shidarezakura, the weeping variety, flowers slightly earlier and is the more dramatic thing to stand under. Yaezakura, the dense double-flowered kind, blooms one to two weeks after Somei Yoshino in heavy pink pom-poms, and there are avenues of it in most cities. And plum blossom, in February, is the older tradition — hanami originally meant plum — with a scent that cherry has none of.

title: The Best Japanese Kitchen Knives to Bring Home
excerpt: Japanese knives are the single best souvenir you can carry out of Japan — functional, beautiful, and something you'll use every day for decades. This guide covers every price point from a ¥4,000 entry knife to the hand-forged blade worth saving up for.
heroImageAlt: Japanese kitchen knives displayed on a dark wooden shop counter
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the knives are different
paragraphs: The short version is geometry and steel. A typical Western chef's knife is ground with a symmetrical edge at a relatively wide angle and made from softer stainless steel that bends before it chips. A traditional Japanese knife is often ground on one side only, at a much narrower angle, from harder steel that holds an edge far longer and is correspondingly more brittle. The result cuts better and tolerates less abuse. That trade is the whole decision, and it is worth understanding before you spend anything.

The hardness is measurable and the difference is not marginal: Japanese blades commonly sit several points higher on the Rockwell scale than European ones. Harder steel takes a finer edge and keeps it for longer, and it will chip if you twist it, drop it, or use it on a bone.

sections.heading: The three shapes worth considering
paragraphs: Ignore the long catalogue and start with three. The santoku is the general-purpose home knife — shortish, flat-bellied, good at almost everything, and the safest single purchase. The gyuto is the Japanese take on a Western chef's knife, longer with more curve, better if you already cook with a chef's knife and want the same motion. The nakiri is a rectangular vegetable knife that looks alarming and is superb at exactly one job.

If you buy one knife, buy a santoku or a gyuto. If you buy two, add the nakiri. If you buy three, add a petty — a small utility knife of twelve or fifteen centimetres that handles everything the big blade is clumsy at, and which most people end up reaching for more than they expected.

The single-bevel traditional shapes — the yanagiba for slicing sashimi, the deba for breaking down fish — are specialist tools. They are beautiful, they are what the knife shops display, and buying one as a first Japanese knife is a mistake unless you specifically intend to use it for that job.

sections.heading: Steel, and the honest trade-off
paragraphs: Carbon steel — shirogami and aogami, white and blue paper steel — takes the sharpest edge and is what most traditional makers prefer. It also rusts if you leave it wet for ten minutes and will discolour within weeks into a grey-blue patina. Stainless resists all of that and gives up a little sharpness and a little edge retention.

Clad or san-mai construction splits the difference: a hard carbon core for the edge with softer stainless sides for protection. For most people buying a knife on holiday, clad stainless is the right answer, and admitting that is not a compromise.

Ignore the decoration when comparing. The rippled damascus layers and the hammered kurouchi finish are cosmetic — they look superb and they tell you nothing about the steel at the edge, which is the only part that cuts.

sections.heading: Handles, which nobody mentions
paragraphs: There are two families. A wa handle is the traditional Japanese one: light, usually octagonal or D-shaped, made of wood, and pushed onto a tang rather than riveted through. A yo handle is the Western style, heavier, riveted, with the blade running through it.

The difference is balance. A wa-handled knife puts the weight forward in the blade and feels quick; a yo-handled one feels planted and familiar. Neither is better and the preference is immediate once you hold both.

One practical note: a wa handle can be replaced when it wears out, cheaply, which is part of why traditional knives are built that way. It is also more vulnerable to being left in water, which will swell and split it.

sections.heading: What each price bracket actually buys
paragraphs: Around ¥4,000–8,000 gets a competent machine-made stainless santoku from an established brand, which will outperform most knives in a Western home kitchen. Around ¥10,000–20,000 is the broad sweet spot: better steel, better fit and finish, often a clad blade and a proper wooden handle.

Above roughly ¥30,000 you are paying for hand-forging, a named smith and frequently single-bevel geometry, which rewards skill and punishes its absence. It is a genuinely different object and it is not a better first knife.

Prices move, so treat these as brackets rather than quotes. The general shape of the market holds: the jump in quality from ¥5,000 to ¥15,000 is enormous, and the jump from ¥15,000 to ¥50,000 is real but far smaller.

sections.heading: Where to buy
paragraphs: Kappabashi in Tokyo is the restaurant-supply district and the obvious destination — several streets of knife shops, many with English-speaking staff, ranging from workaday to serious. Give it a morning; the shops differ substantially and the walk between them is short. It is also where you buy the plastic food models, which is a separate pleasure.

Sakai in Osaka and Seki in Gifu are the traditional forging towns and worth a detour if the knives are the reason for the trip. Tsukiji's outer market has several knife shops that have been sharpening for the fish trade for generations. Department store kitchenware floors carry good mid-range stock with reliable service.
Avoid airport gift shops and souvenir stalls near tourist sites, where the markup is high and the provenance vague. A knife with no maker named and no answer about the steel is a knife-shaped object.

sections.heading: Buying well in the shop
paragraphs: Hold it. The single most useful test is whether the handle sits comfortably in your grip, and it is the one thing no online description conveys. Ask whether the blade is single or double bevel, and if single, whether it is ground for a right- or left-handed user — a left-handed cook with a right-ground single bevel will have a bad time, and left-ground blades usually have to be ordered.

Ask what steel it is. A good shop will answer all three immediately, will offer to sharpen it before you leave, and will often engrave a name into the blade in Japanese characters at no charge. The engraving takes a few minutes, makes it unmistakably a gift, and is the reason to buy in person rather than online.
A shop that cannot answer the three questions is telling you something. So is a shop that pushes the most expensive blade at someone who has just said they cook twice a week.

sections.heading: Getting it home legally
paragraphs: Never in hand luggage. It will be confiscated at security, and this happens constantly. Pack it in checked baggage, in the box, ideally with the blade guard the shop provides and the whole thing wrapped and taped. Keep the receipt accessible.

Most countries permit kitchen knives in checked luggage without issue, but a small number regulate blade length or type on arrival, and the UK in particular has rules worth reading before you buy something expensive. Check your own country's position first.
If you are shipping instead, most reputable shops will arrange it, and for anything above about ¥30,000 that is worth doing for the insurance alone.

sections.heading: Keeping it once you have it
paragraphs: Hand wash, dry immediately, and never put it in a dishwasher — the detergent and the heat will ruin both the edge and a wooden handle. Cut on wood or plastic, never glass, stone or a ceramic plate. Do not use it to cut through bone or frozen food; the thin hard edge will chip.

Learn to use a whetstone. It is less difficult than it sounds, and it is the only way to maintain the edge properly — pull-through sharpeners are designed for wider Western angles and will grind the Japanese geometry away within a few uses. A combination stone of roughly 1000 and 3000 grit covers everything a home cook needs, costs little in Japan, and packs flat.

If you bought carbon steel, expect it to change colour and let it. The patina that forms in the first few weeks is protective, and scrubbing it off returns the blade to bare reactive steel every time.

title: Buying Matcha: Ceremonial vs. Culinary Grade Explained
excerpt: The matcha market is flooded with products that taste nothing like what you drink in a tea ceremony — and the price tag is not a reliable guide. Here's how to read labels, what to taste for, and where to buy the real thing.
heroImageAlt: Matcha powder in ceramic bowls with a bamboo whisk and tea scoop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What matcha actually is
paragraphs: Matcha is powdered green tea from leaves that were shaded for several weeks before harvest. The shading starves the plant of light, which raises the amino acid content — particularly theanine — and lowers bitterness, producing the sweetness and savoury depth that distinguishes good matcha. The leaves are then steamed, dried, destemmed and deveined into a form called tencha, and stone-ground into powder. That grinding is slow, and it is a large part of why the good stuff costs what it does.

Slow is not a figure of speech. A granite mill turns at a low speed and produces something in the region of forty grams of matcha an hour, because faster grinding generates heat and heat destroys the aroma. A single tin represents most of a day on one stone.

This also explains why matcha behaves unlike other tea. You are not brewing leaves and discarding them; you are drinking the whole leaf in suspension. That is why the caffeine hits differently, why the quality of the leaf is so exposed, and why it goes stale so fast.

sections.heading: Ceremonial and culinary are marketing terms
paragraphs: Neither phrase is a regulated grade. There is no certifying body and no legal definition, and a tin labelled ceremonial can be almost anything. What the words usually gesture at is real, though: 'ceremonial' generally means an earlier harvest intended to be whisked with water and drunk alone, and 'culinary' generally means a later harvest with more bitterness, meant to survive being mixed with milk and sugar.

Note that these are largely export-market terms. Japanese producers grade their own output with a house hierarchy and give blends poetic names rather than sorting them into two bins, and a tin bought in a Kyoto tea shop will frequently carry no grade word at all. That absence is not a bad sign.

Treat the label as a hint about intended use rather than a statement of quality, and buy for what you will actually do with it. Whisking an expensive tin into a latte with syrup wastes the thing you paid for; drinking a culinary grade straight will convince you that you dislike matcha.

sections.heading: What to look for instead
paragraphs: Four things carry more information than the grade name. Colour: vivid, almost fluorescent green means shaded leaf and careful handling; dull, yellowish or olive powder means age, oxidation or lower-grade leaf. Origin: Uji in Kyoto, Nishio in Aichi, and Yame in Fukuoka are the established regions and reputable producers say so on the tin. Harvest or milling date, because matcha degrades quickly once ground. And packaging: opaque, airtight and small. A large clear jar is a bad sign regardless of price.

Texture is the fifth, if you get the chance. Good matcha is talc-fine and clings to the side of a scoop; coarser powder feels gritty between the fingers and will not suspend properly no matter how hard you whisk.
Smell it if the shop allows. Fresh, high-grade matcha has a sweet, marine, almost nori-like aroma. Anything smelling flat, hay-like or faintly of dust has been on a shelf too long.

sections.heading: Price is a weak signal on its own
paragraphs: Cost tells you something but not enough. Very cheap matcha — the sort sold in large pouches at a suspiciously low price per gram — is almost always late-harvest and will taste flatly bitter no matter how you prepare it. But expensive matcha in an ornate presentation box is frequently priced for gift-giving rather than for what is inside.

The most reliable purchases sit in the middle: a modest 20 to 40 gram tin from a named producer, bought somewhere with turnover. As a rough anchor, a good drinking matcha runs somewhere around ¥1,500–3,000 for 20–40g, and the tins climbing past ¥5,000 are competition-grade blends whose distinctions are genuinely subtle.
Buying the smallest tin of the better grade beats buying the largest tin of the cheaper one, every time. You will not finish 200 grams before it fades.

sections.heading: Usucha and koicha
paragraphs: There are two preparations and shops assume you know which you want. Usucha, thin tea, is the everyday version: about two grams whisked with sixty or seventy millilitres of water into a foam. Koicha, thick tea, uses roughly double the powder in half the water and is whisked into something closer to warm paint — it is the centrepiece of a formal tea gathering and it is intense.

Koicha requires the top grades, because at that concentration any bitterness is unbearable. If a shop asks whether you want a koicha-grade tea and you are making lattes at home, say no; you are being offered the expensive thing.
A tin sold for usucha will make perfectly good koicha-adjacent tea if you want to experiment, but the reverse is the expensive mistake.

sections.heading: The equipment, and whether you need it
paragraphs: You need a bowl, a bamboo whisk and ideally a small sieve. The whisk — chasen — is the one item with no real substitute: it is carved from a single piece of bamboo into eighty or a hundred tines, and a milk frother produces a different, coarser foam. They are consumable, lasting perhaps a few months of daily use, and cost very little in Japan compared with abroad.

The bowl matters less than people think and is where the money goes if you let it. Any wide bowl works. A chashaku, the bamboo scoop, is charming and a teaspoon does the same job. The sieve is the item everyone skips and the one that most improves the result.

Starter sets containing bowl, whisk, scoop and a small tin are sold everywhere and make an excellent gift — the whole thing is light, packs flat with the bowl wrapped, and is a considerably better present than the tin alone. Buy a spare whisk while you are there.

sections.heading: Making it well enough to tell the difference
paragraphs: Sift about two grams to break the clumps, which is the step everyone skips and the one that causes most bad results. Add roughly 60 to 70 millilitres of water at around 80°C — not boiling, which scalds the powder and makes it harsh. Whisk briskly in a W motion, from the wrist rather than the arm, until a fine even foam forms across the surface.

Good matcha at this point is sweet and thick with a savoury finish. If it is simply bitter, the problem is usually the water temperature or the tea, in that order. If it is gritty at the bottom, you did not sift.
Drink it straight away. Matcha separates within a couple of minutes and the foam is part of the texture, which is why it is served immediately and drunk in three or four mouthfuls rather than sipped.

sections.heading: Where to buy
paragraphs: Established tea houses are the best option and many will let you taste before buying, which settles the question faster than any label. In Kyoto, the old houses around Uji are the obvious destination and worth the short train ride — several have tasting rooms and cafés attached, and Uji makes a good half-day out of the city.

Department store basement food halls carry good producers with reliable stock rotation. Specialist tea shops in any major city are generally trustworthy. Souvenir shops at stations and airports are where old stock goes to be sold in decorative boxes, and the difference in the cup is immediately obvious.

If matcha turns out not to be your thing, the same shops sell gyokuro, the shaded leaf tea matcha's leaf would otherwise have become, and hojicha, roasted and nearly caffeine-free. Both travel better and neither requires equipment.

sections.heading: Getting it home and keeping it
paragraphs: Matcha's enemies are air, light, heat and moisture, and it declines noticeably within a few weeks of opening. Buy small quantities rather than one large tin, keep it sealed, and store it in the refrigerator once opened — letting the tin come back to room temperature before opening, so condensation does not form inside.
Unopened tins travel fine in either checked or hand luggage and weigh almost nothing. If you are bringing back gifts, buy them last and keep them out of a hot car.

One thing to know before you buy for someone else: an unopened tin keeps for a year or so, but the clock on the good stuff started at milling, not at purchase. If there is a date on the tin, the gift is better given sooner.

title: 10 Japanese Drugstore Products Worth Every Yen
excerpt: Japanese pharmacies are overwhelming in the best way — walls of skincare, hair treatments, and stomach remedies at prices that make no sense until you try them. These are the ten products that actually earn their place in your luggage.

factsExpire.what: Tax-free becomes refund-at-departure; the sealed bag and the consumable split end

heroImageAlt: Japanese drugstore skincare and travel products arranged neatly on bright shelves
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the drugstores are like this
paragraphs: Japanese pharmacy chains — Matsumoto Kiyoshi, Sundrug, Welcia, Tsuruha and the rest — occupy a strange middle ground between a chemist and a small department store, and the skincare aisle in particular operates at a standard that is elsewhere reserved for premium brands. The reason is competitive: domestic consumers are unusually informed about ingredients and formulation, and the mass-market brands compete on substance rather than packaging. The practical consequence for a visitor is that the ¥800 product is frequently very good.

The ten below are categories with a representative product named, rather than a ranking. Formulations get revised and packaging gets redesigned constantly in this market, so treat the names as a starting point to show a member of staff rather than a shopping list to match exactly.

sections.heading: 1. Sunscreen
paragraphs: If you buy one thing, buy sunscreen. Japanese formulations are widely regarded as the best mass-market sun protection available, largely because the regulatory environment permits UV filters that are elegant, stable and pleasant to wear — which is what actually determines whether people reapply. Expect fluid, weightless textures that sit under makeup without pilling.

Look for PA++++ alongside the SPF number; the PA rating indicates UVA protection and is the half of the equation most foreign labels omit. The Biore UV range is the cheap and excellent option at a few hundred yen, and Shiseido's Anessa sits above it for a couple of thousand. Both cost a fraction of what comparable products cost abroad.

sections.heading: 2. Sheet masks in bulk
paragraphs: Sheet masks are sold in packs of thirty or more at a price that makes the boutique single-mask model look absurd. The large-volume packs from the mainstream brands — Lululun is the one stacked by the doorway of every branch — are what locals buy in quantity: unfragranced, simple humectant formulas, meant to be used daily rather than as a treat.
A box of thirty runs around ¥1,500 and weighs very little. It is the highest value-per-suitcase-kilo item in the shop and the easiest thing to hand out to several people at home.

sections.heading: 3. Hydrating lotions
paragraphs: The Japanese 'lotion' is not a moisturiser in the Western sense — it is a watery hydrating layer applied before one, and it is the step that makes the routine work. Hada Labo's Gokujyun hyaluronic lotion is the famous one, viscous and unscented, and Naturie's Hatomugi lotion comes in a half-litre bottle designed to be used generously on face and body.
Neither is glamorous, both cost under a thousand yen, and they are the reason people's luggage comes back heavier than it left.

sections.heading: 4. Cleansing oils and balms
paragraphs: Double cleansing — an oil to remove sunscreen and makeup, then a foaming wash — is standard practice in Japan, and the cleansing oil category reflects decades of refinement. The mass-market oils emulsify cleanly, rinse without residue, and cost very little for a large pump bottle. Shu Uemura's is the department-store benchmark; the Biore and Kose Softymo bottles in the drugstore do the same job for a tenth of the price.
If you have only used a wipe or a micellar water, this is the single change most likely to be noticeable. Buy the large size; it is heavy but the price per use is the point.

sections.heading: 5. Foaming face wash
paragraphs: The second half of the double cleanse, and the category where the whipped-foam texture Japan is known for actually originates. Shiseido's Senka Perfect Whip is the one every list mentions, costs a few hundred yen, and produces a dense foam from a very small amount.
Buy a foaming net while you are in the aisle. It costs a hundred yen, it is what the instructions on the tube assume you own, and it roughly doubles how far the tube goes.

sections.heading: 6. Steam eye masks
paragraphs: Self-heating eye masks that warm gently for around ten minutes are a genuinely Japanese invention and difficult to find abroad at a sensible price. Kao's Megurhythm boxes come in several scents, cost around ¥1,000 for five, and are the most reliably appreciated small gift on this list.
They are also the correct thing to have in your bag on a long-haul flight home, which is a good argument for buying two boxes.

sections.heading: 7. Heat patches and pain relief
paragraphs: Adhesive heat pads for shoulders and lower back, and the medicated compresses sold under names like Salonpas, are a staple of Japanese pharmacy shelves and genuinely effective. After a week of walking fifteen kilometres a day they stop being a curiosity and start being a purchase.
In the same aisle: disposable body warmers, sold in packs, which stick inside clothing and stay warm for hours. In winter they are the single cheapest comfort upgrade available in Japan.

sections.heading: 8. Foot care
paragraphs: There is an entire wall of it, aimed at people who walk a great deal, which after a week in Japan will include you. Cooling gel sheets that you stick to the soles overnight, blister plasters that are better than anything sold at home, and gel cushions for specific parts of the foot.

The peeling foot masks — plastic booties containing an exfoliating solution, worn for an hour — are the famous novelty. They work, the results are alarming about a week later, and they are not something to do the night before more walking.

sections.heading: 9. Stomach remedies
paragraphs: Japan has a long tradition of digestive medicine aimed specifically at having eaten too much, which is a useful thing to have on a food-focused trip. Ohta's Isan is the classic — a mildly minty powder in sachets, sold for over a century — and Kampo-based preparations sit alongside the modern tablets.

These are actual medicines rather than supplements. Read the packaging, and ask the pharmacist if anything is unclear; larger branches have one on duty and some products sit behind the counter and require a brief conversation.

sections.heading: 10. Eye drops
paragraphs: The eye drop selection is bewildering by international standards — an entire bay, sorted by symptom, cooling intensity and whether you wear contact lenses. The strongly cooling ones are a specific Japanese taste and are startling the first time.

Worth knowing: some formulations contain vasoconstrictors that are restricted or unavailable in other countries. They are legal to buy and use here; check your own country's rules before bringing a large quantity home.

sections.heading: Tax-free, and how to actually get it
paragraphs: Most large drugstores offer tax-free purchasing to visitors above ¥5,000 in a day at the same store. Bring your physical passport; a photograph is not accepted. Until 31 October 2026 consumables and general goods are counted as separate categories, which occasionally means a basket that looks like it qualifies does not, and consumables leave the shop in a sealed bag. From 1 November 2026 both of those rules end: you pay the full price in store and claim the consumption tax back at the airport, where Customs has to see the goods, so keep them where you can reach them.

Consumable items are sealed in a transparent bag that you are not supposed to open before leaving the country. If you want to use the sunscreen during the trip, buy that bottle separately and pay the tax on it.
The saving is meaningful on a large basket, and the queue at the tax-free counter is usually shortest in the early afternoon.

sections.heading: A note on how to choose
paragraphs: The aisle is overwhelming because almost everything in it is competent, which is a better problem than the alternative. Two shortcuts: the products with the plainest packaging and the largest volume are generally what locals restock rather than what is marketed to visitors, and staff will point you at the right shelf if you show them the back of your hand or say the category name.

Buying three products you will actually finish beats buying twelve that look interesting in a photograph. And if you take prescription medication, check Japan's import rules before you travel — several compounds that are unremarkable elsewhere are restricted here, and that is a border problem rather than a pharmacy one.

title: Where to Buy Authentic Yukata in Tokyo Without the Markup
excerpt: The tourist-district yukata sold near Asakusa are fine, but the ones sold at department store basements and specialist shops are extraordinary — and often cheaper. This guide takes you past the obvious options to the places worth visiting.
heroImageAlt: Folded cotton yukata fabrics and obi sashes displayed in a Tokyo shop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Yukata is not kimono
paragraphs: A yukata is unlined cotton, worn in summer, at festivals, at fireworks displays and around hot-spring towns, and it is the informal end of Japanese dress. A kimono is lined, usually silk, formal, structurally more complex and considerably more expensive. Conflating the two is the most common mistake visitors make, and it matters commercially: a shop quoting a very low price for a 'kimono' is almost certainly selling a yukata, and a shop quoting a very high price for a yukata is relying on you not knowing the difference.

The word itself is a contraction of yukatabira, a bathing robe, which is exactly what it was — something worn after the bath and, later, out to the summer evening. That history explains its rules: no lining, no under-kimono, bare feet in geta, and no occasion formal enough to require anything more.

sections.heading: What you actually need to buy
paragraphs: A wearable yukata is at minimum three items: the yukata itself, an obi sash, and something to hold the whole thing closed underneath — a koshihimo tie, and ideally a datejime belt. Many shops sell these as a set, which is the sensible way to buy your first one. A yukata bought alone, with no obi, is a garment you will not be able to wear.

Men and women wear different sashes and this is the detail most often got wrong. Men wear a kaku-obi, a narrow stiff belt tied low on the hips in a simple knot. Women wear a hanhaba-obi, considerably wider and tied at the back in a bow that takes practice — which is why pre-tied obi that clip on exist and why nobody will judge you for using one.

Add geta and a kinchaku drawstring bag for the complete look, though neither is essential. Geta are worn barefoot and will give you blisters between the toes on the first outing; the standard local solution is to accept this, and the sensible visitor solution is to walk less far than you planned.

sections.heading: The Asakusa question
paragraphs: The shops clustered around Asakusa and Nakamise are convenient and not a scam. What they are is optimised for a specific transaction: a tourist buying one yukata, quickly, in a place with high rent. The quality is generally acceptable, the printing is often digital rather than dyed, the sizes skew towards the middle, and the price reflects the location.

If you want a yukata this afternoon and are not going to think about it again, this is a perfectly reasonable place to buy one. If you have another day, you can do considerably better for the same money.

The rental shops in the same district are a separate proposition and a good one. For a few thousand yen they dress you properly, tie the obi correctly, do your hair if you want, and take it all back at the end of the day. If what you want is to spend an afternoon in Asakusa wearing one rather than to own one, rent.

sections.heading: Department store basements and upper floors
paragraphs: The major department stores — the ones with a kimono floor rather than a kimono corner — carry proper stock, with a summer yukata section from late spring onwards. The advantages are real: consistent sizing including longer lengths, staff who will fit you properly and show you how to tie the obi, dyed rather than printed fabric at the middle price points, and the ability to buy the components separately.

Prices start higher than Asakusa and the value is better. As a rough map: a printed polyester set runs a few thousand yen, a decent cotton yukata with a good obi sits somewhere around ¥10,000–20,000 as a set, and hand-dyed cotton from a named maker climbs from there.

Ask for the yukata section by name and be prepared to spend half an hour. The fitting is the service you are paying for and it is worth taking; being shown how the collar should sit, once, by someone who does it daily, is more useful than any video.

sections.heading: Fabric, and the polyester question
paragraphs: Traditional yukata is cotton, and the better ones use weaves designed for heat — ro and sha are open, gauzy constructions that move air, and chijimi is a crinkled cotton that holds itself off the skin. In a Japanese August this is not a refinement, it is the difference between comfortable and unbearable.

Polyester is common at the cheap end and it has one genuine advantage: it is machine washable and does not wrinkle, which matters if this is going to be a costume worn twice rather than a garment. It is also noticeably hotter. Choose deliberately rather than by price.

Dyed fabric and printed fabric look different at arm's length once you know: on a dyed yukata the pattern appears on both sides of the cloth, while a print sits on the face only and the reverse is pale. Turn a sleeve over in the shop. It is the single fastest quality check available.

sections.heading: The specialist and secondhand end
paragraphs: Specialist kimono shops, found in the older commercial districts rather than the tourist ones, sell to people who wear these clothes regularly and will happily explain the difference between a printed and a hand-dyed pattern. They can be intimidating to walk into and are almost always welcoming once you do.

Secondhand is where the genuinely interesting fabric is, frequently at a fraction of new prices — the recycled-kimono chains and the antique markets, Oedo in Tokyo and Toji in Kyoto, turn up vintage cotton with patterns nobody prints any more. Check the collar and cuffs for staining, check the underarms, and accept that sizing is whatever it is.

One seasonal warning: yukata is summer stock. Shops carry it from roughly April to August and clear it afterwards, so a visitor in November will find the selection thin everywhere except the secondhand shops, which have it year-round.

sections.heading: Fit, which is mostly about length
paragraphs: Yukata are not tailored to the body in the Western sense; the excess length is folded and held at the waist. What matters is that the garment is long enough — roughly your own height is the standard guide — and that the sleeves fall where you want them.

Visitors taller than about 175 centimetres should specify a long size explicitly, since standard stock often will not work and a too-short yukata is immediately obvious. The tell is the hem: it should fall to the ankle. Shoulder width matters second, and everything else is adjusted by the tying.

Men's yukata are worn at close to their full length with the fold taken up in the tying; women's are folded at the waist into the ohashori, the visible tuck below the obi. If you are buying a woman's yukata that is slightly too long, that is fine and expected. Too short cannot be fixed.

sections.heading: Wearing it without getting the important part wrong
paragraphs: Left side over right. Always. The reverse is how the dead are dressed, and it is the one error that Japanese people will notice instantly and find genuinely uncomfortable. The way to remember it: your right hand should be able to slip into the fold against your chest.

Beyond that: the obi sits at the natural waist for men and slightly higher for women, the collar should sit a little away from the back of the neck rather than tight against it, and small steps are simply how the garment moves. Wearing a yukata as a visitor is welcomed rather than resented, provided the left-over-right rule is observed.

Where to wear one: summer festivals and fireworks displays, which is what they are for and where you will be in good company; and hot-spring towns, where walking between baths in the yukata your ryokan provided is the entire local dress code. Wearing one to a restaurant in Ginza in December is a costume, and will read as one.

sections.heading: Washing and keeping it
paragraphs: Cotton yukata can be hand washed in cool water and should be dried flat or on a wide hanger, never wrung. Polyester goes in the machine on a gentle cycle in a mesh bag. Neither should go anywhere near a tumble dryer.

Store it folded rather than hung — there is a standard fold along the existing seams that keeps the lines crisp, and any shop will demonstrate it in thirty seconds if you ask. Hanging a yukata for a year distorts the shoulders.
Keep the obi rolled rather than folded, and if you have bought geta, expect the thongs to loosen with use; they can be re-tightened, and the shop that sold them will usually do it.
